The announcement credits Gapstur with bringing "clear strategic direction" that focused on quality, safety, patient experience and employee engagement. That approach brough national recognitions and designations to its facilities, plus new developments like a genomic program bringing precision medicine into patient care.

> Centene Corporation has created two new positions to lead key segments of its insurance business.

The company said in an announcement that it has named Daniel Finke as group president for markets and commercial and Michael Carson as its group president for Medicare and specialty. Both executives will report to CEO Sarah London, per Centene.

Finke is an experienced insurance executive and will be tasked with overseeing and scaling the company's Medicaid and commercial segments. He joins the insurer from Convey Health Solutions, where he was CEO, and has also previously served as president of Aetna at CVS Health.

Carson, meanwhile, will take on an expanded role in overseeing Centene's Medicare Advantage, Part D, dual-eligible and specialty populations. He joined the company as CEO of WellCare in 2024, and previously held leadership roles at Bright Healthcare and Harvard Pilgrim Health Care.

London said in the announcement that the shift recognizes Carson's significant contributions to the company and the experience that Finke brings to the table in driving operations forward.

"Their collective experience will be instrumental as we continue to strengthen performance across the portfolio and deliver sustainable, profitable growth," she said.

> Cory Mead was named CEO of HCA Florida Palms West Hospital, effective March 30. With more than a decade in leadership roles with HCA Healthcare, Mead most recently served as CEO of HCA Florida Woodmont Hospital.

> Elevance Health unveiled a slew of new leadership appointments within its Health Benefits business and Carelon, the unit leading services such as pharmacy benefits, behavioral health and value-based care enablement.

Kristy Duffey was named president of Carelon Health. The nurse practitioner-turned-executive recently helped scale care models and boost performance at Optum and CINQCARE. She'll be taking over for Peter Haytaian, who's slated to leave the role on May 4 to focus on family commitments but will remain through the end of the year as a special advisor to ease the transition, the company previously announced.

Aimée Dailey was appointed president of government business. She's already attributed with playing "a pivotal role" in expanding Elevance's government programs, and will now have responsibilities covering Medicare, Medicaid, Federal Government Solutions and Group Retiree Solutions.

Additionally, Will Feest, currently chief operating officer for Carelon, will be adding president of Carelon Insights to his title card; Darrell Oliveira was named chief financial officer for Carelon; and Jeff Plante, previously president of Carelon Insights, was dubbed chief financial officer for the Health Benefits segment.

Elevance said the new leaders will help expand and scale Carelon, which reaches over 90 million healthcare consumers. The Health Benefits segment provides coordinated solutions to more than 45 million Elevance members.

> Kurt Small was named president and CEO of CareFirst BlueCross BlueShield, effective May 4.

Small is currently president of Medicaid at Elevance Health, where he has been for nearly seven years. He has over 25 years of healthcare leadership experience, including roles at Blue Cross and Blue Shield of Minnesota, Highmark and Aetna.

At Elevance, he oversaw a Medicaid business with about 8.5 million members. CareFirst, meanwhile, is a nonprofit with 3.5 million members primarily living in the District of Columbia, Maryland and Northern Virginia. It has been without a permanent top executive since last September, with Ja'Ron Bridges serving as interim president and CEO.

> Barclay Berdan, CEO of Texas Health Resources, will retire in September after four decades at the 29-hospital nonprofit.

The executive stepped into his role in 2014, and was credited by the organization in its announcement release for guiding the system "through some of the most complex public health challenges in modern U.S. history while leading significant transformation across the organization’s clinical, digital and operational capabilities."

On deck is Winjie Miao, who is currently senior executive vice president and chief operating officer. She's set for a promotion to president on April 5, priming her to step in as CEO in September when Berdan steps away. Miao has been Texas Health Resources' chief operating officer since 2022, but first joined the organization in 2000.

> Elisabeth Armstrong is the new chief of staff at the National Institutes of Health Office of the Director, filling in the void left with Seana Cranston's resignation earlier in March.

Armstrong, who has a doctorate in bioethics, comes from the Food and Drug Administration, where she served as director of the Office of the Executive Secretariat. Prior to joining government, she conducted healthcare policy equity research for Raymond James & Associates’ Global Equities and Investment, advised and held various ethics positions at biotech and healthcare organizations and was a broadcast journalist, among other roles.

> Cigna Healthcare, the insurance arm of the Cigna Group, announced that it named Stanley Crittenden, M.D., as its new chief medical officer.

In the role, Crittenden will the lead the insurer's clinical operations, and will be tasked with partnering with other key leaders across the company to support the central goals of improving access and simplifying the healthcare journey for both patients and providers.

Crittenden brings years of experience in managed care, value-based care and population health to the role, Cigna said in an announcement. He most recently served as CMO at Quantum Health, and also held leadership roles at Evergreen Nephrology, Anthem and Humana.

Crittenden is also board certified in internal medicine and nephrology, Cigna said.

“I’m honored to join Cigna Healthcare at this important moment in its transformation toward making health care simpler, more personalized and more affordable,” said Crittenden in the announcement. “I am committed to fostering a collaborative and supportive environment, doing everything we can to improve the experience and outcomes of all those we serve.”

> John Haupert, president and CEO of Atlanta-based Grady Health System, will be handing the reins over to current Chief Operating Officer Anthony Saul at the end of this year.

Saul is immediately claiming the president title, and will shuffle into the top spot on Jan. 1, 2027. Haupert will stick around through 2027 in an advisory role to soften the transition, support philanthropic and capital fundraising and provide strategic guidance on a new $1+ billion medical campus the nonprofit also announced this week.

Haupert has headed Grady for the past 15 years. Saul has been around for seven, initially joining as chief financial officer.

> AI-powered prior authorization company Humata Health is bringing Liz Fowler, former director of the Center for Medicare and Medicaid Innovation (CMMI), onto its board of directors.

The company said in an announcement that Fowler's experience at CMMI will support the team's efforts to accelerate Humata's mission to ensure patients get the care they need quickly. At CMMI, Fowler was tasked with rethinking reimbursement in Medicare and Medicaid to drive uptake of value-based care, providing critical insights she can bring to Humata.

Before her stint at CMMI, Fowler held leadership roles at the Commonwealth Fund and Johnson & Johnson. She currently serves as a distinguished scholar at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health and the Carey Business School.

“Liz is a unicorn, a rare leader with deep experience in all realms of the healthcare ecosystem,” said Jeremy Friese, M.D., Humata’s co-founder and CEO, in the announcement. “She understands the inherent complexities of the health system, and her expertise will be instrumental as we work toward our mission of solving these challenges."

From her role driving innovation at CMMI to her track record of bipartisan work on federal health legislation, Liz’s experience will be an invaluable asset as we make AI-driven medical review a seamless process that ensures every patient receives the right care as quickly as possible," Friese said.

> Jeff Balser, M.D., Ph.D., is retiring from his roles as CEO of Vanderbilt Health and dean of Vanderbilt University School of Medicine at the end of 2026.

The academic system's board of directors has kicked of a national search for a successor who would hold both titles, according to the March 12 announcement.

A 1990 Vanderbilt graduate himself, Balser spent years as a cardiac anesthesiologist and surgical intensivist at Johns Hopkins before returning to Vanderbilt in 1998. He was named chair of the Department of Anesthesiology in 2001, dean of the medical school in 2008 and head of the Vanderbilt University Medical Center in 2009. He has served as dean and in the health system's top executive role for the past 17 years.

The organization has grown from a four-hospital system to an eight-hospital system under his tenure, during which its annual net revenue also grew from around $2 billion to nearly $9 billion, according to the announcement. Part of that time was an effort he led to legally and financially separate the medical center and its system from the university as a standalone nonprofit. The organization's cash reserves also have also grown from 50 days to more than 110, with total cash on hand plus investments now exceeding $3 billion.

> Greg Hoffman, chief financial officer of Providence, will retire in June, the organization announced.

Hoffman has been with the major nonprofit system for over a decade, and served as CFO for the past five years. His tenure in the role is marked by a multi-year financial turnaround that finally brought operations into the black during the quarter ended Sept. 30, 2025. The announcement of his retirement also pointed to his role striking up new strategic partnerships, resetting contracts with commercial payers and heading the implementation of an enterprise resource planning system.

Providence said it plans to conduct an internal and national search for Hoffman's replacement.

> Kevin Tabb, M.D., president and CEO of Beth Israel Lahey Health, has given notice to the system's board that he plans to step down after this year.

The physician executive was tapped as CEO of Beth Israel Deaconess in 2011, and stayed at the top through its merger with fellow Massachusetts provider Lahey Health in 2019. Today the organization spans 14 hospitals, employs 42,000 people and cares for 1.7 million patients annually.

Alongside navigating the merger and a pandemic, Tabb is credited with advancing initiatives around care access and connecting services delivered between its locations. Beth Israel Lahey also notched new partnerships: a teaching relationship with UMass Chan School of Medicine and an upcoming cancer collaboration with the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute.

Tabb will remain in his role while the system's board searches for his successor, a process expected to take about eight to 10 months, according to the announcement.

> Health tech company Stellar Health has added Raul Smith, a veteran of Elevance Health, as its chief financial officer.

Smith has 20 years of experience in healthcare leadership, according to an announcement, including six years as president CFO for Anthem's East Region. He has also served as CFO for Duo Health and Gold Kidney Health Plan.

Stellar said that Smith's experience in the health insurance industry will help the company build out its platform. Stellar supports payers in value-based care by making it easier for providers to engage with these complex environments.

In addition, he'll play a key role in driving the financial evolution of its risk-based portfolio, including the tech-enabled accountable care organization, shaco.

"Stellar is already setting the pace for value-based care, and Raul adds the institutional caliber to match our growing scale," said Michael Meng, CEO and cofounder of Stellar Health. "Raul brings the financial authority to stand behind the definitive value we deliver to our payor partners. His leadership solidifies that our ROI is absolute and verifiable—impact that will only continue to compound and get better year over year."

> Wellpoint Tennessee, an Elevance Health subsidiary, has named Rachel Chinetti as president of its health plan.

As president, Chinetti will be tasked with leading the insurer's strategy and operations across the state, including a focus on affordability, access and quality for individuals enrolled in TennCare, its Medicaid program.

She brings almost two decades of experience in Medicaid and long-term services and supports (LTSS) to the role, per an announcement from the insurer. Chinetti has held multiple roles within TennCare and most recently served as a staff vice president within Elevance Health's government unit, where she led a center of excellence in LTSS.

Chinetti is also a native of the state who lives in Nashville, with strong community relationships, the company said.

“It is an honor to serve Tennesseans in this role,” Chinetti said in the release. “Wellpoint Tennessee has a strong legacy of partnership and innovation. I look forward to working alongside TennCare, providers, advocates, and community leaders to strengthen rural and maternal health, enhance long-term services and supports, and deliver more coordinated, person-centered care that helps our members live healthier, more independent lives.”

> James Downing, M.D., will be stepping down from his role as president and CEO of St. Jude Children's Research Hospital near the end of 2026, the pediatric research hospital announced.

The physician executive has been with the organization for four decades, and has sat at its head for the past 12 years. Under his leadership St. Jude underwent the largest strategic expansion in its history, which included the completion of two separate strategic plans requiring nearly $20 billion of investment and over 2,300 new positions; major expansion to St. Jude's main campus; and greater international collaboration.

Prior to that he served as scientific director for eight years, a period in which he spearheaded the Pediatric Cancer Genome Project.

Downing plans to transition into a faculty role at St. Jude's Department of Global Pediatric Medicine after handing over the reins. The organization said a replacement is expected to be named over the summer.

“I’ve watched St. Jude transform the care of pediatric cancer around the world, and I’m grateful to have played a small part as its CEO," he said in the announcement. "It has been the honor of a lifetime to wake up every day and know that I have a purpose, to be a part of this workforce, and to change the outlook for children everywhere.”

>The Department of Health and Human Services announced several leadership changes as the agency looks to advance Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s Make American Healthy Again agenda.

HHS said that Chris Klomp will step into the role of chief counselor at the agency, where he will "oversee all operations of the department." Klomp currently serves as the director of Medicare.

In addition, both Politico and the Washington Post have reported that Jim O'Neill, deputy secretary of HHS and the acting director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, will step down from both roles. Sources told the Post that O'Neill will be offered a position as an ambassador.

The Post reported that the shakeup comes amid significant controversy over the shift at HHS in vaccine policy and other hot-button topics. Kennedy is looking to shift talking points to more politically palatable topics, like healthy food, per the Post.

In addition to the new title for Klomp, Kennedy has tapped Kyle Diamantas and Grace Graham to serve as senior counselors for the Food and Drug Administration as well as John Brooks to step in as senior counselor for the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services.

HHS said that each of these three will also continue to hold their current roles in addition to supporting Kennedy's office.

"I am proud to elevate battle-tested, principled leaders onto my immediate team—individuals with the courage and experience to help us move faster and go further as we work to Make America Healthy Again," Kennedy said in the press release.

>The Federation of American Hospitals announced multiple leadership appointments this week.

The organization's new CEO, Charlene MacDonald, took the role on Jan. 1, and on Jan. 14, FAH revealed the names of key members of her team, including:

McBride brings more than 25 years of overall healthcare experience to the COO role, including more than four years at FAH as its leading voice on patient safety, quality and public health. Broder has been at FAH for more than two years, and will take on an expanded role as chief strategy officer, spearheading efforts to support the organization's mission as well as its long-term stability and growth.

Keefe joined FAH in December 2024 and has more than two decades of policy experience, both at the state and federal levels. Tenoever will continue in the general counsel role, and has held similar titles at other trade associations, FAH said.

“Our exceptional new executive team will be integral to the Federation’s success as we write our next chapter,” MacDonald said in the announcement. “We’re at a critical moment for health care coverage and access, and our team’s proven ability to be strategic, nimble, and relentlessly solutions-oriented will allow the Federation to deliver for our members and the millions of patients they serve.”

>Eduardo Conrado stepped into the CEO chair at Ascension on Jan. 1, taking over for the retiring Joseph Impicciche.

Conrado has been the major health system's president since 2023, and continues to hold that title. He joined in 2018 to serve in digital, strategy and innovation positions. Prior to that, he’d spent 26 years at Motorola Solutions and served on Ascension’s board for five years.

In a blog post published this week, Conrado said his focus as CEO will be for Ascension to strengthen access to care, modernize care delivery and deepen commitments to those most in need—achieved through a combination of mission-driven strategy, capital deployment and talent.

>Jesse Ehrenfeld, M.D., has joined clinical AI company Aidoc as its new chief medical officer.

#5730. New diabetes implant uses electricity to lower blood sugar and promote weight loss

An experimental electronic implant could offer an entirely new way to treat type 2 diabetes. Rather than relying on insulin or conventional medications, the device uses electricity to convert excess blood sugar into a substance that the body can eliminate. In early tests with diabetic mice, the technology successfully regulated blood sugar and also led to weight loss.

The development comes as type 2 diabetes continues to affect a growing number of people worldwide. Unlike type 1 diabetes, type 2 is frequently associated with obesity, limited physical activity, and consuming more energy than the body needs over long periods.

Insulin injections can help reduce blood sugar by allowing muscle cells to absorb glucose from the bloodstream. However, insulin does not eliminate the underlying problem of excess energy. When the body does not use the glucose it absorbs, the surplus can eventually be converted into fat. This helps explain why some people with diabetes continue gaining weight even while receiving treatment.

Researchers led by Martin Fussenegger, a professor in the Department of Biosystems Science and Engineering at ETH Zurich in Basel, have developed an implant designed to address this problem differently. Their findings were published in the journal Science.

A New Diabetes Treatment Powered by Electricity

Fussenegger and his colleagues have spent years developing technologies capable of controlling blood sugar. Their previous designs used engineered genetic networks, but these systems depended on living cells and other biological materials.

That dependence introduced several complications. Biological components can create challenges involving immune compatibility, long-term stability, production, and regulatory approval.

The researchers have now taken a different approach by creating a catalyst made entirely from inorganic materials. It performs its function without requiring living cells, enzymes, or other biological components.

At the heart of the implant is a piece of graphite felt covered with tiny clusters of gold. These gold structures are coated with even smaller platinum particles, creating a specially engineered surface that enables the chemical reaction needed to process glucose.

The researchers designed this nanoscale surface themselves. According to Fussenegger, the materials also demonstrated excellent biocompatibility during experimental testing, suggesting they can interact with living tissue without causing significant adverse reactions.

The system includes an electronic controller enclosed in a 3D-printed housing. Instead of relying on a conventional wired power connection, the implant receives energy wirelessly at a frequency of 13.56 MHz. This frequency is internationally allocated for industrial, scientific, and medical applications.

How the Implant Removes Excess Blood Sugar

The technology works by transforming excess glucose into gluconate, a substance that can be eliminated from the body through urine.

Normally, glucose provides energy for cells. When more glucose is available than the body needs, some of that excess energy can ultimately be stored as fat. By converting part of the glucose into gluconate, the implant prevents that portion from being metabolized and stored in tissues, potentially helping reduce fat accumulation.

The entire process is designed to happen automatically, responding to changes in blood sugar as they occur.

A conventional glucose sensor, similar to those worn on the upper arm by many people with diabetes, continuously measures glucose concentrations in tissue. When levels rise too high, such as after a meal, the sensor communicates through Bluetooth with a smartphone or smartwatch.

The connected device then activates the implant, supplying the electrical energy needed for the catalyst to convert glucose into gluconate.

Once glucose levels return to the desired range, the implant automatically shuts down. This feedback system, known as closed-loop control, is intended to prevent blood sugar from dropping dangerously low.

Blood Sugar Control and Weight Loss in Diabetic Mice

To evaluate the technology, the researchers first conducted a laboratory experiment using a reservoir containing 5 liters of a nutrient solution with glucose. That volume is approximately equal to the amount of blood circulating in an adult human body.

The experiment demonstrated that the catalyst could convert glucose in a solution of this scale, an important step toward assessing its potential for medical applications.

The researchers then implanted the system in diabetic mice. The results showed that the device could precisely regulate the animals' blood sugar levels. The mice also lost weight, suggesting that converting excess glucose rather than allowing it to contribute to fat storage could offer an additional metabolic benefit.

Over six weeks of testing, the implant continued functioning reliably and was well tolerated by the animals.

"The system operates at a very low voltage, and our experiments showed no evidence of tissue damage from either electrical or thermal effects," says Fussenegger.

Although these findings are promising, the device has not yet been tested in humans. Additional research will be necessary to determine whether the technology can operate safely and effectively in people with diabetes.

Could Electronics Transform the Future of Diabetes Treatment?

Fussenegger believes the technology could represent a fundamental change in how diabetes is managed. Rather than using medications to influence how the body processes glucose, an electronic device could directly control the amount of glucose available.

"For decades, we have treated diabetes by telling the body how to manage glucose. We are now showing that we can take control of glucose directly, using electronics rather than drugs," he says. "And the catalyst only activates when glucose levels are too high."

The approach also creates opportunities to connect medical treatments with digital technologies, including the Internet of Things. This refers to networks of devices that exchange information and respond automatically to changing conditions.

The researchers envision electronically controlled treatments that could be manufactured at scale and integrated with existing digital health systems.

Their next objective is to turn the experimental implant into a medical device suitable for further development and eventual clinical testing.

One potential advantage is its relatively simple glucose conversion mechanism. Because the catalyst does not rely on cells or enzymes, the researchers believe some of the technical challenges associated with biological treatments could be easier to overcome.

Much of the supporting technology is also already available. Wireless power transmission systems and external electronic controllers are commercially established, meaning the team would not need to develop every component from scratch.

If future studies demonstrate similar benefits in humans, this approach could open the door to a new class of diabetes treatments in which smart electronic devices help regulate blood sugar directly, potentially reducing reliance on conventional medications.

Materials provided by ETH Zurich. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5729. Cell Therapy for Knee Osteoarthritis Reverses Damage in Early Trial

— It won't be cheap, but could be the disease-modifying therapy the field has long sought

ORLANDO -- A cell-based therapy for knee osteoarthritis (OA) called OSCA not only improved patients' symptoms in a phase IIa trial and appeared safe, but also showed signs of reversing joint damage within a few months, a researcher reported here.

Standard evaluations including the Western Ontario McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC) and Knee Osteoarthritis Outcomes Score (KOOS) showed that a single treatment reduced pain levels by half in the 6-month study, according to Jae-Young Park, MD, PhD, of CHA University in Seongnam, Korea.

But perhaps more importantly, MRI findings at month 6 indicated that some cartilage had regenerated and marrow abnormalities were resolving, he told attendees during a late-breaking abstract session at the American College of Rheumatology's annual meeting.

Orthopedic surgeons should pay close attention: If these results are duplicated with further testing, the treatment could be the first genuine disease-modifying therapy for knee OA, potentially making arthroplasty a quaint relic of a barbaric era in medicine.

OSCA is shorthand for a combination of cord blood-derived mesenchymal stem cells, dubbed osiramestrocel (OS), and cartilage acellular matrix (CAM) taken from pigs, Park explained. He described the proposed mechanism of action as targeting not only the synovium, but also subchondral bone and sensory neurons. The hoped-for result is decreased inflammation, less pain, and structural improvement.

The phase IIa trial tested single doses of this product, injected into the knee joint, in 113 patients randomized equally among two dosing levels (50 or 100 million cells per injection) or placebo. Technically, safety was the primary focus in this early study, with pain, function, structural change, and biomarker effects as exploratory outcomes.

Mean patient age was about 62 and some two-thirds were women. Body mass index values averaged about 25 (which may raise questions about generalizability to the U.S. and other countries where obesity is more common). At baseline, self-reported pain scores on a 100-point scale averaged roughly 67, with mean WOMAC and KOOS values of about 55 and 50, respectively.

Three patients in the lower-dose group and eight receiving the higher dose experienced injection-site reactions, but no other important treatment-related adverse events were noted. Discounting the injection-site reactions, numbers of treatment-emergent adverse events were similar across the three study arms.

Those data may have been the study's primary object, but Park spent most of his talk on the efficacy outcomes. These were all very favorable, even astonishingly so.

Both WOMAC and KOOS scores improved by about 25 points, or approximately half of their baseline values after 6 months. Some improvement was also seen with placebo, but this still left a clinically and statistically significant advantage of 15 points in WOMAC scores and 20-21 points on KOOS. Self-rated pain scores fell 40-44 points from baseline with the two OSCA doses, with differences from placebo of 24-29 points. For the latter outcome, the lower dose outperformed the higher one to a small degree.

Another symptom-focused analysis looked at responses by OMERACT-OARSI criteria, achieved by 77-78% of the OSCA groups versus 39% of the placebo group. Park pointed out that this gap was already apparent just 4 weeks after dosing.

Structural effects were evaluated with the so-called MOCART and WORMS techniques for interpreting MRI images. The former examines cartilage specifically, while the latter was used to assess tibial and femoral bone marrow. The MOCART analysis showed some modest cartilage regeneration -- also greatest with the lower OSCA dose -- and a degree of marrow normalization. For the latter, the higher dose had the greater impact. Notably, the placebo group saw progression of both cartilage and marrow damage.

Finally, serum and urine biomarkers for inflammation and cartilage pathology all showed improvement. For these analyses, the higher dose appeared superior.

Being such a small and short-duration study, many questions remain unanswered. Patients in the current trial will be followed for an additional 6 months, plus a 5-year extension. Those data will give some insight into the therapy's durability. An issue for future studies will surely be whether repeat dosing is needed to maintain or boost structural recovery. Also, the current trial enrolled patients with moderate knee OA, so whether it's more or less effective in patients with milder or more severe disease is another issue that clinicians will want addressed.

Future plans by the developer, Korea-based Kangstem Biotech, aren't yet clear -- a July press release on the study's topline results indicated that the firm is seeking partnerships with global pharmaceutical companies, while making no mention of possible phase III trials.

#5728. A new tactic in the war over out-of-network bills: Health care providers are suing employers

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Herman examined hundreds of pages of court documents for this story, part of STAT’s Out of Pocket, Out of Reach series.

Bob covers the money in health care, focusing on health insurance and hospitals. His stories delve into Medicare Advantage, opaque prescription drug benefits, and how much executives actually make. He is also the author of the Health Care Inc. newsletter. You can reach Bob on Signal at bobjherman.09.

This past August, Joe Hancock, a Kentucky plumbing and heating contractor, opened a just-delivered box packed with hundreds of sheets of paper. Leafing through them, he read seven words no small business owner wants to see: “A lawsuit has been filed against you.”

The complaint, from air ambulance firm PHI Health, claimed Hancock was on the hook for almost $27,000 in medical helicopter bills. They were tied to one of his now-retired employees, who needed an emergency flight after a heart attack.

Hancock, who owns Whitehead-Hancock Plumbing, Heating & Cooling, a family-run business in Frankfort, Ky., that has been around for more than a century, didn’t understand why he was being roped into a lawsuit that featured 31 other companies — for medical charges he was never aware of.

“I was terrified,” Hancock said. “I was like, ‘What in the hell is going on here?’”

He’s not alone. The PHI lawsuit highlights an evolving tactic by health care providers in a raging battle over out-of-network bills. Previously, providers targeted health insurance companies to pay outstanding amounts that were awarded through federal mediation. Now, they increasingly are dragging the insurers’ clients — employers — into court, claiming they are responsible for bills that insurers haven’t fully paid or have delayed paying. The practice is introducing a new shock that could further torch the affordability of workers’ health coverage.

“These big suits naming dozens of employers at a time is really an escalation,” said Garrett Hohimer, a vice president at the Business Group on Health. “And it will cause employers to incur expenses that [come directly] out of their health care plans.”

A 2022 law called the No Surprises Act shielded patients from the financial trauma of many types of unexpected medical bills, but it has also given rise to a vast industry that’s driving up costs across the health care system. The law uses an arbitration process to determine how much health care providers should get paid for out-of-network emergency care, like helicopter rides, for people who have some type of commercial health coverage. STAT has reported that providers are winning most of these arbitration awards, which often are far higher than the amounts in-network providers receive for the same services.

Already, high payments tied to this process have added approximately $20 billion in extra costs to the health care system, Georgetown University researchers have estimated. A large portion of those costs inevitably come out of the bank accounts of America’s employers and consequently lead to higher premiums, emphasizing how even well-intentioned health reforms can add to the financial pressure that’s crushing workers and businesses.

PHI Health, a national chain, is arguably the most aggressive company suing employers, which it claims are not “passive” bystanders in insurers’ refusal to fully pay awards. Other regional physician practices have sued some employers as well. But PHI and its army of attorneys have filed lawsuits against hundreds of companies, demanding they collectively pay tens of millions of dollars in unpaid out-of-network claims that it won in the federal arbitration process.

PHI isn’t just suing small, local firms like Hancock’s. It’s also taking legal action against some of the largest corporations — Amazon, Walmart, Eli Lilly, United Airlines, General Motors, PepsiCo, State Farm, and Toyota, to name a few — as well as unions, counties, cities, states, public school districts, and universities.

PHI has sued other health care organizations, including hospitals, nursing homes, and medical billing firms. It also has gone after nonprofits, such as the Catholic Diocese of Cleveland. In each instance, a worker or family member at these companies took an emergency medical helicopter, often at a cost of tens of thousands of dollars per trip.

Unpacking the business — and secretive inner workings — of the U.S. health care industry

In some cases, PHI wasn’t sure what company it should be suing, but sued anyway. Several lawsuits named specific health insurers and employers as defendants, and then added “ABC CORP” or “XYZ CORP” as a placeholder. If the insurer or employer “is not in fact the plan sponsor … that covers the patient transported by PHI, then the identity of the plan sponsor is unknown to PHI, and this action is instead brought against ABC CORP,” one lawsuit reads.

Katie Keith and Ellie DeGarmo are attorneys at Georgetown’s Center for Health Policy and the Law who have tracked No Surprises Act lawsuits, including those filed by PHI. They said the scores of cases reinforce the bloat in the health care system: above-market prices that providers are winning for not participating in an insurance company’s network, attempts from insurers to not pay at all or profit off lowball offers, and a booming revenue stream for arbitrators.

But trying to wring money out of employers — and, ultimately, from their workers — is a stark divergence from the public statements of physician groups and air ambulance companies, which have painted health insurers as the bad guys for not following the rules.

“It kind of undercuts the narrative that this is provider versus insurance company,” Keith said. “In this case, this is about provider versus everyone who pays for health care and is now stuck with the bill for [arbitration] awards that have gone totally off the rails.”

STAT reached out to more than two dozen employers that were listed in PHI’s lawsuits. Most did not respond to inquiries. Of those that did, most declined to comment.

“Because this matter involves pending litigation … we will not be providing any interviews,” said Clint Mitchell, the division superintendent of Spotsylvania County Public Schools in Fredericksburg, Va. PHI Health is suing Spotsylvania County’s school system for almost $28,000.

Jay Litten, the town manager of Bridgewater, Va., told STAT the town’s health insurer, Anthem Blue Cross Blue Shield, retained counsel and was handling the case. PHI sued Bridgewater in October for more than $37,000 in unpaid awards.

PHI has boasted about its success in the law’s arbitration process. In 2024, it told prospective investors that it was “able to maintain our profitability” by winning more than three out of every four arbitration claims, and it expected “this trend of favorable” outcomes from the process would continue.

The company has some private equity backing, according to financial filings from when the company considered going public in 2023. Its largest shareholder as of 2023 was Q Investments, a family office that has a private equity firm.

PHI declined to make anyone available for an interview. In a statement, CEO Scott McCarty defended the company’s lawsuits, saying the employers PHI has sued “have a duty to their employees and a responsibility to health care providers in their communities to abide by the law and pay for services delivered.”

McCarty said health insurers are asking their employer clients to choose between paying the unpaid arbitration amounts or authorizing the insurer to continue refusing payment.

“Once an employer is on notice of nonpayment and affirmatively endorses that practice, it is no longer a passive bystander,” McCarty said in the statement. “It has made a conscious decision to allow its insurance company not to pay binding federal awards in violation of federal law.”

In PHI’s lawsuits, the company alleges insurers, and now employers, are using an “unlawful scheme to ‘low pay, late pay, or no pay’ providers, including PHI.” All the cases are still pending.

The company also claims insurers float the money from unpaid awards, which are binding decisions, on the stock market as a way to earn extra interest or investment income.

James Gelfand, CEO of the ERISA Industry Committee, a lobbying group that represents large employers, said companies don’t condone insurers delaying payments as a way to make extra money. But he said under the federal law known as ERISA, employers are legally obligated to make sure they spend their health plan assets wisely on behalf of workers. If employers believe the awards are tied to ineligible claims — or are egregiously high compared with what they normally would pay — those payments could violate that obligation.

As a result, the employers’ health insurers “are operating with our blessing when we say, ‘Hey, if the [arbitration] award is inappropriate and wrong, do not pay it,’” he said. “How can we claim to be responsible stewards of people’s money if we’re just like, ‘Oh, here you go!’ That would be crazy.”

Jenny Goins, who is CEO of the National Alliance of Healthcare Purchaser Coalitions and used to oversee health benefits for Kentucky state employees, said “slow-walking the payments” to providers is one of the only ways employers can push back if they believe the awards are based on ineligible or incomplete claims. Medical claims are not eligible for arbitration if, for example, the employer or its health plan doesn’t cover a certain service or if there is certain information or data missing.

PHI has frequently named Anthem Blue Cross Blue Shield, owned by Elevance Health, as a defendant in the lawsuits against employers. Elevance did not make anyone available for an interview. The company said in a statement that PHI is charging prices for air ambulance services that are 700% of what Medicare pays and mileage rates that are 1,500% more than Medicare rates.

“We have already paid PHI substantial amounts for services provided to our members,” Elevance spokesperson Janey Kiryluik said in a statement. “We dispute whether additional amounts are legally owed for claims that were ineligible” for the arbitration process.

PHI said only arbitrators can determine the eligibility of claims. It added that the rates Medicare pays don’t cover the full cost of emergency air care, nor can those prices be considered during the arbitration process.

The bigger issue revealed by the lawsuits, Goins said, is how “broken” the law has become, even though she believed it was well-intended. The issue has now attracted interest in Congress, where lawmakers are proposing various plans to overhaul the arbitration process.

“Greedy people see an opportunity to make more money,” Goins said. “I also see there’s a true opportunity to shine a light on this.”

In September, PHI dropped Hancock’s company as a defendant, one month after its attorneys served him with court papers. Hancock said his heating, cooling, and plumbing business of 30 employees is not self-insured — meaning he buys his health insurance from Anthem, which takes on all the risk of his employees’ medical care.

PHI’s McCarty blamed Anthem in a statement, saying it “does not always receive clear or consistent information from insurers identifying whether a plan is self-funded or fully insured. In this case, after the lawsuit was filed, Anthem’s counsel confirmed that Whitehead-Hancock was fully insured, and PHI promptly dismissed it, without settlement.”

Other businesses are getting released from PHI’s lawsuits, too. It’s unclear if they were wrongfully lumped in, like Hancock’s company, or if they are paying PHI’s demands to clear a costly legal headache.

PHI’s legal team “threw a handful of darts, and they’re going to try to rattle as many cages as they can,” Hancock said. “It’s not right. It shouldn’t be legal.”

STAT’s coverage of the soaring costs of health insurance for workers and employers is supported by a grant from the Commonwealth Fund. Our financial supporters are not involved in any decisions about our journalism.

Bob covers the money in health care, focusing on health insurance and hospitals. His stories delve into Medicare Advantage, opaque prescription drug benefits, and how much executives actually make. He is also the author of the Health Care Inc. newsletter. You can reach Bob on Signal at bobjherman.09.

#5727. Biden Says He Wouldn't Have Run for a Second Term in 2024 If He Knew He Had Cancer

— "I don't think an 80-year-old man with cancer should be running," Biden noted

Joe Biden says he did not know he had cancer while he was president and would not have sought a second term if he already had been diagnosed.

The former Democratic president's comments came in an interview with People magazine before the release of his White House memoir on Tuesday.

"If I had known that I was feeling lousy because I had cancer," said Biden, who turns 84 on Nov. 20, "I would've not gone forward" with a 2024 re-election bid that ended after a disastrous debate performance against Republican Donald Trump.

Biden was diagnosed with metastatic prostate cancer months after leaving office in 2025.

"I don't think an 80-year-old man with cancer should be running" for president, Biden said in the interview.

Still, he argued that the June 2024 debate, less than 5 months before Election Day, was not a seismic event even if it accelerated Democrats' concerns about his age -- he was 81 at the time -- and his ability to defeat Trump.

"First of all, I thought there'd be another debate, which there wasn't," Biden said. "But notwithstanding the fact that there wasn't another debate, it didn't disturb me because it wasn't consequential."

Within weeks, Biden announced he was ending his campaign and endorsing his vice president, Kamala Harris, who secured the nomination and lost to Trump in the general election.

Biden insisted he was able to perform his duties while he was in office. He said age itself was not disqualifying and meant he had experience and deep personal relationships with world leaders.

"I believe that on an objective basis, I was the best-equipped person to do the job," he said.

His son Hunter told the BBC in August that the cancer had spread and was causing his father pain. "It's very painful and it's very debilitating in many respects," he said.

Since Joe Biden left office, his son has become a higher-profile public presence, sparring with Republicans on social media, posting lengthy thoughts on the nation's direction, and launching his own cryptocurrency.

Joe Biden defended his son's public persona and his decision to pardon Hunter Biden after the younger Biden's 2024 conviction on federal felony gun charges and his guilty plea to federal tax charges. Hunter Biden also had faced years of scrutiny and withering Republican attacks over his international business dealings.

Hunter Biden has said the pardon damaged his father's legacy, but the former president said Trump's penchant for vengeance made it necessary.

"He goes after people without any basis, whether they're viewed as an enemy. I knew what he would do," Joe Biden said. "If I hadn't pardoned -- not just some of my family members, anyone who's dealt with me -- he would go back and try to do harm to them."

Biden called his son "one of the brightest men I know," adding, "I'm really proud of him."

While medical cost trend remains a pressure point for health insurers, leading companies cited some positive trends, too, heading into the final months of 2026.

Through the first nine months of the year, profits were $15.9 billion at UHG, rising from $12 billion a year ago.

The healthcare giant has been in the midst of a critical financial turnaround since mid-2025, and in the most recent quarter, it highlighted some of the progress that it's logged over the past year at one of its biggest pain centers: Optum Health.

When the company posted an uncharacteristically poor quarter to start 2025, Optum Health was cited as one of the main pressure points. During its most recent call, Optum CEO Patrick Conway, M.D., said that the transition centered on a "continued return to value-based care principles" that sit at the core of Optum Health.

UnitedHealth also led the way on revenue in Q3, posting $112.7 billion. That's down slightly from $113.2 billion the company, reported in the third quarter of 2025.

CVS Health had the second-highest profit and revenue in Q3, bringing in $2.2 billion in earnings for the quarter. This marks a significant reversal from the prior-year quarter, when the company posted a nearly $4 billion loss.

CVS' revenue in the quarter was $108.4 billion, increasing from $102.9 billion in the third quarter of 2025.

The company's financial performance wasn't what dominated the headlines in Q3, however, as CVS shocked the industry in announcing plans to split its pharmacy business off and form two companies. The break-up is expected to close in the first half of 2028, and would establish CVS Pharmacy as its own company while Aetna and Caremark would remain together as CVS Health.

CVS CEO David Joyner said that the shift represents "a structure and plan that are built to win and represent the best path to create value over the long term."

The Cigna Group and Elevance Health were on par with one another in Q3 on profits, both earning $1.4 billion. Cigna wins out on revenue, though, with $73.7 billion, while Elevance reported $51.4 billion.

By comparison, Cigna posted $1.9 billion in profit and $69.7 billion in revenue in Q3 2025.

Core to the third-quarter conversation was the company's newly-unveiled Lead to One healthcare transformation strategy, which puts an emphasis on building a personalized experience for its members and customers.

Elevance Health, meanwhile, increased its profit slightly year over year from $1.2 billion in Q3 2025. Revenues in the prior-year quarter were $50.7 million.

The company was one of several insurers in the quarter that noted positive signs in its Medicaid plans. While its leaders told investors that 2026 remains a "trough year" for its Medicaid business, improvements are likely in the cards for 2027.

That trend is supported by state rate setting that more fully accounts for the rising cost of care and the acuity of people enrolled in Medicaid, executives said. The member mix is only expected to increase in acuity as states roll out work requirements at the beginning of this year.

Similarly, Centene CEO Sarah London said the company sees an opportunity for "long-term growth" in the Medicaid market as part of its Q3 report. She noted similar trends around rate setting from states.

London added that the insurer has made significant progress on focus areas for improvement, such as behavioral health.

Centene posted a $71 million loss in the quarter, slimming its losses significantly from $6.6 billion in the prior-year quarter. That massive loss a year ago was backstopped by a one-time impairment charge of more than $6 billion.

Revenues in Q3 were $50.6 billion, up slightly from $49.7 billion in the third quarter of 2025.

The insurer has had momentum around new sign-ups and has also done well in recapturing enrollments that were impacted by market exits, Rechtin said.

Humana posted a $162 million profit in the third quarter, down from $195 million a year ago. Revenues were $41.15 billion, growing from $32.6 billion in the prior-year quarter.

#5725. What we learned about the hyperscalers from earnings season

GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala

Recently Amazon.com Inc., Google owner Alphabet Inc. and Microsoft Corp. reported earnings within roughly 24 hours of each other, and this earnings season told us more about long-term artificial intelligence strategy than any keynote or press release this year. Beneath the headlines lie three very different strategies.

Here’s what I took away: Amazon will be the long-term winner because its open, platform-first approach gives customers the broadest choice of models and silicon, and it’s showing that size doesn’t limit scale. Microsoft is a solid second, protected less by strategy than by the customers it already has locked in. And Google will be a distant third, with impressive technology built on a fragile business foundation and a closed, Gemini-first strategy that runs counter to where enterprises are heading.

The most remarkable part of the earnings season was that Amazon’s Amazon Web Services business has found a way to buck the law of large numbers. It’s growing 39.3% at its size. AWS revenue reached $46 billion, marking its sixth straight quarter of acceleration and its fastest growth in nearly five years, putting the business at an $184 billion annualized run rate, according to Amazon’s third-quarter release.

To put that in perspective, the last time AWS grew this fast was in the fourth quarter of 2021, when it posted 40% growth on $17.8 billion in quarterly revenue. AWS is now more than two-and-a-half times that size and is growing at essentially the same rate. The roughly $13 billion it added year over year is about three-quarters of what the entire business generated in a quarter back then.

The law of large numbers is supposed to catch every business. The largest cloud provider on the planet is accelerating instead.

Amazon Chief Executive Andy Jassy projected AWS growth of more than 40% in both 2027 and 2028. Operating income reached $17.8 billion at a 38.7% margin, and backlog climbed to $578 billion, up from $244 billion at the end of 2025. On the earnings call, Jassy indicated AWS could reach $1 trillion in as little as five years, giving Amazon two businesses that do north of a trillion dollars in revenue.

Bedrock is the most underappreciated piece of Amazon’s strategy and, in the long term, the most important. Microsoft built its AI identity around OpenAI, and Google around Gemini. Both host third-party models, but each has a house favorite that its roadmap and pricing orbit around. AWS made model neutrality the product.

According to an AWS Builder Center guide, Bedrock offers more than 100 models from providers including Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta, Mistral, DeepSeek, Google, xAI and Nvidia. In the third quarter alone, Amazon added OpenAI’s GPT-6 family, Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5, xAI’s Grok 4.7, and Moonshot’s Kimi K3, per Amazon’s quarterly release.

The open-weight wave makes this even more important. Bedrock already runs DeepSeek, Qwen, Mistral, Kimi, Gemma, Nemotron and OpenAI’s gpt-oss models as fully managed services, as AWS has detailed. As open models close the gap, enterprises will fine-tune smaller, cheaper models for specific tasks and reserve frontier models for the hardest problems. The platform that lets them route across all of them under a single security and governance model wins. A cloud built around a single-model company has a conflict of interest every time an open model gets good enough to replace it.

Customer spending is validating Bedrock’s value, as Fortune 500 spending on Bedrock rose nearly sevenfold year over year and token volume grew nearly 17-fold, Jassy said on the earnings call.

The second advantage is silicon, which is tightly linked to Bedrock. Most of Bedrock’s inference runs on Trainium, which lets AWS keep prices low while protecting margins, according to TIKR’s call coverage. Customers using Amazon’s custom silicon saved more than $2 billion in the third quarter alone, as noted in the call transcript.

The bigger news was Jassy’s commitment to sell Trainium outside AWS starting in late 2027. “We believe we’re going to have a very significant business selling chips externally,” he said, according to Yahoo Finance. Training is periodic, whereas inference is a perpetual cost that scales with every agent and transaction. Selling Trainium racks brings AWS’ price-performance to enterprise data centers, sovereign environments and neoclouds, and gives organizations that need on-premises inference a credible alternative to Nvidia.

AWS has the broadest infrastructure footprint, the broadest model selection, and silicon that lowers the cost per token. The downside is the bill: a 2026 capex of roughly $220 billion, per 24/7 Wall St., and negative $33.5 billion in free cash flow, according to TradingKey. That spending is backed by contracted demand. If the growth rate continues, investors should be happy to see Amazon spending ahead of demand, but all eyes will be on free cash flow.

Who builds on AWS: Builders, including digital natives, AI labs, independent software vendors and large enterprises with mature engineering teams seeking model choice, cost control and no dependence on a single model partner.

Of the three hyperscalers, Microsoft’s business is the most predictable because it’s very hard to disrupt and isn’t a disruptor. What it is now is likely what it will be in the future. Azure grew 48% to $33.2 billion, the first time Microsoft has disclosed Azure revenue in dollars, according to CNBC.

But the most notable data point concerned lock-in. Customers with more than 50,000 Copilot seats grew more than eightfold year over year, including Capgemini, Hitachi, Truist and the U.K.’s HMRC, according to Microsoft’s earnings call. That’s Microsoft’s true AI strategy: Upsell AI to the hundreds of millions of workers already living in Office, Teams and Windows. Switching costs are enormous, and Microsoft will capture a large share of enterprise AI spend regardless of how its models compare.

Google and others have tried to disrupt the Office franchise for decades but haven’t posed a serious threat. In the AI era, a company like Canva or Zoom could introduce an entirely new way to create documents and begin to erode that business, but until there is a material loss of share, that installed base seems safe.

Microsoft’s strategy has downsides. The company leans heavily on OpenAI, a partner that increasingly acts like a competitor. On the same earnings call, Microsoft Chief Financial Officer Amy Hood said some third-party capacity deliveries were delayed. Microsoft also didn’t update its total paid Copilot seat count, leaving open how deeply those seats are used.

Who builds on Microsoft: Large, Microsoft-standardized enterprises, especially in regulated industries and the public sector, prioritize knowledge-worker productivity within the tools they already use.

Google Cloud’s headline numbers were impressive. Revenue grew 103% to $30.7 billion, and the operating margin was 36.2%, according to highlights from Alphabet’s earnings call. But a strong quarter doesn’t necessarily signal durability, and the earnings exposed three structural problems.

First, look at what is driving growth. According to Alphabet’s investor relations, CFO Anat Ashkenazi said tensor processing unit system sales were a “meaningful contributor” to cloud revenue. Hardware sales are lumpy and concentrated among a few large buyers, which is a different business from recurring cloud consumption.

Second, the core business funding all of this is showing cracks. Search made up 49.7% of Alphabet’s revenue, below half for the first time in the company’s history. That trend is likely to continue given the diversity of AI platforms. A year earlier, it was 55.3%. Also, Search grew only 12%, down from 19% in Q1 and 17% in Q2. YouTube ad revenue grew 9.2% to $11.21 billion, short of analysts’ $11.43 billion expectation. That’s down 15% from a year earlier and 13% from last quarter, adding only $152 million over the last quarter.

Third, spending is outpacing cash. Capex reached $51.4 billion, while free cash flow was negative $9.1 billion. Alphabet expects capex to exceed $300 billion in 2027, according to CNBC. The core business’s decline is becoming significant as the capex arms race continues.

Google has world-class research, Gemini and TPUs. Against that, it has a Gemini-first strategy that sits awkwardly with the open-weight wave, an ad business under AI pressure, and a history of sunsetting products, which remains the biggest objection I hear from chief information officers. Also, Google has always struggled with its enterprise strategy.

In 2018, I wrote this post for CIO.com asking whether Google was ever going to get serious about enterprise, and nothing much has changed. It seems to roll out products that have promise but never makes them best-in-class. As an example, Google Meet is good but not great, and Docs, Gmail and Drive are the same. They’re low-cost, but there are always better alternatives. Why would we expect their AI strategy to be different?

Who builds on Google: AI-native startups, research-heavy organizations,and BigQuery shops willing to accept platform risk. It’s a harder sell to a regulated enterprise making a 10-year commitment.

Neither is likely to make a long-term dent in the hyperscaler market, for one simple reason: They lack the flywheel. Amazon has retail and advertising; Google has search; and Microsoft has Office and Windows, each massive cash-generating businesses that can fund a multiyear compute buildout. The AI infrastructure race is capital-intensive, and IBM and Oracle are running it without that engine.

Oracle’s numbers look impressive on the surface, with cloud infrastructure revenue up 121% to $7.4 billion in its September quarter and RPO at $664 billion. The problem is how it’s financing that growth. Capex hit $28 billion in a single quarter, free cash flow was negative $5.4 billion, and debt has reached $125 billion, according to CNBC. After a $20 billion equity sale, it’s now selling another $10 billion in bonds, as Yahoo Finance reported.

Its database business can’t fund this buildout, so Oracle is relying on borrowed money and customer prepayments. That’s a fragile way to compete with companies that can self-fund.

IBM has largely stayed out of the compute race. Revenue grew 5% to $17.1 billion, led by Red Hat, according to IBM’s earnings release. IBM’s presentation reports $7.8 billion in year-to-date free cash flow, roughly what Amazon or Microsoft spends on capex in two weeks. IBM will matter as a hybrid-cloud integration layer, not a primary AI platform.

The biggest takeaway from earnings season is that the hyperscaler AI race now has a predictable order. Amazon is growing nearly 40% at an $184 billion run rate by doing what it has always done: building an open platform from silicon to agents, offering the broadest shelf of frontier and open-weight models, and preparing to take its inference silicon beyond its own data centers. Microsoft is a strong second, monetizing its existing customer base. Google is a distant third, betting that superior technology can outlast disruption to its core business while asking customers to adopt a closed stack.

To be clear, when I say “distant third,” that’s a forward-looking statement. Currently, Google’s cloud business is only slightly smaller than Azure’s, so my basis for “distant third” is openness, customer trust, enterprise go-to-market and the ability to fund the buildout.

When AI becomes a line item in IT budgets, customers will gravitate toward the platform with the lowest inference costs, the broadest selection of models and the deepest operational track record. Openness wins platform wars.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#5724. STAT+: Doctors on Kennedy’s influential preventive care panel have major conflicts of interest, filings reveal

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Chelsea covers the Department of Health and Human Services with a particular focus on power and influence at the top. Confidential tips can be sent via Signal at chelseacirruzzo.42.

WASHINGTON — Federal officials have granted blanket waivers to every member of an influential, yet little-known federal panel that evaluates preventive medical services, allowing them to serve despite some having clear financial stakes in decisions they might make.

The waivers, signed by a top federal official and obtained by STAT, show a willingness by health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s department to overlook financial conflicts of interests, though Kennedy frequently decries corporate influence in health care. In the case of two members, the documents show that they own private medical practices that could profit should the panel recommend particular types of care.

Other conflicts being waived include stock holdings in pharmaceutical and medical device companies and employment at public research universities that provide medical care. Some members of the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force, especially the newer ones, have more extensive conflicts than others.

#5723. Scientists reverse liver cell aging and cut Alzheimer’s-linked protein in half

The liver may hold an unexpected key to fighting two of the most serious diseases associated with aging: Alzheimer's disease and heart disease. Scientists have discovered that restoring the function of aging liver cells can dramatically reduce harmful substances in the bloodstream, raising the possibility of treating diseases that affect organs far beyond the liver itself.

In a new study involving older rats, researchers at the Keck School of Medicine of USC found that an experimental drug called cinaciguat reversed important signs of aging in specialized liver cells. After just two weeks of treatment, levels of amyloid beta, a protein associated with Alzheimer's disease, dropped by half. Levels of LDL, commonly called bad cholesterol, also returned to those seen in younger animals.

The findings, published in the Journal of Biological Chemistry, also revealed a previously unknown way that liver cells communicate with one another. This discovery could help scientists develop treatments that restore the liver's ability to remove potentially harmful substances from the blood, possibly reducing the risk of Alzheimer's disease and atherosclerosis, a condition in which fatty deposits accumulate inside arteries.

Why the Liver Could Be Important for Alzheimer's

Although Alzheimer's primarily affects the brain, scientists are increasingly interested in how other organs might influence the disease. The liver plays a central role in filtering the blood and removing unwanted compounds, including substances that may contribute to disease when they accumulate.

The USC findings suggest that restoring this natural cleaning process could offer a different approach to preventing certain age-related illnesses. However, the results have so far been demonstrated only in rats, and additional studies are needed to establish whether the same benefits occur in humans.

"We need to do further translational work to see whether our findings might point to new therapies," said corresponding author Laurie DeLeve, MD, PhD, professor and vice chair for scientific affairs in the USC Department of Medicine. "We're hopeful, though, because the findings line up with a lot of epidemiological results showing age as a major risk factor for Alzheimer's and atherosclerosis, and liver damage as a risk factor for Alzheimer's."

Targeting the liver could be particularly valuable in Alzheimer's research, where efforts to develop treatments acting directly in the brain have faced an estimated 98% failure rate in clinical trials. One major obstacle is the blood-brain barrier, a protective system that limits which substances can enter the brain from the bloodstream. While this barrier helps shield the brain from harmful compounds, it also makes delivering certain medications extremely difficult.

"If we're right that the liver is impactful, what do we do about that?" said first author Sam de Leve, MA, a USC lab technician and child of Laurie DeLeve. "Rather than trying to get a drug through the blood-brain barrier, which is obnoxiously difficult, we could direct drugs to the liver, an organ where there might be more therapeutic impact and certainly an easier job of drug delivery."

Scientists Restore the Aging Liver's Natural Filters

To understand how liver aging affects the bloodstream, the researchers focused on a relatively understudied group of cells known as liver sinusoidal endothelial cells (LSECs).

These cells form the lining of tiny blood vessels inside the liver. Unlike most blood vessel walls, they contain numerous microscopic openings that function somewhat like the holes in a sieve. These openings allow larger molecules circulating in the blood to reach neighboring cells called hepatocytes, which carry out much of the liver's work processing and removing substances from the body.

As the liver ages, the openings in LSECs gradually become smaller or disappear. This makes it harder for certain large molecules to reach the cells responsible for clearing them, allowing more of these substances to remain in circulation.

One substance affected by this change is amyloid beta. This protein is especially important in Alzheimer's research because it can accumulate in the brain and form plaques, one of the disease's defining features.

Previous observations showed that the liver becomes less effective at removing amyloid beta as it ages. The researchers suspected that the gradual closing of the openings in LSECs might help explain why more of the protein remains in the bloodstream of older animals.

To investigate, they administered cinaciguat to aged rats for two weeks. They then compared the treated animals with two untreated groups, one consisting of older rats and the other of younger rats.

The results were striking. Cinaciguat restored the structure and function of the aging LSECs, reopening their microscopic pores and improving their ability to help clear substances from the blood. Amyloid beta concentrations fell by approximately 50%, reaching levels comparable to those in young rats. The untreated older animals showed no similar improvement.

The researchers also measured low-density lipoproteins (LDL), often referred to as "bad" cholesterol because elevated levels contribute to fatty deposits inside arteries. Over time, these deposits can restrict blood flow and increase the risk of heart disease.

Initially, LDL was included as a comparison measure rather than a substance expected to respond to treatment. Unlike larger molecules, LDL particles are small enough to leave the bloodstream without passing through the microscopic openings in LSECs. The scientists therefore expected cinaciguat to have little or no effect on LDL levels.

Instead, they discovered that LDL concentrations in treated older rats also fell to levels observed in young animals.

"We said, 'Wait, why did that go down? Clearly, there's more to this story,'" Sam de Leve said.

The unexpected finding suggested that the drug was doing more than simply reopening the liver's aging filters. It appeared to be restoring another important aspect of liver function.

Because previous research had shown that hepatocytes function better when LSECs are present, the team began examining how these two types of cells communicate.

Their investigation uncovered a previously unknown sequence of biochemical signals that helps coordinate the liver's ability to remove substances from the bloodstream.

A Hidden Communication Pathway Between Liver Cells

The researchers found that cinaciguat activates an enzyme called soluble guanylate cyclase inside LSECs. This triggers the cells to release a growth factor known as HB-EGF, which sends a signal to nearby hepatocytes.

In response, hepatocytes alter their surfaces in ways that allow them to capture more LDL and amyloid beta from the blood. This helps explain why the treatment reduced both substances, even though they do not rely on the same filtering mechanism.

Normally, aging interferes with the ability of LSECs to release HB-EGF. Cinaciguat restored this signaling process, allowing the liver cells to communicate more effectively and supporting the removal of substances that otherwise tend to accumulate with age.

The discovery identifies a potential new target for future drugs. Rather than focusing exclusively on the physical openings in LSECs, researchers may be able to develop therapies that restore the chemical signals responsible for helping the liver work efficiently.

Could Liver Rejuvenation Help Prevent Alzheimer's and Heart Disease?

According to the researchers, this is the first study to demonstrate that a drug can fully restore the structure and function of aging LSECs, including their ability to support the clearance of substances from the bloodstream.

It is also the first to show that a treatment directed at the liver can bring age-related elevations in circulating amyloid beta and LDL back to youthful levels.

These findings raise the possibility that cinaciguat, similar medications, or treatments targeting HB-EGF could eventually be used to counteract certain effects of liver aging. If those changes translate into meaningful protection against disease, they could provide new strategies for preventing Alzheimer's and cardiovascular problems.

For now, however, the findings represent an early step. Lowering amyloid beta in the bloodstream does not necessarily mean that amyloid plaques in the brain will decrease or that Alzheimer's disease can be prevented.

The researchers plan to continue studying cinaciguat in rats to determine whether its effects on amyloid beta actually translate into measurable protection against Alzheimer's disease.

They also hope the findings will encourage scientists studying other conditions, particularly atherosclerosis, to investigate how restoring liver function might influence disease development.

"We hope that people who are in fields like atherosclerosis research read this, and want to grab the idea for themselves," Sam de Leve said. "There are six different ways someone could go with this, and we can't do them all. So please, scoop us. We'd love it."

Additional researchers involved in the study include Xiangdong Wang, Helia Alavifard and Lily Dara, all affiliated with the Keck School of Medicine of USC.

The research received federal funding from the National Institutes of Health [R56AG071480, 5R01DK100580].

#5722. Ibuprofen and Kidney Injury: Study Reveals Who Is Most at Risk

— Higher AKI risk seen only in certain patients

Use of ibuprofen was associated with higher rates of acute kidney injury (AKI) among hospitalized adults, but the excess risk was concentrated almost entirely in certain patients, according to a retrospective active-comparator cohort study.

Compared with patients given oxycodone for acute pain, those who received at least 24 hours of ibuprofen had higher adjusted rates of the following:

The heightened risk was driven primarily by high-risk populations: postoperative patients (IRR 1.70, 95% CI 1.28-2.27) and critically ill patients in the intensive care unit (IRR 1.65, 95% CI 1.29-2.11), reported Todd Miano, PharmD, PhD, of the Perelman School of Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia, and colleagues.

In contrast, patients deemed low risk -- those younger than 60, not critically ill, not recovering from surgery, and with preserved baseline kidney function (estimated glomerular filtration rate >60 mL/min/1.73 m²) -- had no elevated AKI risk associated with ibuprofen use (IRR 0.94, 95% CI 0.75-1.18).

These findings "suggest that there may be a subset of patients who can safely be treated with NSAIDs [nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs], such as younger patients with preserved kidney function who are not critically ill and are not postoperative," the authors wrote in JAMA Network Open.

However, current hospital practice did not appear to reflect that distinction. Even among low-risk patients in the study, 87% were prescribed oxycodone over ibuprofen.

"NSAIDs cause nephrotoxic effects, primarily through vasoconstriction of afferent arterioles in the glomerulus, which can reduce kidney blood flow, leading to ischemic AKI in vulnerable patients," Miano and team explained. "Most evidence regarding NSAID-AKI risk comes from outpatient settings, where patients often use NSAIDs for extended durations. In contrast, hospitalized patients typically receive NSAIDs for at most a few days."

While low-risk patients may safely tolerate ibuprofen, they "are often prescribed oxycodone," which carries an "extensive adverse-effect profile" and risks long-term dependence, the authors emphasized. "Thus, our analysis suggests that outcomes might be improved with enhanced risk stratification and individualized analgesic prescribing that effectively identifies patients at low risk of NSAID-associated AKI."

For this study, the researchers reviewed records for 78,656 hospitalized adults admitted to three Philadelphia hospitals within the University of Pennsylvania Health System from January 2004 through June 2017. Patients with end-stage kidney disease, baseline serum creatinine over 2.0 mg/dL, recent unresolved AKI, or other contraindications were excluded. Median patient age was 59, 48% were women, 59% were white, and 31% were Black.

Overall, 72,343 patients received oxycodone and 6,313 received ibuprofen. In the unweighted raw data, inpatients given ibuprofen were younger (median age 52 vs 59 years), had fewer comorbidities, and had a lower crude AKI rate (5.1% vs 6.2%) than those given oxycodone. Median follow-up was 3.0 days.

Over 270,472 days of patient follow-up, 4,799 AKI events occurred (17.7 events per 1,000 days). AKI was defined by changes in serum creatinine and initiation of KRT according to Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) criteria and staged over 7 days after onset. Most AKI events were stage 1 (79%), 15% were stage 2, and 6% were stage 3.

In a post-hoc subgroup analysis, the IRR of AKI was 1.48 (95% CI 1.18-1.86) among patients with concomitant nephrotoxin exposure and 1.15 for those without such exposure (95% CI 1.00-1.32).

The authors noted that prescribing decisions cannot hinge on nephrotoxicity alone. "While our analysis was focused on kidney outcomes, other NSAID-mediated adverse effects (e.g., bleeding) also inform prescribing decisions," they wrote. "Research evaluating the broader comparative safety of these classes is needed to optimize inpatient analgesia."

Patients who received both ibuprofen and oxycodone on the index date were excluded, which may limit generalizability to those treated with both drugs.
