#5692. Red Hat accelerates agentic adoption across hybrid environments

Enterprise ambitions for artificial intelligence are outpacing the infrastructure and budgets needed to support them. Red Hat AI faces a familiar enterprise challenge: turning ambitious plans for artificial intelligence into production deployments that deliver measurable returns.

Organizations must also decide how to deploy and manage increasingly complex AI workloads across existing infrastructure without letting costs spiral. At Red Hat Summit 2026 in May, Red Hat Inc. outlined its approach to those challenges through expanded platform capabilities, automation and an open-source development process that relies on community contributions.

“I think everybody here loves that because that does lead to sovereignty as well,” said Rob Strechay, principal analyst at theCUBE, during the event. “They’re actually building on top of open source and enhancing it in a way that provides more value in supporting it, which is key to their success.”

This feature is part of SiliconANGLE Media’s ongoing coverage of the AWS Financial Services Symposium. (* Disclosure below.)

Deploying and managing AI workloads across hybrid cloud environments presents new operational challenges for enterprises. Red Hat’s answer is Red Hat AI 3.4, an updated version of its enterprise AI platform that supports agentic AI deployments and large-scale inference across hybrid environments.

The company also announced two new managed services: Red Hat AI Inference and Red Hat OpenShift Virtualization Service on IBM Cloud. Red Hat AI Inference is designed to integrate real-time AI inference directly into clients’ production workflows, while OpenShift Virtualization enables clients to migrate and run virtual machines at scale. Both services are intended to accelerate hybrid cloud adoption.

“What’s really going to drive inference demand exponentially is AI agents,” said Joe Fernandes, vice president and general manager of Red Hat AI. “We provide a platform where customers can deploy and manage their AI agents across a hybrid infrastructure environment.”

The next piece of Red Hat’s agentic strategy comes in the form of Ansible Automation Platform 2.7, which connects AI-generated insights to governed infrastructure actions. Its self-service automation capabilities allow authorized users in locations such as branch offices and factory floors to manage servers and networks within established controls.

“Customers are now able to use their own data to calculate savings and efficiencies,” said Sathish Balakrishnan, vice president and general manager of Red Hat’s Ansible business unit. “Every action, whether it’s triggered by humans, an event or an AI agent, passes through the same [access controls], approval gates, audit trails, content signing and credential management.”

AI budgets are booming: according to theCUBE Research, Analysts project that AI cloud spending could approach $2.5 trillion by 2026, growing at roughly 44% year-over-year. However, that investment does not always return concrete value. Research shows that 50.7% of organizations rely on public AI tools such as ChatGPT and Copilot but only 20.2% report enterprise-wide AI deployments built on a governed framework.

“Most people are token consumers and that is part of the reason they’re trying to figure out how do they get to production,” Strechay said. “How do they get out of these death-by-pilot situations and become token producers so that they can offset the cost or at least lower the cost so they can get to the [return on AI investment] of those applications? You can use [OpenShift] infrastructure along with things like vLLM and some of the other things in Red Hat AI to get and become efficient in how you produce your tokens.”

Part of Red Hat’s strategy for helping customers manage sprawling AI budgets is its partnership with Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. Together, AMD and Red Hat are encouraging enterprises to rethink the financials of AI. Rather than opting for the newest, most expensive hardware, clients might have better results if matching compute resources to the workload, according to John Hampton, corporate vice president of global enterprise technical sales at AMD.

“So many of these enterprises just ran out and bought big [graphics processing unit] clusters because they knew they had to solve for AI,” he said. “Enterprises are coming to us and saying, ‘This is exploding. It’s good that we’re using AI, but we can’t afford this anymore.’”

Red Hat has also joined forces with Intel Corp. to help customers determine which combination of hardware and software best suits their workloads. As enterprises look to reduce inference costs, the companies are emphasizing the value of choosing the right mix of CPUs and GPUs rather than relying on a single approach.

“As we’ve gone through this with our customers in the industry, we’ve seen that people often have just assumed, ‘I’ve got a hammer. I need the nail to hit it with,’” said Bill Pearson, vice president of data center and AI at Intel. “Once they take a step back to say, ‘Wait a minute. I have these [central processing units] in my data center’ or ‘I need to figure out how to balance the right number of CPUs with the right number of GPUs to achieve that outcome I’m looking for,’ they’re actually going to get better results at a better price point for delivering lower-cost tokens.”

Red Hat announced several collaborations at the summit, including Red Hat AI Factory with Nvidia Corp. The partnership includes support for Nvidia’s Blackwell architecture and upcoming Vera Rubin platform, as well as participation in Nvidia’s OpenShell project for AI agent sandboxing and secure execution.

“Moving AI from corporate experimentation to an industrial engine requires a sovereign, consistent foundation across the hybrid cloud,” said Chris Wright, chief technology officer and senior vice president for global engineering at Red Hat, in the announcement. “Through our strategic co-engineering efforts with Nvidia, Red Hat provides the architectural control and open source innovation enterprises need to scale agentic AI with confidence.”

Red Hat’s other partnership announcements focused on agentic AI and edge computing. Boomi LP, which brands itself as a data activation company, is collaborating with Red Hat on a single, integrated stack for deploying agentic AI at scale. The partnerships with Panasonic Connect and Voyager cover edge computing solutions and space edge micro data centers, respectively.

Red Hat’s expanding ecosystem of partnerships reflects the growing range of enterprise applications for agentic AI. The challenge for organizations is determining how those capabilities can address their specific business needs, according to Matt Hicks, president and chief executive officer of Red Hat.

“From the board level down … you have a feeling of, ‘We have to be able to harness what this technology can do,’” said Matt Hicks. “The people that will be the most successful with AI are the people that have the most questions. People that know business, they know their domain. Those are the ones [that] have no barriers to what they can do and change. It’s just about getting started.”

Sovereign AI has become an increasingly important consideration for enterprises seeking greater control over their data and infrastructure. Gartner Inc. forecasts that the sovereign cloud infrastructure-as-a-service market will grow at a compound annual rate of 36% through 2028.

Red Hat is expanding support for sovereign cloud while allowing customers to keep the infrastructure they already invested in. That includes collaborations with Core42, which specializes in sovereign-by-design infrastructure, and Sopra Steria, a longstanding European collaborator on sovereign AI initiatives.

Red Hat is also extending its software security capabilities as enterprises adopt agentic AI. Fedora Hummingbird Linux is a container-native operating system designed for agent-first development, with an automated software delivery pipeline. Meanwhile, Red Hat Hardened Images provides a catalog of minimal container images designed to reduce vulnerabilities and strengthen software supply-chain security.

At this point, sovereign AI and governance play an essential role in giving customers choice and control, according to Ashesh Badani, senior vice president and chief product officer of Red Hat.

“Whether an organization is meeting jurisdictional mandates or reclaiming its data from proprietary silos, we are providing the capabilities and platforms to build a more self-determined future,” he said in a Red Hat press release.

#5691. Newly elected doctors and scientists hope to restore trust in science. It won’t be easy

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Nicholas Florko covers trust in science for STAT, aiming to help readers understand the lived experiences of people who distrust science and to probe why that distrust exists and its consequences. Reach him on Signal at nickflorko.44

Last week, doctors and scientists across the country persuaded Americans to vote them into office. Now comes the hard part: Convincing those who didn’t trust them to believe in their mission.

Doctors and public health officials ran pro-vaccine, pro-science campaigns and won over voters even in traditionally conservative areas. Candidates endorsed by the organization 314 Action, which works to elect Democratic doctors and scientists, flipped 10 congressional seats in last week’s election.

“What we saw in the results is that when these scientists really leaned into their scientific and medical backgrounds, that only provided their potential constituents with more trust,” said Shaughnessy Naughton, the founder of 314 Action. “They are looked at as truth tellers and that really is what people want.”

But the midterm results also clearly demonstrate that Americans remain deeply divided on core scientific issues, with some communities remaining distrustful of the cornerstones of public health policy.

South Carolina elected a pediatrician, Annie Andrews, as the first Democrat to represent the state in the Senate since 2005, but it also voted for 18 officials who publicly pledged to remove Covid vaccines from the market, according to the anti-vaccine advocacy group Americans for Health Freedom.

Across the nation, more than 120 lawmakers publicly opposed to Covid shots were elected to office, according to Americans for Health Freedom. Anti-vaccine sentiment in statehouses has the potential to reshape vaccine policy. Last year, several states passed into law bills that vaccine advocates say would curb vaccine distribution and uptake.

On a statewide level, not all elections went pro-science either. While much attention has been paid to Ohio’s decision to elect Democrat Amy Acton, who led the state’s Covid response, as its next governor, Florida’s next governor will be Byron Donalds, who has said removing all state vaccine requirements would be a “step in the right direction.” Donalds’ challenger, David Jolly, publicly pledged to “bring back science, data, math, vaccines, and public health.”

Brian Castrucci, a Republican who leads the de Beaumont Foundation, which promotes public health, told STAT newly elected public health experts must now answer the question: Why should I trust you?

“We can answer that question, but it’s not going to be by telling people they’re wrong,” Castrucci said.

The newly elected class of doctors and scientists seem particularly well suited to make the case for why their advice on topics like infectious disease should be heeded, several public health experts said. Andrews, for example, has taken to social media to encourage vaccination and has encouraged other doctors to do the same. Castrucci called El-Sayed “one of the best communicators I have ever met in my career .”

“Having leaders who can really communicate how devastating these policies have been and the consequences, I think, is really, really helpful,” said Jeanne Marrazzo, CEO of the Infectious Disease Society of America.

Abdul El-Sayed, a Democrat who will represent Michigan in the Senate, has written about the need to improve communication with those who are skeptical of science. “Yelling ‘trust the science!’ at someone who’s afraid of vaccinating does little to allay their underlying fear. Rather, it gives them more reason not to trust  — you, the vaccine, ‘the science,’” he wrote in a column for the Detroit Metro Times in 2024.

In an interview with STAT Wednesday, he argued that “the root cause of the distrust in public health has less to do with distrust in science and a lot more to do with distrust with greed.”

El-Sayed said he hopes to build trust through his efforts to “reinvigorate a movement for public health that is willing to stand up to the power of big corporations,” and to “show the grifters for who they are.”

El-Sayed has made no secret of his desire to use his new power to investigate the actions of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., telling STAT prior to the election that he is eager to “grill” the secretary.

Democrat Richard Pan, a physician elected to represent Sacramento County, Calif., in the House of Representatives, told STAT that while building back trust is going to be difficult, the first step is to “expose the corruption and bad decision-making” of the current administration.

“This administration and RFK Jr. and the people who he has appointed … have all undermined the idea that you can actually trust the federal government,” he said.

Following the election, several Democratic lawmakers, including Patty Murray, vice chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, renewed calls for Kennedy to step down or be fired. A number of Democratic lawmakers have been calling for Kennedy’s ouster for more than a year, citing a lack of confidence in his ability to “carry out the duties of his office.”

Democrats hope gaining the power to subpoena Trump administration officials will allow them to make headway on the investigations they launched when they were in the minority.

“We’ve not even really been able to get information out of RFK and the department,” Rep. Lauren Underwood (D-Ill.), co-chair of the House Democratic Policy and Communications Committee, told STAT. The Democratic majority in Congress means “we’re going to be able to do really vigorous oversight, help people understand how we are fighting for them, and then giving them accurate information,” she added.

While much of the work of congressional investigations occurs behind closed doors through document requests, subpoenas, and sworn depositions, it could also mean Kennedy is brought before congressional committees now under Democratic control, to answer for various policy decisions under oath. Some lawmakers are indicating he will be a frequent guest on Capitol Hill.

“Unless RFK Jr. is interested in spending the next two years in front of Congressional committees, he should go ahead and resign now,” Sen. Raphael Warnock (D-Ga.) tweeted after the election. Andrews has called Kennedy her “professional archnemesis for decades.”

El-Sayed acknowledged Wednesday that perhaps too much focus is on Kennedy himself, rather than his decisions. “Any investigation that we’re doing is about trying to correct the problems and address the flaws and the faults, rather than trying to achieve any sort of retribution,” El-Sayed said.

Several other Democratic lawmakers agreed that their intention in the next Congress will not be to weaponize or politicize science, but to restore faith in the existing system.

“Democrats will work to restore our scientific infrastructure and integrity and end this administration’s politicization of science,” Sen. Mark Warner (D-Va.) said in a statement. There is also hope among some Democrats that these inquiries can be bipartisan. Republicans are “not all happy with what’s happened to the science programs,” said Zoe Lofgren (D-Calif.), who wants to lead the House Science Committee.

Still, there could be risks in aggressively investigating Kennedy. Research suggests that  political fights over vaccines can be a net negative for vaccine acceptance. A 2015 paper found that statehouse debates over the HPV vaccine, for example, resulted in “decreases in support for HPV vaccine requirements, state immunization programs, and confidence in doctors and in government.”

It’s an open question whether engaging in a political debate with Kennedy will serve to  deepen skepticism of public health measures, or whether polarization over vaccines has already hit a ceiling, said Sarah Gollust, a professor at the University of Minnesota School of Public Health.

“I’m not sure it can get worse in terms of how politically charged the vaccine issue has been since Covid-19,” said Gollust, one of the 2015 paper’s authors. “We’ve never been here before. We are in very new territory.”

When asked about this potential risk, Pan downplayed the number of ardent Kennedy supporters who currently exist and would be further emboldened by Democrats’ fights with the HHS secretary. “There’s only a very small number of people who really believe in RFK Jr.,” Pan said.

Exactly how true that is remains up for debate. Several candidates endorsed by Kennedy’s MAHA movement did lose elections last week. And Kennedy’s views on vaccines are not always top of mind, even for self-described MAHA movement followers. An April 2026 survey of self-described MAHA voters found that just 10 percent identified re-evaluating vaccine safety as their top priority.

Nevertheless the number of parents opting their children out of vaccines continues to grow across the country. Data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention indicate that vaccine exemptions grew in 41 states and the District of Columbia between the 2024 and 2025 school years.

Even if Democrats can convince a sizable group of Republicans to trust their vaccine advice over Kennedy’s, a small and growing number of vaccine skeptics can cause public health havoc.

Though Andrews was able to convince more than 1 million South Carolinians to support her pro-science message, it was a relatively small group of vaccine skeptics in Spartanburg County, in the northwestern corner of the state, that prompted the state’s 2025 measles outbreak, which at the time was the largest in the United States since measles was formally eliminated in 2000. (Pennsylvania’s current outbreak has since topped South Carolina’s record, with more than 1,500 cases.)

There are some signs that pro-vaccine messages are beginning to resonate in these communities. Andrews’ message of impeaching RFK received an ovation in Spartanburg County during the campaign, and she did perform better there than Democratic candidates of the past. But as of now, the region still has a vaccination rate low enough that it is vulnerable to continued resurgences of measles.

As Andrews acknowledged in an op-ed during the campaign: “Trust doesn’t snap back like a rubber band. It takes years to build and minutes to burn.”

CareSource launches $1M grant program to support AI-powered solutions" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Nonprofit insurer CareSource is launching a $1 million program that aims to back responsible AI solutions in healthcare.

The initiative, launched through the CareSource Foundation, is seeking proposals for ways to advance and identify deployments for AI that can drive better outcomes and address barriers for individuals enrolled in Medicaid or who otherwise struggle to access care.

The program will provide up to $1 million over the course of two years to ensure that the tool can deliver on meaningful and scalable benefits for the communities it serves.

Erhardt Preitauer, CEO of CareSource, said in an email to Fierce Healthcare that AI offers the potential to improve not just patient care but the experience for providers too as they navigate complex conditions.

"I'm a big believer that when technology, healthcare and the people in our communities rally around a shared purpose, magic can happen," said Preitauer. "Leaving no stone unturned is the only way we can make healthcare work better for people, and AI gives us the power to explore every possibility."

The program will include two phases. First, interested applicants can submit shorter proposals, with the goal of generating interest. Applications that are selected to move on will be tasked with submitting a more fleshed-out proposal, including details on implementation, AI governance and sustainability.

CareSource is aiming to identify solutions that are ready for implementation and has the potential for scale. Potential focus areas include care coordination, member engagement, behavioral health and rural healthcare. Solutions should use AI to support care delivery, but it should not replace human judgement or oversight, the insurer said.

To be eligible, a qualified nonprofit organization must be leading the effort, according to the announcement. Technology companies, academic researchers, healthcare organizations and community-based groups can also play a role as partners.

#5688. Scientists solve 30-year-old mystery and discover a hidden defense against inflammation

Scientists have solved a biological mystery that remained unanswered for more than three decades, uncovering an unexpected way the immune system protects the body from its own inflammatory response. The breakthrough reveals that a chemical signal responsible for attracting immune cells to fight infections also helps prevent those same defenses from damaging healthy tissue.

The discovery came from researchers at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSK), who took an unusual approach to studying inflammation. Rather than relying on mice, a standard choice for biomedical research, they turned to zebrafish. That decision helped them identify a long-mysterious enzyme and uncover a protective mechanism that had previously escaped scientists.

The findings, published October 7 in Nature, could advance research into cancer, inflammatory bowel disease, and asthma. They also raise the possibility of developing treatments that strengthen the body's natural defenses against inflammatory damage.

The mystery began in 1992, when researchers at McGill University investigated a molecule that helps direct immune cells toward sites of infection. Known as 5-oxoETE, or 5-oxo-6,8,11,14-eicosatetraenoic acid, this fatty signaling molecule acts as a chemical alert when the body needs to respond to a threat.

At the time, scientists observed an enzyme that could both produce and break down 5-oxoETE. Enzymes are proteins that help chemical reactions take place, but in this case, researchers could not identify the human gene responsible for making the enzyme.

That missing genetic information created a major obstacle. Without knowing which gene produced the enzyme, scientists could not easily manipulate it in experiments or determine how problems with its activity might contribute to disease. Researchers assigned the enzyme a descriptive name based on its chemical function, but its genetic identity remained unknown for more than 30 years.

The breakthrough finally came through the work of Yanan Ma, PhD, a postdoctoral researcher at MSK's Sloan Kettering Institute. Building on earlier investigations by former lab colleague King Lam Hui, PhD, Ma identified the human gene that produces the enzyme, giving researchers a way to examine its function much more closely.

How the Immune System Can Damage Healthy Cells

Ma works in the laboratory of cell biologist Philipp Niethammer, PhD, whose research examines how cells respond to injuries, infections, and other forms of stress. His team focuses on inflammation, tissue repair, and regeneration, biological processes that also play important roles in cancer and numerous other diseases.

When harmful bacteria enter the body, chemical signals help recruit specialized white blood cells to the affected area. One of those signals is 5-oxoETE, which attracts immune cells equipped to attack invading microorganisms.

Although this response is essential for fighting infections, it carries risks. The substances immune cells release to destroy pathogens can also injure surrounding healthy tissue.

"They flood the site with toxic substances to kill the bacteria," Dr. Niethammer says. "But this can cause damage to healthy cells if it gets out of control."

Niethammer's laboratory had already spent years investigating the molecular reactions involved in 5-oxoETE signaling. Researchers were gradually identifying how the different components of the system worked together, but the unknown enzyme remained a major missing piece.

Why Zebrafish Succeeded Where Mice Could Not

Most biomedical experiments involving animals use mice or rats because their biological systems share many similarities with humans. However, these familiar laboratory animals had a significant limitation for the question Ma and her colleagues wanted to answer.

"Mice and rats are the primary model used in biomedical research," says Dr. Ma, who received a prestigious Marie-Josée Kravis WISE Fellowship in 2023 for her work on the pathway. "It makes sense -- they're mammals, and there's about an 80% overlap between their genes and ours."

Despite those similarities, mice lack a known immune cell receptor capable of recognizing 5-oxoETE. Without that receptor, researchers cannot investigate the complete signaling process in mice.

Zebrafish, however, have retained the necessary biological machinery.

"This means that you can't study the pathway in mice," Dr. Ma says. "But the pathway is intact in fish. So picking the right alternative model was critical to advancing our understanding of how the human body responds."

Using zebrafish allowed the scientists to explore how the signal operates in a living organism and eventually helped reveal a function that had gone unnoticed for decades.

Scientists Finally Identify the Missing Enzyme

Before investigating the process in zebrafish, Ma and Hui began searching for the enzyme's genetic origins using cultured human cells.

They selected several genes that might be responsible and systematically switched them off, looking for changes in the enzyme's activity. One candidate produced a decisive result.

When Ma disabled a gene called DHRS7, the enzyme stopped functioning. The experiment established that DHRS7 was the gene researchers had been searching for since the early 1990s.

Additional tests involving the rodent version of the gene showed almost no enzyme activity. That result was consistent with the absence of the 5-oxoETE receptor in mice, suggesting that rodents had lost key functions associated with this signaling system.

Identifying DHRS7 resolved the long-standing mystery. It also connected Ma's research with a separate investigation underway in the same laboratory, led by postdoctoral researcher Miklos Lengyel, MD, PhD.

"Typically, when you have a paper with two first authors like Yanan and Miklos, there is just one story that two people contributed to equally," Dr. Niethammer says. "But this paper is not like that. In this paper, there are two separate projects led by two different authors that came together as one larger discovery. And I think that's extremely important to note."

A Surprising Result Turns Expectations Upside Down

While Ma investigated the mysterious enzyme, Lengyel was using zebrafish to study colitis, an inflammatory condition affecting the colon. His experiments involved disabling selected genes to understand how they influenced intestinal inflammation.

One experiment produced an especially puzzling outcome.

Lengyel removed a gene called hcar1-4 (the zebrafish version of the human gene OXER1). This gene produces the receptor that recognizes 5-oxoETE and allows cells to respond to its signal.

Because 5-oxoETE helps attract immune cells and initiate inflammation, removing its receptor should theoretically weaken that response.

"So if you remove the receptor that detects the signal, you'd expect less inflammation, not more," Dr. Lengyel says.

Instead, the zebrafish developed intestinal inflammation on their own, even though no infection was present.

The researchers initially considered whether neutrophils, the white blood cells normally recruited by the signal, might be responsible. However, removing those immune cells did not eliminate the inflammation.

This unexpected behavior suggested that the 5-oxoETE pathway was doing something much more complicated than simply activating the immune system.

Disabling an Inflammatory Signal Makes Inflammation Worse

The connection between the two research projects became clear after Ma identified DHRS7 as the gene responsible for producing the enzyme involved in 5-oxoETE signaling.

Lengyel then disabled DHRS7 in zebrafish, preventing the production of the enzyme and disrupting the signaling process.

Based on the molecule's established role in attracting immune cells, the researchers expected inflammation to decrease. Instead, they observed the same surprising pattern seen when the receptor was removed: inflammation increased.

"It made absolutely no sense," Dr. Lengyel says. "I had to prove using several different methods before the rest of the lab was convinced."

The findings pointed to a previously unrecognized function. The signaling pathway did not simply help initiate the immune response. It also appeared to prevent unnecessary damage to healthy cells.

That dual responsibility explained why eliminating the pathway had such an unexpected effect. By disabling the system, scientists had removed not only an inflammatory signal but also an important source of cellular protection.

The Immune System's Hidden Protective Shield

Further experiments revealed how this protection works.

When immune cells attack dangerous microorganisms, they release highly reactive substances that can harm nearby healthy cells. The 5-oxoETE pathway helps tissues withstand this chemical stress, reducing the risk that the body's own defenses will cause unnecessary injury.

"This makes sense when you think about it," Dr. Niethammer says. "These immune cells unleash chemical warfare against a pathogen, and organisms have evolved an elegant way of protecting healthy cells at the same time."

The researchers found that zebrafish intestinal cells became particularly vulnerable when either 5-oxoETE or its Hcar1-4 receptor was missing. Even the normal bacteria living in the intestine produced enough low-level chemical stress to cause problems when this protective system was disabled.

The team traced the cellular protection to a group of enzymes known as NUDIX hydrolases. These enzymes help maintain cellular health by removing damaged DNA building blocks before they can interfere with normal biological processes.

Without the protective signaling pathway, intestinal cells could no longer withstand the chemical stress associated with ordinary gut bacteria. Some cells died, setting off an inflammatory response despite the absence of an invading pathogen.

The results revealed that the body uses the same molecular system both to call immune cells into action and to protect healthy tissue from the consequences.

"As it turns out, this signal isn't just an alarm, it's also a shield," Dr. Niethammer says.

Potential Implications for Cancer and Inflammatory Diseases

Understanding this protective mechanism could have important implications for diseases involving excessive or poorly controlled inflammation.

The 5-oxoETE signaling pathway is known to be disrupted in conditions such as cancer, inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), and asthma. By identifying its previously unknown protective role, researchers have gained a new perspective on how those disruptions might contribute to tissue damage.

In human cancers, mutations affecting DHRS7 and OXER1 (the human version of hcar1-4) have been identified in tumors of the gastrointestinal tract and uterus.

Research has also linked mutations that prevent OXER1 from functioning properly with poorer outcomes in patients with colorectal, pancreatic, and kidney cancers.

The findings suggest that strengthening the pathway might eventually help healthy tissues tolerate damaging conditions more effectively. One possible application involves protecting the intestine from oxidative stress associated with cancer treatment.

"More research is needed, but there's a possibility that activating the pathway could increase the resilience of the gut to oxidative stress -- which might help counteract damage caused by radiation therapy or chemotherapy," Dr. Lengyel says.

The discovery also has implications for diseases affecting mucosal tissues, the protective linings found in areas such as the intestines and respiratory tract.

In people with IBD, researchers have previously associated lower concentrations of 5-oxoETE in intestinal tissue with worse disease outcomes.

Evidence from asthma research points to another possible protective function. An independent study involving primates found that blocking OXER1 weakened the immune cell response but also caused protective mucus-producing cells in the airways to disappear.

Together, these observations suggest that attempts to suppress inflammation must account for the protective roles certain inflammatory signals perform. However, further research will be necessary to determine whether targeting this pathway can produce safe and effective treatments in humans.

How Physical Injury Activates the Same Defense System

The researchers are also investigating how this signaling pathway responds to physical damage, not just infection or chemical stress.

That aspect of the work is being explored by doctoral student Zaza Gelashvili, MS, who studies how cells detect mechanical forces associated with tissue injury.

When cells experience physical stress, changes to their membranes can initiate the same chain of molecular reactions involved in inflammation.

One early step occurs when stressed cell membranes release arachidonic acid, a fatty molecule that serves as the starting material for producing 5-oxoETE.

Gelashvili, a co-author of the Nature study, led a separate investigation into the molecular signals associated with physical wounds. That research was published in Nature Communications earlier in 2026. His contributions were also recognized with the 2026 Chairman's Prize from the Gerstner Sloan Kettering Graduate School of Biomedical Sciences.

"There's a mechanical component to the pathway that's upstream of what Yanan and Miklos have been studying," explains Gelashvili, a co-author on the study who led a separate study on physical wound signals that was published in Nature Communications earlier this year; his work was also recognized with the 2026 Chairman's Prize from the Gerstner Sloan Kettering Graduate School of Biomedical Sciences. "You can think of it as the first step in a chain reaction: Physical stress unlocks the raw material, oxidative stress drives the conversion, and DHRS7 amplifies the signal."

The research suggests that the body combines information about different forms of cellular stress to coordinate its response. Physical damage can initiate the process, chemical stress can influence the conversion of signaling molecules, and DHRS7 helps strengthen the resulting signal.

Rather than operating as separate responses, these processes appear to work together to help the body recognize danger while limiting unnecessary harm to healthy cells.

"What we are really studying is a pathway that integrates two completely different kinds of stress -- mechanical and metabolic -- and converts them into a single, coordinated, protective response," Dr. Niethammer says.

Additional researchers contributing to the study were Yohannes Ambaw, Leehyeon Kim, Ritchie Ly, Siyang Peng, Meysoon Quraishi, Tobias Walther, and Robert Farese Jr., all affiliated with MSK.

Financial support came from the National Institutes of Health (R35GM140883); an MSK Basic Research Innovation Award; a Starr Foundation Program for Discovery Science grant; a Tow Foundation fellowship; a Marie-Josée Kravis Women in Science Endeavor (WISE) fellowship; a Crohn's Colitis Foundation Research Fellows Award (1268111); an Experimental Immuno-Oncology Scholars fellowship; and core facility services supported in part by MSK's National Cancer Institute Cancer Center Support grant (P30CA008748).

#5687. Opinion: I research MAHA and Black Americans. The relationship is complicated — and fascinating

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Ezell is an epidemiologist and assistant professor at the University of Chicago Medical Center.

When one thinks about the key supporters of MAHA, they likely don’t envision Black people, and rightfully so. A 2025 poll from KFF and The Washington Post found that only 30% of Black Americans support the MAHA movement, compared with 43% of white Americans.

But the data belie a stark reality: On an issue-to-issue basis, Black people are strikingly aligned with MAHA, at least in terms of their concerns around the movement’s tentpole issues. I’ve been studying why, or rather how, this came to be.

According to a May poll from Global Strategy Group, 47% of Black people, compared with 35% of white people, strongly agree with the statements “I am concerned about environmental toxins and pesticides” and “I am concerned about ultra-processed foods and artificial ingredients in our food” — key MAHA flashpoints.

The same poll found that 51% of Black people, a staunch Democratic voting bloc, either strongly or somewhat agreed with the statement “I am skeptical of vaccines,” compared to 58% of Republicans and 28% of Democrats. Moreover, the poll found that 26% of Black people strongly or somewhat support eliminating fluoride from public drinking water, a not-so-secret desire of health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. This figure nearly mirrors the 28% of Republicans who also want the additive nixed from our water supply, while

This crossover makes some sense. MAHA is perhaps the sole part of the Trump administration’s sprawling attempt to remake American society that can be said to be, at least on the surface, apolitical. Its broad agenda amplifies everyday public health issues like food quality and safety while elevating thorny but universally relevant topics like Big Pharma’s role in the overmedicalization of Americans.

This explains why a number of people on the left who would seem to be politically opposed to MAHA sometimes begrudgingly, and sometimes warmly, endorse it. In recent months, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), who appears to have 2028 ambitions, has glowingly discussed her conversations with MAHA activists and characterizes the MAHA cause as nonpartisan. Uber-progressive physician and Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed actively campaigned on some of MAHA’s hallmark principles.

Many in clinical medicine have also come out in support of MAHA, or at least components of it. In The Atlantic, emergency physician Craig Spencer encouraged public health practitioners to swallow their pride in service of the lightning-in-a-bottle moment for reform that MAHA was serving up, aligning with a number of respected public health influencers who’ve encouraged the same kind of acquiescence.

To some, including me, this sudden embrace of MAHA and pandering to the movement’s voters looks like acute Stockholm syndrome. And that’s largely because its intentions are often assumed a priori to be politically neutral, and its origins are rarely questioned.

A January tweet from California Gov. Gavin Newsom’s press office noted that “MAHA started in California,” highlighting the likely 2028 Democratic presidential contender’s statewide ban on ultra-processed foods in 2025. In early October, Democrat Rep. Chellie Pingree (Maine), who made MAHA a centerpiece of her successful reelection campaign, tweeted that she’d “been fighting for a food system that puts people and farmers first long before the ‘MAHA movement.’”

But Black scholars and activists played the biggest role in bringing to light the systemic fissures in our health care and food systems that MAHA — and some left-leaning opportunists — now assume a gatekeeper role over.

Throughout the 1960s and 1970s, Black activists around the country began to lead coordinated efforts to address the harms caused by industrial pollution in the U.S. and tackle the industrialization of the food system.

In 1969, Fannie Lou Hamer, a Black organizer, pioneered land cooperatives in Mississippi to usher in food sovereignty, aiming to curb her Black contemporaries’ increasing reliance on large, sprawling food production systems. Hamer foresaw what would become a reality in the 21st century: a loss of community control over food production and the proliferation of ultra-processed, unhealthy foodstuffs, a talking point deeply embedded in Kennedy Jr.’s Eat Real Food initiative.

In 1978, Black residents in Warren County, N.C., began organizing to protest a landfill that was poised to store some 60,000 tons of cancer-causing PCBs (polychlorinated biphenyls) in their rural, low-income community. Over the next several years, as legal motions to stop the state government-endorsed plan were quashed, hundreds of Black demonstrators would be arrested in nonviolent protests against the site. It wasn’t until two decades later that the protesters’ persistence would pay off: An $18 million site detoxification process was initiated in 2002 and completed in 2004.

It’s evident Kennedy, a trained environmental lawyer, learned a great deal from cases like these. When running as a presidential candidate in 2024, Kennedy made several direct appeals for addressing environmental injustice, the racially inequitable distribution of environmental harms in minority communities. For instance, during a visit to Loyola Marymount College while on the campaign trail, Kennedy discussed the legacy of polluting facilities and noted, “We’ll have a cleaner environment if rich people and white people have to bear the equal burdens for people who are poor among the minorities.”

This was a racial justice battle cry, virtually right out of “Dumping in Dixie,” a seminal environmental justice text authored by the godfather of the movement, Robert Bullard.

This past “woke” iteration of Kennedy is deeply at odds with the present version, considering the term “environmental justice” is now essentially forbidden in research grant applications submitted to the National Institutes of Health, and that the NIH has substantially curbed funding for studies focused on racial disparities.

Ultimately, MAHA’s template is a retread, warmed over and confusedly repackaged for the anti-science and contrarian crowd keen on bringing the culture wars as deep as possible into public health.

To this end, Kennedy’s subtle homages to Black activism have been undercut by his public commentary and policy, which in addition to distorting and cherry-picking aspects of evidence-based science, is imbued with MAGA’s distinctive brand of political grievance and racial myopia.

Even as Kennedy and his MAHA consorts have cribbed from the Black activist playbook, they’ve actively undermined and misrepresented Black identity and culture. Part of this has been accomplished by playing into the fears that many Black people harbor against doctors and the medical establishment, including by using disinformation to gin up concerns about vaccines in Black communities, a population already highly skeptical of immunizations. Going back to the Tuskegee experiments, where Black men’s treatment for their syphilis was withheld, Black populations have held significant distrust for clinicians and medical research.

In a Kennedy-produced documentary, “Medical Racism: The New Apartheid,” a piece of unabashed agitprop released in 2021, the current health secretary recruited Nation of Islam Minister Tony Muhammad to help peddle the fantastical claim that vaccine-makers are nefariously targeting Black kids as a means of widening racial disparities.

And this tactic isn’t new. Republicans and anti-abortion activists have long sought to curry the support of Black people by claiming abortion is a subversive tool being used by white liberals and medical elites to facilitate Black genocide.

On a podcast before the 2024 election, Kennedy argued that Black people have a stronger immune response to certain antigens than other races, thereby warranting a change in their vaccine scheduling, a scientifically debunked notion that he nevertheless doubled down on during his Senate confirmation hearing.

He has also been a vocal cheerleader for a controversial study to assess the effects of hepatitis B vaccine dose timing on a cohort of infants in the small West African country of Guinea-Bissau, where local officials recently raided the offices of an RFK-Jr.-allied research group supporting the study.

The most positive reflections on MAHA have largely centered around the trope of the genteel “MAHA mom,” a racially coded term painting white mothers as singularly focused, doting caregivers who just want their kids to be healthy. Contrast this with Kennedy’s thoughts on Black parents. In a 2024 podcast, he advocated “reparenting” Black kids with ADHD, a population he said was “just standard put on Adderall, SSRIs, benzos, which are known to induce violence.”

It’s no surprise that prominent Black politicians haven’t accepted the Faustian bargain that MAHA represents and rallied around MAHA as their white peers have. Kennedy’s vision of and prescription for Black America is antiquated and dangerous. The spoils MAHA may otherwise offer — if we’re willing to whitewash its ethos — are no consolation.

With the midterms serving up a colossal defeat for MAGA, it stands to reason that MAHA’s day of reckoning may not be too far off. Calls for RFK. Jr’s impeachment are already bubbling among Democratic party leaders, a group that no longer needs to actively curry favor with MAHA proponents.

Only time will tell if the movement and its baggage can thrive without a titanic political force like MAGA behind it. Public health will be better off if it doesn’t.

Jerel Ezell is an epidemiologist and assistant professor at the University of Chicago Medical Center.

Carelon agrees to pay $10M to settle ghost network, coverage denial allegations in New York" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Carelon will pay more than $10 million across two settlements in New York over mental health networks and coverage denials.

The company, a division of Elevance Health, will pay $2.35 million in penalties, fees and costs as well as up to $8 million in restitution for members who paid out-of-pocket for out-of-network mental healthcare, to reimburse those whose claims were improperly denied or to overhaul its networks.

New York Attorney General Letitia James said in an announcement that the settlements resolve two investigations from her office that determined the company misled members by directing them to seek care from providers that were out-of-network—through so-called "ghost networks"—and improperly denied coverage for treatment for substance abuse disorder.

James noted that Carelon administers behavioral health benefits for multiple plans, including Anthem Blue Cross, EmblemHealth, Independent Health and the Empire Plan, which covers state and local government workers.

Across these insurers, Carelon manages behavioral health benefits for more than 4 million people in the state, James said.

The alleged behavior also goes against a 2015 agreement with the AG's office, where the company agreed that it would maintain accurate provider networks and "use approved criteria" when denying substance abuse treatments.

"When someone is ready to seek help for a mental health condition or addiction, every day matters," said James. “Carelon left New Yorkers calling provider after provider who could not see them and made it harder for people to get the treatment to which they were entitled."

"These settlements will help people get the care they need and put money back in New Yorkers’ pockets," she said.

Elevance Health said in a statement to Fierce Healthcare that it is committed to ensuring patients have access to the most up-to-date provider information.

"Carelon Behavioral Health is committed to helping people find and access high-quality mental health and substance use disorder care. Accurate, up-to-date provider information is an important part of that effort," the company said. "We continue to invest in tools and processes that support accurate provider information and work closely with providers and other partners to help connect consumers with the care they need."

Carelon was hit with a lawsuit in April over the alleged ghost networks and their impact on the Empire Plan in particular. In the case, plaintiff's attorneys conducted secret shopper calls to analyze Carelon's network, calling 300 providers. Just 17% of those contacted took insurance and were open to new patients.

These "ghost networks" have also drawn concern in other markets, such as for maternal care services in Medicaid and in Medicare Advantage. A study released last month found that commercial plans also routinely have inaccurate provider directories.

#5685. Scientists discover mysterious “lonely” brain waves linked to memory loss

You walk out of the grocery store, ready to head home and make dinner. But as you scan the crowded parking lot, a frustrating question comes to mind. Where did you leave your car? You try to picture the spot, but the memory refuses to surface.

Remembering personal experiences like these depends on episodic memory, which allows us to recall events from our lives. These memories help form the foundation of long-term memory, whether they involve a childhood milestone, such as the first day of elementary school, or something that happened just minutes earlier, like parking your car.

This ability tends to weaken as we grow older. The sights, sounds, and other details associated with past experiences can become increasingly difficult to retrieve. Scientists still do not fully understand why this happens. Although some memory decline is a common part of aging, the changes can become far more severe in people developing Alzheimer's disease.

A new study from researchers at the University of California, Berkeley, offers important clues about what may be happening inside the aging brain. Neuroscientist Omer Sharon and his colleagues, working under the direction of former Berkeley sleep researcher Matthew Walker, discovered a connection between disrupted brain waves during deep sleep, declining memory performance, and the accumulation of tau, a protein associated with Alzheimer's disease.

The findings suggest that tau buildup in the brain's frontal cortex is linked to changes in the coordinated electrical activity that helps preserve memories overnight.

"This is the first time we've shown this relationship between tau and how it messes with memory consolidation by attenuating traveling slow waves that originate in the frontal cortex," said Sharon, a postdoctoral researcher at UC Berkeley's Center for Human Sleep Science.

The research was published in Nature Neuroscience.

How Deep Sleep Helps the Brain Store Memories

Sleep involves several distinct stages, each associated with different patterns of brain activity. Rapid eye movement sleep is particularly recognizable because the eyes move beneath closed eyelids and most dreaming takes place during this stage. However, another stage, known as non-REM sleep, is especially important for maintaining healthy brain function.

During this deeper stage of sleep, when dreaming is limited or absent, large groups of neurons briefly become inactive and then active again in a coordinated sequence. These synchronized changes produce slow electrical waves that spread across the brain, typically beginning in the frontal cortex.

"Each slow wave reflects an enormous population of neurons switching off and back on together," Sharon said. "Our study shows that for memory, it's critical that these events cascade in sequence across large parts of the brain. This coordinated shutdown has been observed only during deep sleep, and may be one reason why we sleep."

The researchers found that this carefully organized activity becomes less coordinated as tau accumulates in the aging brain. Instead of traveling together across broad regions, the waves become more scattered and cover shorter distances. These changes are associated with weaker memory consolidation, declining cognitive abilities, and Alzheimer's disease.

Alzheimer's Protein Linked to Disrupted Brain Waves

To investigate the relationship, the scientists monitored sleeping brain activity using electroencephalograms (EEGs). They compared cognitively healthy young adults in their early 20s with older participants ranging from their mid-60s to mid-70s.

The differences were striking. In younger participants, groups of slow waves moved together across distances roughly equivalent to the width of a hand on the scalp. Among older adults, the waves typically traveled less far and appeared more independently, rather than moving in coordinated groups.

The team also examined whether these changes were associated with tau accumulation. Working with Dr. William Jagust, a UC Berkeley professor emeritus of public health and neuroscience, the researchers used positron emission tomography (PET) scans to examine the brains of older participants. This imaging technique uses radioactive tracers introduced into the bloodstream to reveal biological activity and the distribution of specific substances.

The scans showed that greater tau buildup in the frontal cortex was associated with a breakdown in the longer traveling waves normally seen during deep sleep.

Importantly, these changes were present in people who had not developed Alzheimer's disease.

"These people did not have Alzheimer's," Sharon said. "They had tau in their brains, but with subclinical impacts. Their memory decline was within the normal range for their age."

Sharon explained that early Alzheimer's related changes can vary considerably in severity. The amount of tau present in the brain is associated with cognitive performance, even when a person's memory abilities remain within the expected range for their age.

Mysterious "Lonely Waves" Linked to Memory Loss

The researchers wanted to determine whether the altered sleep patterns were associated with actual differences in how well people remembered information.

To test this, participants learned pairs of associated words in the evening. The following day, they were asked to recall what they had learned, allowing the scientists to evaluate how effectively the memories had been retained overnight.

Participants whose slow brain waves traveled shorter distances and appeared more isolated generally remembered fewer word associations. The researchers called these disconnected patterns "lonely waves."

The team also tracked a subset of participants over several years to see how their brains changed with time. Among those whose frontal cortex tau levels increased, the slow waves became less coordinated, and their ability to retain newly learned information overnight declined.

These observations provide evidence of a relationship between tau accumulation, changes in deep sleep brain activity, and worsening episodic memory. However, they do not establish that tau buildup directly causes memory loss or that disrupted waves are the mechanism responsible.

Additional Tests Strengthen the Connection

Because PET scans are costly and require specialized facilities, the scientists sought another way to investigate the relationship between Alzheimer's related proteins and sleep activity.

They collaborated with neurologist Yo-El Ju at Washington University in St. Louis to analyze spinal fluid from a separate group of older adults. The goal was to determine whether measurements of Alzheimer's associated proteins would reveal patterns similar to those seen with brain imaging.

Unlike PET scans, the spinal fluid measurements could not identify tau accumulation specifically within the frontal cortex. Nevertheless, the results pointed in the same direction.

People whose sleeping brains produced more isolated slow waves had higher ratios of tau to amyloid, another protein closely associated with Alzheimer's disease, in their spinal fluid.

The consistency between these independent groups and testing methods strengthened the researchers' confidence in the findings.

"It's collected in a totally different place and in a different cohort, so I think that adds to the strength of the evidence," Sharon said.

Together, the sleep recordings, brain scans, spinal fluid analyses, and memory assessments suggest that tau accumulation is associated with a particular disruption of brain activity during deep sleep.

"This longitudinal correlation suggests that Alzheimer's disease pathology is associated with a disruption of this main sleep feature," Sharon said.

What Deep Sleep Reveals About the Aging Brain

Although memory often declines with age, the new research indicates that the process may involve more than simply growing older. Changes associated with Alzheimer's disease, particularly tau accumulation in regions responsible for generating widespread slow waves, may help explain why some people experience greater difficulty retaining memories.

"It's not just about age," Sharon said. "It's how much pathology you have in frontal areas where global waves originate."

Sleep quality also appears to be part of the picture. Although it can be difficult to define or measure precisely, the organization and movement of slow brain waves may provide important indicators of how effectively the brain performs its nighttime memory functions.

The findings raise the possibility that changes in deep sleep activity could eventually help researchers better understand or identify early memory problems. They also point toward potential targets for future treatments aimed at protecting memory as people age.

For now, however, a central question remains unanswered. Scientists still need to determine whether accumulating tau contributes to the breakdown of synchronized sleep waves, whether changes in those waves influence tau accumulation, or whether the relationship involves additional processes.

"We can see tau and lonely waves rising together over time," Sharon said. "What we cannot yet say is which leads -- and that question will shape how we design interventions."

The study's additional co-authors include Xi Chen, James Westphal, Chelsea Brown, and Vyoma D. Shah of UC Berkeley, along with Jason Dude of Washington University in St. Louis.

Funding came from grants awarded by the National Institute on Aging at the National Institutes of Health. Sharon also received support through a Glenn Foundation for Medical Research Postdoctoral Fellowship and a Weill Neurohub Fellowship.

#5684. Opinion: 3 things new governors must do to lead on health

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Cohen is former secretary of health and human services for North Carolina and former director of the CDC. Montz is former chief deputy at the Virginia Department of Medical Assistance Services and former deputy administrator and director at the Center for Consumer Information and Insurance Oversight at CMS.

As former state health leaders, we know the challenges and opportunities facing the 21 new governors stepping into their roles on Jan. 1. Health is what lets people go to work, raise their kids, and enjoy the years they’ve earned. Health is also the largest line item in most state budgets and a primary driver of the affordability crisis for American families.

To succeed in harnessing the power of state government to improve health and well-being and tackle affordability, new governors need to do three things: hire operators, see the trouble that’s already here, and set a focused agenda.

A governor’s three most consequential health appointments are the state’s health and human services secretary, Medicaid director, and public health officer. The attributes that matter most in these leaders include, foremost, a track record in getting things done in and with government. Look for leaders who have managed large government teams, legislative processes, and stakeholder associations.

Expertise matters, especially in this moment. The Medicaid director should understand evolving federal financing rules, eligibility systems and operations, and the state’s Medicaid delivery system, which is often managed care. The public health officer should have run an outbreak response.

Relationship and communication skills are paramount in managing a large government agency through change. The governor’s health leaders need to have the trust of legislators of both parties, hospitals, health centers and other health care providers, local leaders, consumer groups, and community partners. This team will be the state’s public face and primary communicators in a crisis.

Issues that are already hitting states hard will become even more challenging in the coming year. Governors-elect should be briefed on them now.

Medicaid eligibility requirements: In expansion states, work requirements and more frequent redeterminations of Medicaid eligibility are set to go live on Jan. 1, 2027. These new road rules require expansion adults ages 19 to 64 to document 80 hours a month of work, school, or service and to prove eligibility for Medicaid every six months. Experience shows that coverage losses will be high and come from paperwork, not because residents aren’t eligible for Medicaid anymore. These federal mandates will have major local impact. Governors should know:

Measles: The U.S. has already recorded more cases of measles in 2026 than in any year since 1991, nearly all among unvaccinated people. An international review this week will assess whether the country has lost its elimination status. On day one, governors should know kindergarten vaccination rates by county, confirm outbreak plans and surge staffing, and have a crisis communication plan at the ready for when an outbreak hits.

Medicaid program integrity: Medicaid program integrity is a concern for every state, and governors should expect CMS scrutiny to continue. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services has required all 50 states to submit Medicaid provider revalidation plans and has withheld federal payments from at least one state. New executive health teams should assume a review is coming and give the state’s fraud and inspector general units the resources they need and make program integrity the state’s own priority.

Aligning priorities across program and funding silos is a core job of the governor and their health team. With sustained leadership and clear focus, a state can unlock enormous untapped potential across Medicaid, public health, social services, insurance regulation, the state employee health plan, and rural health funds. This should include clarity of which levers states control and which require federal partnership (such as Medicaid or ACA waivers and financing changes). Governors should prioritize action in those areas that the state can drive.

Governors should elevate key priorities to name in the first State of the State, fund in the first governor’s budget, and show results within two years. Strong candidates for priorities are:

Coverage: Ten states still have not expanded Medicaid access. For these states, four of which have new governors coming in January, expansion should be a priority. It’s still the biggest lever for coverage, rural hospital sustainability, and funding. In any state, governors can create a public option to make premiums more affordable and give struggling small employers relief.

Affordability: The first affordability priority for new governors — indeed, for all governors —  should be relief that families feel soon. Options to consider include capping out-of-pocket costs for high-use medications, making primary care available before the deductible kicks in, and reining in pharmacy costs through pharmacy benefit manager reform and drug price transparency.

States can also protect patients from surprise and excessive bills by limiting facility fees, strengthening hospital financial assistance standards, and adding medical debt protections.

Lasting affordability also requires bringing down the overall cost of care — something that is a shared responsibility across hospitals, insurers, and drug manufacturers. Governors can set cost growth targets and compel public reporting. They can use combined state purchasing power to drive value-based payment and cut administrative waste. They can also pay for care models that improve access and chronic disease management, such as value-based primary care and technology-enabled models aligned with Medicare’s ACCESS model.

Rural health: Every state received a Rural Health Transformation Program award, averaging about $200 million a year through 2030, and later funding depends on meeting the commitments in each state’s application. It’s critical to avoid the “peanut butter” approach — spreading the dollars over so many priorities that the money is thin for all. Set a few measurable goals, such as keeping obstetric and emergency services open, building regional referral networks, and building and maintaining primary care and behavioral health access. Plan for how to sustain the work after federal funding ends.

States should approach artificial intelligence thoughtfully as they invest rural health and other state funds. Used well, AI holds promise to improve access, health, and the work of state government. Used poorly, it can drive up costs and deny care.

To guide AI investment, governors should set clear, simple rules that protect consumers through disclosure, consent, and clinician review, aligned with other states. Use Medicaid managed care contracts and state purchasing to require disclosure of AI use and reporting of outcomes, steering vendors toward tools that improve access and affordability rather than AI automation billing wars. Start small with initiatives inside state government where AI can support your workforce including by piloting AI in chatbots, call centers, and eligibility processing, with human review of any decision that denies or ends coverage.

A divided government in Washington likely means few federal solutions are coming soon. States have always been laboratories of innovation, and that power has never been more critical to harness than at this moment.

Mandy Cohen, M.D., M.P.H., is former secretary of health and human services for North Carolina and former director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. She is a national adviser at Manatt, a legal and consulting firm. Ellen Montz, Ph.D., is former chief deputy at the Virginia Department of Medical Assistance Services (Virginia Medicaid) and former deputy administrator and director at the Center for Consumer Information and Insurance Oversight at the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services. She is a managing director at Manatt.

BJC Health, St. Luke's reveal plans to merge" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Missouri-based BJC Health and St. Luke's Hospital are planning a merger.

The providers announced on Wednesday that they have signed a letter of intent to come together, bringing the community hospital into the fold with the Show Me State's largest health system. The pair expects the deal to improve access and improve local care in the St. Louis region.

St. Luke's said in the announcement that the letter "follows a deliberate and thorough evaluation process," conducted by its board of directors and leaders "to identify the best path forward for St. Luke’s and the communities it serves."

The providers said they intend to spend the next several months building a definitive agreement to merge and complete the needed regulatory approval process. In the interim, St. Luke's patients can continue to see their regular physicians.

BJC said in the announcement that it is committed to supporting local, community care while also allowing St. Luke's to tap into the resources available across its ecosystem. It intends to provide key support for the hospital's clinical technology and equipment as well as backing infrastructure and facility upgrades and provider recruitment and retention efforts.

St. Luke’s is a well-respected hospital, known for clinical quality, patient experience and the personal attention given to everyone in our care,” said Andy Bagnall, CEO of St. Luke’s, in the announcement. “At the same time, the demands of health care delivery and our communities’ needs are changing rapidly."

We believe that together with BJC, we can strengthen patient care in St. Louis in ways we could not easily do on our own," Bagnall said.

Nick Barto, CEO of BJC Health, called St. Luke's "a trusted leader in our region with a reputation for excellence."

"Together, we will build on that foundation through our aligned clinical strengths and complementary services," Barto said in the announcement. "Our shared goal is to expand access to differentiated, high-quality care while ensuring St. Luke’s can continue serving the growing communities of West St. Louis for generations to come.”

#5682. Agents may soon be the main workload, and most of the time they’re doing nothing

As AI agents take on more enterprise work, agent sandboxing has become a basic requirement rather than an afterthought. Every agent that writes code, runs tools or drives a browser needs hard walls around it. Those walls also can’t come at the cost of runaway compute bills.

Google LLC’s answer is Agent Substrate, an open-source project built on Kubernetes that the company donated to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation alongside its gVisor sandbox. Customers have raised the same problem for the past 18 months: They need to run agentic workloads securely and efficiently on the infrastructure they already have, according to Brandon Royal (pictured, left), product manager, AI agents and infrastructure, at Google Cloud.

“Any agent needs to be fully isolated,” Royal said. “Whether it’s accessing tools or using a computer or a browser, there needs to be some level of isolation, period, full stop.”

Royal and Benjamin Elder (right), staff software engineer at Google, spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how agent sandboxing is central to Google’s open-source Agent Substrate. (* Disclosure below.)

Agent Substrate starts with hardened sandbox runtimes densely packed on Kubernetes clusters. All traffic passes through a layer that applies policy and understands identity, so an agent can reach nothing it hasn’t been explicitly granted, Elder explained. The project also keeps secrets out of the agent’s hands by injecting credentials on the wire.

“Don’t expose credentials to the sandbox,” Elder said. “Don’t let the agent touch the credentials. Instead, when it requests to do something, you can make a decision about outside the sandbox.”

Security is only half the equation. Agents in a swarm spend much of their time blocked, waiting on a large language model call or on a human to follow up. Agent Substrate snapshots those idle agents out of memory and CPU, stores them offline and restores them when they’re needed, freeing resources across the cluster, according to Elder.

“Should you be holding compute while you’re getting coffee? Because you might come back in five minutes. You might come back in five hours or five days,” Royal said. “We don’t know.”

Google is already building on the project. Gemini Managed Agents now runs on Agent Substrate and gets the same density, efficiency and security guarantees, Royal noted. Google Cloud also recently introduced Agent Compute Engine to host AI agents.

“Agents are going to become the predominant workload in the future,” Royal said. “Maybe it’s six months, maybe it’s 12 months, but we see this as a really big area of growth.”

Here’s the complete video interview, part of SiliconANGLE’s and theCUBE’s coverage of KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA:

#5681. Extra weight may be aging your brain faster than you think

Carrying excess weight may affect more than physical health. New research from the University of Georgia suggests that having a higher body mass index may also speed up cognitive decline, potentially causing memory and thinking abilities to deteriorate more quickly with age.

Some cognitive changes are a natural part of getting older. Remembering information, thinking clearly, and processing new details can become more difficult over time. For healthy adults, however, these changes are usually relatively mild and develop gradually.

The new findings suggest that excess body weight may accelerate this process. Researchers found that people with higher body mass index (BMI) experienced faster declines in memory, overall cognitive performance, and executive functioning. These abilities are essential for everyday activities such as concentrating, planning, organizing tasks, and regulating emotions.

To investigate the connection, the research team analyzed data from a nationally representative study that tracked more than 8,200 adults over age 50 for 24 years.

Higher BMI Linked to Faster Cognitive Decline

The results revealed a consistent relationship between body weight and cognitive health. Each one-point increase in BMI was associated with a faster rate of cognitive decline, suggesting that even relatively small differences in body weight could matter over time.

The association was strongest at the eighth year of the study, and adults older than 65 showed the most pronounced effects.

Despite the concerning findings, researchers also identified a potentially encouraging opportunity to protect brain health. Managing body weight may help slow cognitive decline, with possible benefits becoming apparent within just two years.

"We found that if people managed their weight, they could significantly lower their rate of cognitive decline in just two years," said Suhang Song, the study's lead author and an assistant professor at the University of Georgia's College of Public Health. "That makes BMI one of the most easily modifiable risk factors when it comes to aging well."

How Excess Weight May Affect the Aging Brain

Obesity, generally defined as a BMI of 30 or higher, has been associated with poorer brain health. However, scientists are still working to understand exactly why carrying excess body weight may interfere with memory and other cognitive abilities.

Several biological processes could help explain the connection. Excess weight may promote inflammation, impair blood circulation, and contribute to insulin resistance. Together, these changes could increase the likelihood of cognitive impairment, Alzheimer's disease, and other forms of dementia.

The findings are particularly relevant given how widespread obesity has become in the United States. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, approximately two in five Americans meet the criteria for obesity when BMI is used as the sole measure.

Some scientists argue that BMI alone does not provide a complete picture of obesity. They support a broader definition that also considers waist measurements and medical conditions associated with excess weight. Using those additional criteria, the estimated proportion of Americans classified as having obesity rises to 75%.

Weight Management Could Help Protect Brain Health

The potential connection between obesity and cognitive decline is especially concerning as dementia becomes increasingly common. More than 7 million Americans currently live with dementia, and researchers expect that number to double by 2050.

Although the study does not establish that excess weight directly causes cognitive decline, its findings highlight body weight as a potentially important factor in maintaining cognitive health. Because weight can be managed, researchers believe it could offer an opportunity to reduce the risk of worsening memory and thinking abilities as people grow older.

"There are no cures for dementia," Song said, "which is why it is critical to identify and address any modifiable risk factors we can find to prevent it."

The research was published in the Journal of Neurology. Coauthors from the University of Georgia College of Public Health include Meng Hsuan Sung, Zhuo Chen, Janani Rajbhandari, Grace Bagwell Adams, Mahmud Khan, Ye Shen, and Xiao Song. Qianhui Xu and Xia Song also contributed to the study.
