#5679. Duet nabs $15M series A, plans to launch first NP-led ACO in 2027

Duet nabs $15M series A, plans to launch first NP-led ACO in 2027" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Nurse practitioner-owned primary care practice network Duet secured $15 million in series A funding to expand its clinic network and grow its partnerships and team.

Kairos led the funding round, with participation from Lerer Hippeau.

Kairos co-founder and co-CEO Alex Fiance said in a statement the company is “one of those rare businesses where everybody wins.”

“It reaches patients in need, helps clinicians become business owners, and brings costs down for the payers and the U.S. government by catching problems early,” Fiance said. “We believe Duet has the potential to reshape care across the country in a highly scalable way and are excited to help fuel their growth.”

Duet is the largest network of independent NP-owned primary care practices in the U.S., the company says. It helps practices earn compensation through its various partnerships with insurers, including Anthem, Cigna and Centene.

Duet Founder and CEO Jonathan Goldberg told Fierce Healthcare the company’s platform “combines practice advisors with AI-powered tools” to offload administrative work and give NPs more time for patient care.

“Our technology identifies people who are drifting out of care and gets them scheduled. It threads together patient data ahead of every visit, so an NP knows who is at risk and what to focus on,” Goldberg said. “And we help extend care into the home for those who need extra attention with remote technology and wraparound support.”

Goldberg continued, “There’s a lot stacked against small practices. Our mission is to help NPs show up for people that the system has overlooked.”

Patients visiting Duet clinics had an overall NPS of 92 across approximately 400,000 visits a year, Goldberg said.

“Patients often comment that this is the first time they felt heard, had someone take the time to read through their chart, or had a condition diagnosed that other clinicians had dismissed,” Goldberg said. “The clinical results follow from that. Practices that join Duet see preventive screenings for conditions like breast cancer and colon cancer rise 30%, and ER visits fall 20%. We also bring back 25% of the patients who are unengaged, and those are the patients who tend to end up worse off.”

The company has raised $22.5 million to date and works with more than 130 clinics across 21 states, executives say.

Goldberg said the company plans to use the fresh capital in three main ways: serve more clinics, deepen its value-based care partnerships with insurers and add engineers to its team. He added that Duet is launching an accelerator program in 2027 to help clinics “start strong.

Alongside the funding round, Duet announced it plans to launch the first-ever NP-led Medicare Accountable Care Organization (ACO) in 2027.

NPs will design and govern the company’s new model, which Goldberg says will allow practice owners to maintain “their autonomy while getting the technology and resources to strengthen their care.”

“NPs already practice prevention first, and this gives them a way to be recognized for it,” he said.

#5678. Agricultural Visionary: Stefan Soloviev's Path to Innovation

Entrepreneur Stefan Soloviev has created an indelible impression in the global agribusiness landscape. Known for his innovative approach and dedication to sustainability, his journey provides essential insights into successful entrepreneurship in this challenging yet rewarding industry.

Breaking Ground: Stefan Soloviev's Foray into Agribusiness

When talking about Stefan Soloviev, one cannot ignore his impressive transition into the agribusiness sector. He recognized the immense potential in this industry, which is evident in his ownership of Crossroads Agriculture, managing more than 70,000 acres of farmland from New Mexico to Colorado1. #5676. American Cancer Society revises guidelines, urges routine PSA screening for prostate cancer

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Annalisa (Nalis) Merelli is focused on boys’ and men’s health: She looks into reproductive health, trending treatments, screening approaches, mental health, and everything in between.

In a major change to screening guidelines, the American Cancer Society recommended on Thursday that American men between ages 50 and 69 at an average risk of prostate cancer should test their prostate-specific antigen (PSA) blood levels every two years.

The prior guidelines, released in 2010, left testing for average-risk men to their discretion, after assessing cancer risk with a physician.

Similarly, PSA testing recommendations were strengthened for high risk groups — Black men and men with a strong family history of prostate cancer. They are now encouraged to get PSA-based screening yearly starting at 45. Black men in particular disproportionately die from prostate cancer, and the guideline authors said they hope that increased surveillance will reduce the number of Black patients presenting with cancers at advanced stages.

Then, starting at 70, the decision on whether to continue screening becomes individualized as the balance of benefit and harm is not as clear after that age. Screening should be interrupted after 80, or in men who are not expected to live another 10 years.

The changes reflect recent findings that screening through PSA levels reduced disease specific mortality for certain men, bringing the indicator back into specialists’ good graces. Once a preferred biomarker to identify risk of prostate cancer, routine PSA screening had fallen out of favor — and was dropped from the guidelines in 2010 — for its lack of specificity, which resulted in many men undergoing follow-up procedures when they had no cancer, or very slow-growing tumors.

The U.S. Preventive Service Task Force, a federally appointed panel of outside experts, has not changed its guidelines since the new evidence became available in 2025, and continues to recommend against routine, population-wide PSA screening, suggesting instead individualized decision-making. But the panel, whose recommendations determine the preventive services that insurers must cover, has announced an upcoming update.

The cutoff for PSA levels to be considered high is established as 3.0 nanograms/milliliter or higher for men aged 45 to 69 years old. This is an important clarification, said James Eastham, chief of urology at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center. “Most PSA blood tests in the United States, when they’re reported, say under 4.0 [ng/ml] is normal, but it really should be under 3,” he said. “I think [the update] will hopefully help primary care physicians refer folks a little bit earlier.”

To limit the risk of overdiagnosis and overtreatment, the guidelines also now recommend two elevated PSA readings, followed by an MRI scan and/or testing for other biomarkers of prostate cancer, with the aim of reducing the number of patients undergoing biopsies. “We just wanted to give a little bit of flexibility for folks who cannot easily obtain an MRI,” said William Dahut, chief scientific officer at the ACS and a contributing author of the guidelines, about including both biomarkers and MRIs as a possible step following elevated PSA levels. However, he noted that an MRI would still be recommended prior to biopsy, should a biomarker test come back abnormal.

Though there are a variety of biomarkers, the guidelines don’t recommend one over the other. Dahut said ACS researchers  intend to look more closely at biomarkers to establish which may be more effective in predicting a more aggressive cancer.

“I think the new guidelines are certainly a balanced approach for early detection of prostate cancer,” said Eastham. “There have been many men undergoing unnecessary biopsies, and many low risk cancers that were subsequently overtreated,” he said. By recommending some steps between an elevated PSA and a biopsy, he said, the new recommendations reflect the evidence that while being a good biomarker, PSA alone would identify too many men as biopsy candidates.

Finally, the guidelines emphasize the importance of active surveillance in men with slow growing cancer: “If you screen more men, you’re going to find more men with early-stage disease, and we need to be strong in our position that that does not mean that you need to rush for therapies or that you need to have therapies at all.”

For Eddie Baynes, a 56-year-old prostate cancer survivor and advocate, the new guidelines “hit the nail on the head” when it comes to recommending routine PSA screening. As a Black man, he knew he was at higher risk of developing prostate cancer, yet it wasn’t until the fraternity he belonged to organized a screening event that he, at 52, started getting regular PSA tests with his bloodwork. Though routine screening wasn’t part of the ACS recommendation at the time, it led to a cancer diagnosis and a prostatectomy.

That’s why he’s been advocating for men to get PSA levels tested, and relatively frequently. With the new guidelines, men like him will start routine screening earlier than he did. “Part of my advocacy is getting tested more frequently. So now, just to have that announcement coming from the American Cancer Society, it just makes what I’ve been urging individuals to do for a while stronger,” he said.

#5675. Experts say high blood pressure guidelines are missing half the equation

For decades, one of the most common recommendations for lowering high blood pressure has been simple: eat less salt. But a new scientific report suggests that this advice may be missing an equally important part of the equation.

Researchers say that increasing potassium intake, rather than focusing only on reducing sodium, could lead to better blood pressure control. By addressing both nutrients together, this approach could strengthen efforts to prevent hypertension and reduce the risk of serious cardiovascular problems.

The potential impact is enormous. High blood pressure, also known as hypertension, affects more than 1.28 billion adults worldwide and is a major risk factor for cardiovascular disease, including heart attacks and strokes. Although public health recommendations have traditionally emphasized cutting sodium, researchers now argue that getting enough potassium deserves just as much attention.

Sodium and potassium are essential minerals that help regulate fluid balance, nerve signaling, and muscle function. Both also influence blood pressure, but they affect the body in different ways.

Eating too much sodium can cause the body to retain additional fluid, increasing the pressure inside blood vessels. Potassium helps counter some of sodium's effects by supporting the kidneys in removing excess sodium through urine. It also contributes to the normal functioning of blood vessel walls, which plays an important role in maintaining healthy blood pressure.

In a new report, physicians and health experts argue that dietary recommendations should address these two minerals together. Rather than treating sodium reduction as the primary solution, they propose combining it with greater potassium consumption to achieve stronger results.

"It is time to view dietary interventions holistically because food components interact and physiology is integrative across systems," said Naomi Fukagawa, M.D. Ph.D., professor of medicine emerita at the Robert Larner, M.D. College of Medicine at the University of Vermont and first author on the report. "Growing evidence shows that increasing dietary potassium as well as reducing sodium intake work together to better manage hypertension."

A Major Rethink of Blood Pressure Guidelines

The report, published in the peer-reviewed American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, was supported by the IAFNS Sodium in Food and Health Implications Committee.

The researchers examined the scientific evidence underlying current sodium and potassium recommendations, along with practical ways to reduce sodium consumption and increase potassium intake. They also explored the obstacles to implementing these changes and identified areas where additional research and updated public health policies could help improve outcomes.

One of the central concerns is that many people consume too much sodium while getting nowhere near enough potassium. Both dietary patterns can contribute to elevated blood pressure, making them important targets for prevention and treatment.

Despite widespread efforts to encourage people to limit salt, average sodium consumption continues to exceed recommended levels. Meanwhile, potassium intake remains "far below optimal levels in both developed and developing nations," according to the authors.

This imbalance suggests that focusing primarily on what people should eat less of may be overlooking an important opportunity to improve cardiovascular health by encouraging them to consume more of a beneficial nutrient.

Potassium is naturally present in many familiar foods, including fruits, vegetables, legumes, and dairy products. Bananas, potatoes, beans, leafy greens, and yogurt are examples of foods that can help increase potassium intake.

Another possibility is replacing some sodium chloride, the main ingredient in ordinary table salt, with potassium salts. These substitutes can help reduce sodium while simultaneously increasing potassium, potentially addressing both dietary goals at once.

However, creating these products presents challenges for food manufacturers. Adding too much potassium salt can produce an unpleasant metallic taste, limiting how much can be used without affecting flavor. Manufacturers must therefore find a balance that improves nutritional content while keeping foods appealing to consumers.

Increasing potassium is also not appropriate for everyone. People with kidney disease or those taking certain medications may have difficulty regulating potassium levels, so potassium supplements and potassium-based salt substitutes should be used with medical guidance when these concerns apply.

A New Strategy for Fighting High Blood Pressure

The researchers emphasize that reducing sodium remains essential. Their proposal is not to abandon existing advice, but to expand it by recognizing that potassium intake is another major factor in blood pressure regulation.

The authors conclude that "dietary sodium reduction is a foundational strategy for hypertension prevention and management. However, new evidence supports a broadening of the current approach that focuses solely on sodium reduction and provides equal emphasis on increasing potassium intake."

For the more than one billion people living with hypertension, this shift in thinking could have significant implications. Instead of concentrating almost exclusively on reducing salt, future dietary recommendations may increasingly emphasize the combined benefits of consuming less sodium and more potassium.

The underlying message is straightforward: better blood pressure control may depend not only on what people remove from their diets, but also on what they add.

Happy Thursday. We’ve got a great lineup for you today, including an inside look at shuffles within the Senate’s health committee, and what it might mean for “Medicare for All.”

The American Cancer Society released a major update to its guidelines today, recommending testing for prostate-specific antigen blood levels every two years starting at age 50 for men with an average risk of prostate cancer. Men in high-risk groups, like Black men and men with a significant history of prostate cancer in the family, are urged to get tested annually starting at 45. The guideline’s authors hope that increased surveillance will reduce the number of Black patients presenting with cancers at advanced stages, as this demographic is disproportionately represented in prostate cancer mortality.

The changes reflect recent findings that screening through PSA levels reduced disease-specific mortality for certain men. It had fallen out of favor for its lack of specificity before recent findings returned it to specialists’ good graces. Read more from STAT’s Annalisa Merelli.

The Senate health committee is in the spotlight once again.

Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee members announced they will vote next week on whether to nominate Heidi Overton as commissioner of the Food and Drug Administration. Republicans are still in power in this lame duck session, but Overton’s approval is not a given, STAT’s Margaret Manto explains, since a key Republican hasn’t said whether he backs her.

And colleague John Wilkerson noted Tuesday that Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) plans to move the party towards supporting “Medicare for All” once he becomes chair of the committee in January. But he’ll have a new Republican colleague to spar with.

Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.) announced yesterday that he will forgo his leadership of the Senate homeland security committee to join HELP as the top Republican next year. Why is this bureaucratic shuffling noteworthy? The senator used the homeland security committee’s unusually powerful subpoena authority to accuse Anthony Fauci, without evidence, of conspiring to cover up the origins of the Covid-19 pandemic. Committee members voted along party lines to hold the former National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases director in contempt of Congress.

Moving to the health committee will allow Rand to fight with Sanders over Medicare for All and all manner of other health issues.

(Most of the information about Paul came from John Wilkerson and our D.C. Diagnosis newsletter. If you want puns and great updates about which senators STAT reporters are chasing down in the bowels of Congress, you can sign up here.)

Body mass index is a flawed measure for obesity, but it remains deeply entrenched in global medical systems. If the world replaced it, obesity rates would increase and millions of people’s obesity diagnoses could flip, according to a new study.

Experts took a framework developed last year that offers a new understanding of how weight can impact a person’s health outcomes and applied it to obesity rates in the United States, the United Kingdom, China, and Spain. After analyzing 844,000 participants, the researchers calculated that BMI-based obesity missed 6.2% of adults compared to the new metric.

The measure ditches BMI’s focus on a person’s height and weight to include where fat is stored in a person’s body, most notably abdominal fat. It could have major implications for accurately assessing the mortality risk from obesity. Read more about the study from STAT’s Andrew Joseph.

Two new First Opinion pieces explore how the movement’s history informs its present. In one, professor Jerel Ezell argues that MAHA has coopted strategies from Black environmentalists fighting systemic health and food system fissures for decades. “Even as Kennedy and MAHA have cribbed from the Black activist playbook, they’ve actively undermined” Black Americans, he writes.

In another, professor Gavin Yamey argues that it’s not surprising key leaders are standing by convicted rapist Russell Brand, given the movement’s history of cozying up to violent men. “There is a rot of toxic masculinity and violence at MAHA’s core,” Yamey writes. Read more.

If you’ve ever spent months cycling through different doses of the same drug to find one that works, it could be your pharmacogenes at work. This set of genes affect how your body responds to prescription drugs, impacting what dose works for you and potential side effects.

Scientists have just identified thousands of new variants in these genes, thanks to a study using data from nearly 100,000 Americans through the National Institute of Health’s All of Us program. The advances are partly due to the program’s collection of genetic data from diverse backgrounds.

The study found that every participant carried at least one variant in the 16 pharmacogenes they studied, and that one in four participants had taken a medication that could be affected by these variants — everything from selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors to chemotherapy. Anil Oza has the write up.

#5673. Ring Drone Cam Becomes a Reality for Homeowners Eager To Level Up With Smart Home Security

If you remember Rosie from “The Jetsons,” congratulations—the future is here.

Amazon’s Ring announced the launch of two new products on Tuesday, offering homeowners room-to-room surveillance and smart home functionality in brand-new ways.

First, there’s an indoor security drone. The Ring Drone Cam is a security camera that takes flight in your home, including upstairs, to monitor your house activity, day and night.

At a demonstration in New York on Monday, Ring CEO Jamie Siminoff showed how the drone could be used as a home monitoring tool and as a crime “deterrent.”

“If someone is going around your house at night, and your motion detector goes off on your Ring doorbell, imagine if you see spotlights and something flying across the window,” Siminoff said, according to CNBC. “You’re probably not going to go into that house.”

Secondly, there is the Ring Rover Cam. Seen by most as an upgrade to Amazon’s 2021 Astro home robot, this free-roaming bot is being pushed more for companies to patrol offices, warehouses, and other workspaces.

But it is a clear indication of where the technology for your home may head next.

The Ring Drone is being touted as a product meeting the moment of consumers eager to keep their most powerful asset protected at every level.

“For years, customers told us they wanted eyes in the places a fixed camera couldn’t reach, and peace of mind in the spots they’d never want one,” said Siminoff in the company’s press release.

“The honest answer wasn’t more cameras; it meant reimagining what a security device could be. That kind of invention is hard, and it takes time. But we kept at it until we got it right—and that's Ring Robotics. It’s not just a new category of security; it’s the beginning of a future where proactive, autonomous protection is something every home and every business can have.”

Priced at $250, the Ring Drone flying indoor security camera is a first-of-its-kind Ring camera, “built from the ground up with AI at its core,” according to the company.

Spec and key features include the following:

Custom flight routes: Homeowners can set routes and a schedule, and Ring Drone flies them automatically. You can also deploy it on demand, as the promo video shows.

Automatic incident response: When a Ring camera, sensor, or alarm is triggered, Ring Drone automatically flies to previously set patrol points to investigate.

Wall-to-wall coverage: With a 148-degree field of view and the ability to rotate 360 degrees, Ring Drone provides a whole-room view in 2K video.

Captures video day or night: Two built-in LED lights activate automatically in low-light environments, so you always get clear, crisp video.

Seamless Ring integration: Works with Ring cameras, doorbells, sensors, and alarms out of the box, and can be controlled from the newly updated Alexa Home Map.

The Ring Drone was announced as part of the launch of Ring Robotics, which takes everything “customers already love and trust about Ring and puts it in motion,” according to the company announcement.

While the Ring Drone is presented as a home product, the company’s debut of Ring Rover is designed for business.

An autonomous security robot, the $1,000 device is designed to give a roving security to offices, warehouses, and other larger footprint facilities.

Admittedly, the company created the Ring Rover after receiving feedback from Amazon Astro customers who said the feature they loved seeing is security on the move.

“As leaders in home and business security, the Ring team took that feedback, leveraged the best of Astro, and built something new—not a home robot that also does security, but a purpose-built security robot,” reads the press release.

Key features and capabilities of Ring Rover include the following:

Full-spectrum scanning: The Ring Rover can travel to any saved checkpoint or room with one tap. It can then execute a complete 360-degree scan to ensure total coverage.

Customizable patrol schedules: Set automated monitoring routes that fit your business schedule, allowing Ring Rover to patrol off-hours when a workspace is empty.

Automated event investigation: Triggers from connected Ring devices prompt Ring Rover to autonomously navigate to designated patrol points to assess the situation.

Height-adjustable periscope camera: An extendable mast allows the camera to see above shelving, counters, and obstacles. Height settings can be customized and saved for specific stops.

Visible and audible deterrents: Equipped with an integrated siren, light tower, and two-way audio, Ring Rover signals an active security presence and enables direct real-time communication.

Continuous 4K video recording: Streams and records up to 4K video during motion and patrols, capturing footage along the entire route for later review.*

The Ring Drone Cam ships in the U.S. on Jan. 27, pending approval from the Federal Communications Commission, while the Ring Rover Cam will begin shipping to users on Dec. 16, the company said.

#5672. 5 Exciting Ways to Invest in Real Estate

When it comes to exploring enticing investment opportunities, real estate often stands out as an excellent solution for making and growing wealth. No matter how the world around us changes, there will always be a demand for property in attractive areas. This has led countless people to diversify their portfolios over the years, buying rental properties, second homes, and even office spaces.

In recent years, as the world has continued to evolve, the marketplace for real estate investors has evolved with it. Today, people no longer need to buy and flip entire properties to make money. There are numerous tips for getting started and ways you can start your journey into the property world, and some options are actually simpler and more affordable than you might expect. Here are some of the best, most interesting ways to invest in real estate, if you want to avoid the traditional buy and flip strategy.

Not all real estate investments have to include purchasing actual bricks and mortar in the physical world. The digital landscape has evolved drastically in recent years, introducing new opportunities for innovative entrepreneurs to make money buying virtual assets. As the concept of the metaverse continues to gain traction, digital real estate is growing increasingly attractive.

With digital real estate, companies purchase a section of the blockchain in a metaverse landscape, where they can build online experiences, or simply store other assets. In 2021, sales on four of the biggest metaverse platforms for real estate reached a whopping $501 million. This indicates learning how to invest in digital real estate could be a worthwhile strategy for any consumer. Not only is it potentially profitable, but the digital real estate also requires less work to manage and maintain than a physical house or property.

Even if you’re not familiar with this form of property-based investing, you probably know the term crowdfunding. Made popular by sites like GoFundMe and Kickstarter, the crowdfunding strategy involves individuals pooling their resources together to fund a product or business. In the real estate world, investors can work together to purchase a property, such as a corporate space, warehouse, or block of flats, reducing the initial cost of a purchase.

The approach allows investors to participate in products that would have been impossible to access in the past because of high capital requirements. Individuals can use this strategy to diversify their portfolios with a variety of different locations and property types. Plus, you’ll earn a passive income through rental profits, and property appreciation.

Another real estate investment strategy gaining increasing attention in recent years is REITs. These are basically investment vehicles responsible for owning and operating income-generating assets, such as rental properties and office blocks. They’re traded on traditional stock exchanges and provide individuals with an opportunity to invest in the market, without directly owning a property or having to manage the investment themselves.

REITs can come with several attractive features, including regular distributions of dividends, and the ability to explore a range of different sectors. You can even use this strategy to spread your portfolio across industrial, residential, and commercial properties. They’re also a highly liquid investment option, making them appealing to beginners.

Finally, one interesting way to invest in real estate, without buying a physical property outright, is to spend some of your money on shares in PropTech startups. PropTech, or Property Technology startups, are companies focused on developing tools and real estate designed to transform the property landscape. They develop things like property management solutions, smart home technology, and virtual reality applications for tours.

If you already have experience in the world of stocks and shares, investing in a PropTech company could be an excellent way to utilize your existing knowledge and diversify your portfolio. It’s also a chance to get your foot in the door with a company that’s actively disrupting the real estate space, and the market as we know it.

Investing in property has become a much more diverse and versatile opportunity for individuals in recent years. No matter how much money you can afford to spend, or where your expertise lies, you can find plenty of ways to expand your portfolio with disruptive real-estate investment strategies.

#5671. Scientists discover new Alzheimer’s drug that repairs DNA damage and reduces brain inflammation

Scientists at King's College London have identified a promising new strategy for fighting Alzheimer's disease that could address several of the condition's damaging effects at the same time. Their research suggests that an experimental drug originally developed for spinal cord injuries may help repair damaged DNA, reduce inflammation, and target biological changes associated with the disease.

The drug, known as KCL-286, produced encouraging results in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease. Unlike treatments that focus primarily on the buildup of toxic proteins in the brain, this approach targets additional processes that can begin long before the disease reaches its advanced stages.

One particularly promising advantage is that KCL-286 has already completed Phase 1 human safety and tolerability trials as part of its earlier development. This could significantly shorten the path toward further clinical testing, although its effectiveness against Alzheimer's in humans has not yet been established.

"KCL-286 is a first-in-class, orally bioavailable small molecule that has already successfully cleared Phase 1 human safety and tolerability trials. This will dramatically cut down the traditional multi-year timeline required for new drug development," commented Professor Jonathan Corcoran, Professor of Neuroscience at the Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology & Neuroscience at King's College London.

The drug is a small molecule that can be taken by mouth, making it potentially more convenient to administer than treatments that require injections or infusions.

Why Alzheimer's Disease Is So Difficult to Treat

Alzheimer's disease involves a complicated series of changes in the brain, making it particularly challenging to develop effective treatments. Two of its best-known features are the abnormal accumulation of proteins called amyloid-beta and tau.

Amyloid-beta can collect into sticky deposits between nerve cells, while abnormal tau proteins can form tangles inside them. These changes interfere with normal brain function and are associated with the progressive loss of neurons, the specialized cells responsible for transmitting information throughout the brain.

Much of the effort to develop Alzheimer's treatments has focused on these two proteins. Although medications that remove amyloid-beta have demonstrated modest but measurable clinical benefits, they do not fully address the many biological processes involved in the disease.

Researchers are increasingly investigating other changes that may contribute to Alzheimer's, including damage to DNA and inflammation in the brain. Both can appear early in the disease process, making them potentially valuable targets for treatments designed to slow its progression.

In the new study, KCL-286 helped repair breaks in DNA and reduce inflammation in mice with Alzheimer's-like disease. These findings suggest that targeting several harmful processes simultaneously could offer a broader approach than focusing on amyloid-beta or tau alone.

"Our findings demonstrate that KCL-286 not only targets DNA damage but also reduces inflammation, two processes that occur very early in Alzheimer's disease progression. This highlights its potential as a disease-modifying therapy rather than simply addressing symptoms," said Dr. Maria Goncalves, who project-managed the drug development.

How Vitamin A Pathways Could Help Fight Alzheimer's

The drug works by activating a particular protein involved in the retinoic acid pathway, a biological system associated with how the body processes and uses vitamin A.

Vitamin A is best known for supporting healthy vision, but it also plays important roles in cellular development, gene regulation, and nervous system function. Retinoic acid, a substance derived from vitamin A, helps control the activity of genes involved in several essential biological processes.

Earlier research found that disruptions in this pathway were associated with the formation of amyloid-beta deposits in the brains of rats. These deposits resemble a major pathological feature of Alzheimer's disease, suggesting that the pathway may be relevant to the condition.

KCL-286 activates a specific protein within this system, offering researchers a way to influence biological processes connected to brain health and cellular repair.

The drug had already demonstrated an ability to promote the repair of DNA double-strand breaks in earlier research involving neuropathic pain, a type of pain caused by damage or dysfunction in the nervous system.

That discovery led scientists to investigate whether the same mechanism might also help address DNA damage associated with Alzheimer's disease.

DNA contains the genetic instructions that cells need to function properly. Although cells have natural systems for repairing damaged DNA, some forms of damage are particularly serious.

One example is a DNA double-strand break, which occurs when both strands of the DNA molecule are severed. These breaks can disrupt normal cellular activity and threaten cell survival if they are not properly repaired.

"DNA double-strand breaks are like a rope snapping completely in two, rather than just fraying at the edges. We found that KCL-286 promotes repair of these breaks, allowing us to target a key feature of Alzheimer's disease," said Professor Corcoran.

The researchers had another reason to suspect that KCL-286 might be useful against Alzheimer's. Previous work by the same team at King's College London identified molecular pathways shared by acute spinal cord injury and Alzheimer's disease.

Because the two conditions involve some overlapping biological mechanisms, the scientists believed that a drug developed to address nervous system damage after spinal cord injury might also improve certain Alzheimer's-related changes in neurons.

Their new findings support that possibility, showing that KCL-286 can influence several cellular pathways involved in the disease.

A Promising New Direction for Alzheimer's Treatment

The results highlight a potentially important shift in Alzheimer's research. Rather than concentrating on one hallmark of the disease, scientists are exploring treatments that address several interconnected causes of brain damage.

KCL-286 is particularly interesting because it targets DNA damage and inflammation, two processes that can emerge early in Alzheimer's progression. Its previous human safety testing also provides a potential advantage over entirely new drug candidates that have not yet entered clinical development.

However, the Alzheimer's findings remain preclinical. Additional studies and human clinical trials will be necessary to determine whether the drug can safely slow disease progression or improve outcomes in patients.

Natasha Hill, one of the first authors on the paper, said: "To develop an effective treatment for Alzheimer's disease, we need to tackle multiple aspects of the disease. KCL-286 was able to target multiple disease-relevant cellular pathways, some of which are initiated very early in the disease course."

#5670. AI agents carry memory and storage like people, so their data needs guarding while in use

As AI agents move into production on Kubernetes, cloud engineering teams at financial companies face a security problem that encryption alone can’t solve. Container orchestration has become the default foundation for AI workloads, and the data those agents use is now the main target.

Payment networks feel that pressure more than most because every transaction carries customer data and regulatory exposure. Protecting data while it is being processed, and not just while it is stored or moving, has become central to running agents at scale, according to Krishna Mayuram (pictured), senior principal engineer and vice president of cloud engineering at Mastercard Inc.

“What we call confidential computing is when you are launching these applications in a highly secure, virtualized secure environments or confidential environments or confidential containers, you are able to protect the data in use,” Mayuram said. “We have protected data at rest, data in motion. Now, what is happening to the data in use?”

Mayuram spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed cloud engineering, security problems and the challenges of protecting data in use. (* Disclosure below.)

Mastercard runs its platforms on Red Hat Inc.’s OpenShift, a Kubernetes platform that Red Hat is extending to support AI agents. Red Hat has also brought confidential containers to OpenShift on bare metal. Agents act much like microservices and need the same elastic infrastructure, Mayuram explained.

“We need to scale the platform, that’s Kubernetes which gives horizontal scaling, vertical scaling, if you will, and also the agents, just like applications, require all the elastic capabilities of Kubernetes,” Mayuram said.

Scale increases the risk, especially for a company that operates under many countries’ laws. Mastercard recently added trust services for agentic commerce. Internally, the same idea applies, with guardrails at every step from development to deployment, according to Mayuram.

“The business is distributed, the industry is very distributed, and we have different laws of the land. So all these things need to be encompassed with guardrails,” Mayuram said. “Whether agents or regular, the guardrails remain the same. The enterprise security remains same.”

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has shelved the fast-track drug review initiative launched during the Trump administration by former Commissioner Marty Makary, Reuters reports. But critics pointed to possible preferential treatment for companies meeting demands of President Trump, such as offering ‌drugs at lower prices. No new drugs have gotten a voucher since Makary’s departure, and a key component of the program — an executive council of political appointees that oversaw drug reviews ​and had a central role in speeding approvals — has gone dormant.

#5667. Scientists discover a surprising clue to autism's origins hidden in the placenta

Scientists are still working to understand why autism develops. Genetics are known to play a major role, but researchers have also found that conditions during pregnancy can influence the likelihood of autism spectrum disorder.

A new study from Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory (CSHL) has uncovered a surprising connection between inflammation during pregnancy, changes in the placenta, and the development of autism-like traits in male mice. The findings suggest that certain developmental disruptions may begin much earlier than previously recognized, potentially offering new clues about autism's origins.

"To truly understand autism spectrum disorder, we have to look beyond the brain," CSHL Associate Professor Lucas Cheadle says. "Our work suggests that maternal immune activation and changes within the placenta are a gateway to autism for some unique individuals."

Scientists Identify an Early Window of Vulnerability

To investigate how inflammation affects fetal development, Cheadle and his colleagues triggered an immune response in pregnant mice at different stages of pregnancy. They used a substance that mimics the immune system's reaction to a viral infection without actually introducing a virus.

The researchers discovered that mouse fetuses were especially vulnerable when inflammation occurred 12.5 days into pregnancy. According to Irene Sanchez Martin, a postdoctoral researcher in Cheadle's laboratory, approximately one-third of the fetuses showed developmental abnormalities within just 24 hours.

Scientists have investigated the effects of maternal immune activation for decades, but these findings reveal signs of developmental disruption earlier than researchers had previously observed.

Even more striking was the difference between male and female fetuses. Across every experiment, autism-like traits appeared only in males, while females continued developing normally.

This unexpected distinction could provide insight into why autism is diagnosed substantially more often in boys than girls. What makes the finding especially intriguing is how early the difference appeared, before many of the biological changes normally associated with sex-specific development.

"It's really fascinating, because we're looking at an age which precedes hormonal surges. It precedes sexual differentiation in the brain and many other regions. So, it's surprising there would be a sex-based difference this early."

A Surprising Connection Between the Placenta and Autism

To determine why some developing mice were affected while others appeared protected, Cheadle and Sanchez Martin examined the placenta, the organ that connects a developing fetus to its mother and supports its growth throughout pregnancy.

Their attention centered on specialized cells called spongiotrophoblasts, which occupy a region of the mouse placenta where maternal and fetal cells interact.

In fetuses that developed normally, this part of the placenta remained healthy. However, male fetuses showing developmental abnormalities also had visible damage to these specialized cells.

Spongiotrophoblasts play an important role in helping the mother's immune system tolerate the developing fetus. This protection is essential because the fetus carries genetic material from both parents and is not genetically identical to the mother.

The researchers found that maternal immune activation could interfere with this protective function. When these placental cells become damaged, the mother's immune response may begin affecting the developing fetus in harmful ways.

Why Female Fetuses May Have a Hidden Advantage

The findings raise another intriguing question: Why were male fetuses vulnerable while females appeared unaffected?

One possibility is that male embryos produce distinctive proteins that can trigger an unfavorable maternal immune response following a viral infection. Another explanation is that female embryos possess some form of protection that helps them withstand inflammation during this sensitive developmental period.

Cheadle says, "A protective mechanism may exist within the female that could be harnessed to help the male. We're trying to understand how autism emerges in both sexes," he explains. "The evidence says that there are potentially different mechanisms."

These possibilities suggest that biological pathways involved in autism-like development may differ between males and females. Understanding those differences could help researchers identify why some individuals are more vulnerable to certain environmental influences during pregnancy.

Cheadle's team plans to investigate both male and female mice more closely to uncover the mechanisms responsible for these contrasting responses. Their work could eventually identify new targets for treatments and lead to strategies for intervening earlier in developmental processes associated with autism.

Although the findings come from experiments in mice and do not establish that the same mechanisms cause autism in humans, they highlight an unexpected possibility: Important clues to autism's earliest development may lie not only in the brain, but also in the placenta and its interactions with the maternal immune system.

#5666. ‘Landman’ Season 3 Is Filming at Taylor Sheridan’s 600-Acre Texas Ranch—Which He Previously Charged Paramount $50K a Week To Use

Actor and director Taylor Sheridan has created an impressive slate of ranch-themed TV shows, but what is perhaps more remarkable is that some of them have been filmed on his very own properties.

The “Yellowstone” creator, 56, boasts an extraordinary property empire that’s estimated to be worth more than $600 million. And one of his most recognizable properties—the 600-acre Bosque Ranch near Fort Worth, TX—will reportedly be a filming location in Season 3 of the Sheridan-produced show “Landman.”

One of the series’ cast members, musician Clayton Q, confirmed the plans in a Nov. 6 Instagram post.

“Hey, y’all, Clayton Q here. I’m here at the world-famous Bosque Ranch right here in Weatherford, TX,” he said in the video. “Taylor Sheridan’s horse ranch. We got a lot of stuff going on. I’m on location today.”

Season 3 of the series began filming in October and is expected to premiere in mid-2027. It comes at a slight delay, as the season was green-lit in December 2025.

The Bosque Ranch Headquarters website confirms the legendary spot has been used to film a handful of projects, including “Yellowstone,” “Lawman: Bass Reeves,” and “Lioness.”

According to the Wall Street Journal, Sheridan had reportedly charged Paramount $50,000 a week to film at the ranch. His cattle was rented in herds, priced at $25 a cow.

Sheridan snapped up the property in 2013 for a whopping $264 million. At the time, the ranch served as a home base for his family, who had relocated to the Lone Star State from Los Angeles, where he previously worked as an actor on shows such as “Veronica Mars” and “Sons of Anarchy.”

Today, the home remains Sheridan’s primary residence, although he and his wife, actress-model Nicole Muirbrook, also spend time with their son at another property they own in Texas—the Four Sixes Ranch he purchased for $320 million in 2022.

“The main headquarters where we live is more of a horse ranch, because I’m pretty deep into the horse deal. And then the ranch out by Jacksboro is more where we run the cattle,” he explained in a 2020 interview.

Sheridan also has a $4.95 million ranch in Wyoming’s Star Valley, which he reportedly acquired in August 2024. The 179-acre homestead is known as Papa’s Creek Ranch and is located about 65 miles from Jackson Hole.

Despite his jaw-dropping portfolio, Sheridan hasn’t always been well-off financially. In an August 2026 interview with Town and Country magazine, he recalled a time when he was down on his luck.

“I was homeless twice,” he said. “I lived in my car. Sometimes I’d go to Ojai, just somewhere where I could safely sleep. I did that for six months.”

The multihyphenate noted that the struggle was technically his own choice.

“I could have decided at any point, ‘I’m going to get a full-time job and I’m going to give up this dream,’” he said of his acting career. “And I chose to sleep in my car over that.”

However, when he became more successful, after his stint on “Sons of Anarchy,” he developed a strategy to make sure he could solidly stand on his own two feet from there on out.

After turning to screenwriting, he sold his first screenplay for a drama called “Hell or High Water.” Afterward, he “bought a little house on an acre on a river in Wyoming.”

“We moved there, and I wrote a check for it,” he said. “Then, as I would start to have more success, I would buy a little bit more land beside it and get a couple horses. I’m still so averse to having to ever owe anybody anything.”

Sheridan explained that now that he’s built a career tied so deeply to ranching, he can avoid Los Angeles, a city he disliked living in.

#5665. The Efficacy of Broad Match + Audiences Strategy in Real Estate

When considering digital marketing strategies, the realm of real estate is no different from any other industry. The key objective remains the same - reaching the target audience with an impactful, compelling message that can inspire action. An increasingly popular approach adopted by real estate agents is the broad match + audiences strategy. This approach leverages the power of Google AdWords' broad match feature and combines it with audience targeting to attain superior marketing results.

The real estate sector thrives on the availability of a vast array of properties, each with a unique combination of attributes that appeal to different prospective buyers. Recognizing this immense diversity and matching it with the correct buyer is a daunting challenge that real estate agents constantly grapple with. This is where the broad match + audiences strategy steps in, optimizing the process by expanding reach while ensuring relevance.

The broad match feature in Google AdWords is a type of keyword match that allows your ads to show whenever someone searches for that keyword or a related phrase. It can include searches that are misspellings, synonyms, related searches, and other relevant variations.

With the broad match feature, you're casting a wide net over an extensive range of search queries. It brings with it the advantage of gaining visibility across a wider spectrum of potential buyers who might not use the exact keywords that you've selected for your campaign.

In the real estate industry, property attributes can be incredibly diverse, ranging from "3-bedroom apartments in New York City" to "colonial-style houses with large gardens in Austin". By leveraging the broad match feature, agents can reach potential clients who use various search terms that directly or indirectly relate to their listing.

Audience targeting is a method used in digital marketing to segment audiences based on specific criteria like demographics, interests, buying behavior, etc. Google AdWords allows you to target your ads to specific audiences, ensuring they are seen by those who are most likely to be interested in your offerings.

In the context of real estate, audience targeting can be a game-changer. For instance, if an agent specializes in selling luxury homes, they can target audiences with high-income levels and a demonstrated interest in luxury living. Alternatively, if an agent focuses on properties suitable for first-time buyers, they can target younger audiences who have recently started searching for homes.

The marriage of broad match keywords with audience targeting may seem counter-intuitive at first, considering one aims at breadth and the other at specificity. However, the combination forms a robust strategy that takes the best of both worlds - wide reach and precise targeting.

The broad match feature ensures a wide reach, allowing real estate agents to surface their listings to a large number of prospective clients. But, broad match alone can lead to high impression counts with low conversion rates as the ads may be presented to irrelevant audiences. This is where audience targeting steps in to bring precision.

When used in conjunction, the broad match feature ensures that your ads reach a wide array of searchers, while audience targeting ensures these ads are shown to a specific subset of this wide audience who are most likely to be interested in your property listings.

This synergistic approach allows real estate agents to achieve two key objectives:

In the dynamic and competitive world of real estate, digital marketing strategies need to be both comprehensive and precise. The broad match + audiences strategy does precisely that - it maximizes the reach of property listings while maintaining relevance to the audience. As such, it is not surprising that this strategy is being widely adopted by savvy real estate agents seeking to gain a competitive edge in the digital realm. The power of a wide-reaching yet finely tuned marketing strategy should not be underestimated in a market as diverse and competitive as real estate.

#5663. A $35 Million Home Just Hit San Francisco’s Market, Marking the Most Expensive Listing of the Year

San Francisco’s most expensive home of the year just hit the market and is expected to draw interest from potential buyers flush with cash from the AI boom.

The home at 2770 Broadway officially went on the market on Monday with a nearly $35 million price tag.

The seven-bedroom, 6.5-bathroom home is already drawing inquiries, listing agent Neil Ward of Compass told SFGate.

Located in the exclusive Gold Coast neighborhood, the home sits on a 50-foot-wide, double-width lot, with breathtaking views of the San Francisco Bay, Golden Gate Bridge, Palace of Fine Arts, and other famed landmarks, according to the listing.

The home was designed in 1894 by Reid & Reid, the same architectural firm responsible for the iconic Fairmont Hotel. While many Gold Coast homes of this age, most of which are generational properties, need complete renovations after being sold, Ward told SFGate that the potential buyer of 2770 Broadway can “walk in with their toothbrush and their furniture.”

A 2007 renovation by architect Jim Jennings and Van Acker Construction brought together the home’s original turn-of-the-century grandeur with the functionality needed for modern family living.

The home’s 9,000 square feet are spread across four floors, where prospective buyers will find herringbone-patterned floors, arched openings, and fine millwork, all evidence of the home’s architectural greatness.

The property also features a two-car garage, wine cellar, and sport court in the rear of the house.

The home was purchased by San Francisco business executive David Chamberlain in 1989, according to SFGate. He was CEO of companies such as Shaklee, Stride Rite, and Genesco, but also had a deep connection with his city, serving as president of the San Francisco Opera and the San Francisco Chamber of Commerce.

After his death earlier this year, Chamberlain’s two daughters decided to sell the home.

Ward told SFGate that he thinks the property will sell for its $35 million asking price, which would make it the most expensive home sold on the multiple listing service in San Francisco this year.

“It is a really, really rare product that does not hit the market,” Ward said.

Between the home’s turnkey condition and the city’s competitive ultraluxury home market, Ward thinks the home’s time on the market will be brief.

“I’ve done this for over 35 years. I was here for the dot-com boom and everything in between. Nothing comes close to what’s taking place right now,” Ward said.

San Francisco is experiencing what some real estate brokerages are calling a “mansion shortage,” according to NPR. The AI boom, much of which is concentrated in San Francisco, has caused demand for luxury single-family homes in the area to skyrocket, while the supply remains stagnant.

Home to major AI companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic, the San Francisco market had a median of just 37 days on the market, according to Realtor.com data, two weeks less than the national median of 61 days.

Some listings have had over 50 offers, and 44 homes were sold for at least $1 million over asking in June alone, according to a report from NPR.

In October, the sale of a home in San Francisco’s Presidio neighborhood broke the record for the highest sale above asking. The 1966 midcentury home was listed for $18.5 million and sold for $28.5 million, an eye-watering $10 million premium.

#5662. Scientists turn viruses into weapons against deadly superbugs

Viruses are usually associated with causing infections, but some can actually help fight them. Scientists are now working to turn these bacteria-killing viruses into treatments for dangerous infections that no longer respond to conventional antibiotics.

An international team of experts has taken an important step toward making this approach safer and more practical for medical use. Led by the German Society for Infectious Diseases (DGI), the group has developed the first internationally coordinated clinical guidelines for personalized phage therapy, a treatment that uses carefully selected viruses to attack harmful bacteria.

The effort involved 20 professional organizations, 18 international experts, including representatives from regulatory agencies, and two patient advocacy organizations. Together, they established more than 60 recommendations covering how phages should be selected, tested, manufactured, administered, and monitored. The guidelines also address laboratory infrastructure, quality control, treatment documentation, and priorities for future research.

The consensus statement was published in the journal Nature Medicine. Until now, doctors and researchers have lacked a unified international framework for many of the essential procedures and quality standards involved in using phages as medical treatments.

How Bacteria-Killing Viruses Could Fight Antibiotic Resistance

Antibiotic resistance is making bacterial infections increasingly difficult to treat around the world. As some bacteria develop defenses against commonly used medications, doctors may find themselves with few effective options.

One possible alternative involves bacteriophages, commonly called phages. These are viruses that naturally infect bacteria and can destroy them. Unlike many antibiotics, which can act against a broad range of bacteria, phages typically target particular bacterial species or even individual strains.

That precision makes phage therapy especially interesting, but it also creates a challenge. A virus capable of killing one strain of bacteria may have little or no effect on another. Before treatment begins, specialists must therefore determine whether a particular phage can successfully attack the bacteria responsible for a patient's infection.

Personalized phage therapy may be considered when established treatments have failed, are unavailable, or cannot be used safely. Research so far suggests that properly manufactured and administered phages generally have a favorable safety profile. However, controlled clinical trials have not yet provided sufficient evidence to establish how reliably the treatment works.

For that reason, the new guidelines do not recommend phage therapy as a routine treatment for bacterial infections. Instead, they emphasize carefully evaluating individual patients and using the approach only when the circumstances justify it.

Early Results Show Promise Against Difficult Infections

Although major questions remain, early clinical experiences suggest that phage therapy could benefit some patients with difficult infections.

In a Belgian case series involving 100 people who received phage treatment, 77 percent experienced an improvement in their clinical condition. In 61 percent of cases, tests could no longer detect the bacteria that the treatment had targeted.

These findings are encouraging, particularly for infections that are difficult to control with existing medications. However, observational studies cannot establish whether phages were responsible for the improvements or determine how well the treatment would perform in a controlled clinical trial.

Larger, carefully designed studies will be needed to clarify the effectiveness of phage therapy and identify which patients are most likely to benefit.

Finding the Right Virus for Each Bacterial Infection

A central challenge in personalized phage therapy is finding the correct virus for each patient.

Because phages are highly selective, laboratories must test whether a candidate virus can kill the specific bacterial strain involved in an infection. This process, known as a "phage match," should be completed as quickly as possible before treatment begins.

Timing matters because bacteria can change their susceptibility to phages during an infection. If multiple bacterial pathogens are present, specialists should test all of the relevant organisms rather than focusing on just one.

The guidelines recommend that treatment decisions involve a team of specialists, including the patient's physicians, clinical microbiologists, and recognized phage experts. This collaborative approach is intended to help clinicians select appropriate phages and determine whether treatment is justified.

The recommendations also establish expectations for cooperation among laboratories, phage manufacturing facilities, pharmacies, and clinical teams. Consistent testing methods and regular proficiency assessments should help ensure that results from different facilities are reliable and comparable.

Another priority is collecting detailed information about every treatment. The guidelines call for cases to be systematically documented and entered into registries, allowing researchers to compare clinical experiences, identify problems, and investigate unanswered questions.

"The standardization of quality criteria for the production of phages for personalized use, as well as the identification of infrastructural requirements, are essential components of the guideline and important prerequisites for reliable treatments," says Dr. Annika Claßen.

Claßen, a researcher with the German Center for Infection Research (DZIF), played a leading role in developing the recommendations. She also directs the "Translational Bacteriophage Research Group" at University Hospital Cologne.

Other major contributors include PD Dr. Silvia Würstle, Prof. Maria Vehreschild, and Dr. Simone Lieberknecht-Jouy of Goethe University Frankfurt. Vehreschild serves as deputy coordinator of the DZIF research area "Healthcare-Associated Infections," where Claßen, Würstle, and Lieberknecht-Jouy are also involved in research.

German Hospital Begins Using Personalized Phage Therapy

The potential of this approach is already being explored in clinical practice.

"The guideline provides physicians, pharmacists, and regulatory authorities with a common framework for safely and responsibly incorporating phage therapy into clinical practice," says PD Dr. Würstle, the corresponding author of the guideline.

At Frankfurt University Medical Center, Würstle is overseeing the development of the facilities and procedures needed to provide phage therapy in accordance with the new recommendations.

The medical center reports that ten patients have been successfully treated through its guideline-based phage therapy program since February 2026. The treatments use viruses individually selected to target the bacteria causing each patient's infection.

Among the pathogens treated are Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus, two bacterial species associated with infections that can be particularly challenging to manage, especially when antibiotic resistance is involved.

The method of delivering the phages depends on the infection and the patient's medical needs. Treatment may involve intravenous administration, inhalation, a nasal spray, or application through a sterile hydrogel.

These different delivery methods illustrate how personalized phage therapy can be adapted to specific clinical situations rather than relying on a single treatment approach.

New International Standards Could Shape the Future of Phage Therapy

Building a reliable system for phage treatment requires coordination across numerous medical and scientific specialties.

The guidelines highlight PhageNET DZIF, a network established and coordinated by Claßen, as an important platform for exchanging scientific knowledge and clinical experience.

By bringing together expertise in microbiology, clinical medicine, pharmacy, manufacturing, and regulation, the new framework aims to help specialists understand both the possibilities and the limitations of personalized phage therapy.

The recommendations were developed through a structured consensus process under the AWMF (Association of the Scientific Medical Societies in Germany). They are valid from January 5, 2026, through June 29, 2030, with the responsible committee reviewing them annually to determine whether updates are needed.

While phage therapy still requires stronger evidence from controlled clinical trials, these international standards establish a clearer path for its responsible development. For patients facing infections that conventional antibiotics cannot adequately treat, bacteria-killing viruses may eventually provide another valuable option.

#5661. Google DeepMind releases new advanced robotics AI model and next-generation gene prediction model

Alphabet Inc.’s artificial intelligence research lab, Google DeepMind, Tuesday debuted the next generation of Gemini Robotics, the company’s most capable vision-language-action model to date for creating an “AI brain” for robotics.

Separately, DeepMind announced AlphaGenome 2 today, a next-generation AI model that can predict how DNA sequences and their variations affect human cell types, creating a powerful biological tool for fighting disease and drug development.

DeepMind said Gemini Robotics 2.5 enhances dexterity, reliability and safety to help engineers bring robots out of the lab and into dynamic, unstructured, real-world environments where they can coordinate alongside humans.

The company said that with the release of Gemini 4 Argon, the research division has been able to accelerate robot research and reach into physical AI. The new robotics AI model was tested across over 200 distinct tasks and the company said it anticipates scaling even further.

Argon, the company’s frontier artificial intelligence large language model, rolled out in late September, bringing advanced reasoning to the enterprise. Using the capabilities behind this new, flagship model, DeepMind said it allowed Gemini Robotics 2.5 to increase the breadth and speed with which robots can learn new skills and apply them to real-world scenarios.

The 2.5 version makes a significant jump in optimization and performance across three key areas. Boosted dexterity means robots running on 2.5 can perform more tasks with greater accuracy, including using everyday tools to handle delicate, flexible objects. With increased reliability, the new model successfully packed automotive parts with a 96% success rate during real-world proof-of-concept tests at Mercedes-Benz. Finally, DeepMind enhanced safety with improved physical steerability and introduced a new benchmark for testing against jailbreaks.

In evaluations, Robotics 2.5 now achieves a 30% to 100% success rate depending on the task and completes tasks 20% to 30% faster compared with the previous version’s baseline.

The company said that, like previous models, it natively works with many different types of robots, including Apptronik Inc.’s Apollo 2 humanoid robots and the Franka Duo platform with two-fingered parallel grippers.

“This is what we built Apollo for: useful work alongside people in real industrial settings,” Apptronik co-founder and Chief Executive Jeff Cardenas said. “Pairing Apollo 2 with Gemini Robotics, we saw the models improve dramatically in just a few weeks of post-training and carry over to Mercedes-Benz production with very little drop-off.”

Gemini Robotics 2.5 is rolling out today via DeepMind’s robotics partners, including Agile Robots SE, Apptronik and Boston Dynamics Inc.

AI models such as AlphaGenome help drug development and biotechnology companies turn genetic data into testable leads. By predicting how DNA changes affect gene activity and which cells in the body those changes act in, they can guide researchers to promising drug targets and help prioritize experiments.

Announced today, AlphaGenome 2 adds finer detail about specific cell types and states, potentially revealing disease-related effects that broader tissue-level models miss. These predictions guide research rather than replace experimental validation; the model is not approved for clinical or diagnostic use.

The problem researchers face is that every cell in the body carries the same DNA; however, different genes are activated at different times to differentiate cells and adjust their behavior. For example, a heart muscle cell or an immune cell fighting an infection may have the same DNA, but they use the blueprint to produce different proteins, enzymes and other tools to do their job.

DeepMind used global efforts from the Human Cell Atlas, a scientific consortium that mapped gene expression in millions of cells, to give the world an unprecedented view of how different cells use genes. However, predicting the paths and variations that drive activation and expression changes remains a major challenge.

Professor Sarah Teichmann, co-founder of the Human Cell Atlas and professor of Stem Cell Medicine at the University of Cambridge, said what makes Alphagenome 2 so powerful is “how it adapts directly to new single-cell data without retraining, predicting how DNA variants act in newly profiled cell states,” and that it can adapt even from very small samples.

According to DeepMind, the new model can predict core experimental readouts of DNA function as the previous generation, including gene expression, histone modification and chromatin accessibility – but also adds DNA methylation, which is a significant part of epigenetics, which explains how behaviors, environment and life experiences can influence gene activity.
