#5659. Gene editing could replace a lifetime of medication, but there's a catch

Imagine receiving a single treatment that could keep your cholesterol under control for decades, potentially eliminating the need for daily medication. Advances in gene editing are bringing that possibility closer to reality. But scientists say the same technology that could revolutionize medicine also raises difficult questions about safety, permanent genetic changes, and unintended consequences.

Gene therapy is already being used to treat certain serious illnesses. These treatments can introduce working copies of genes, silence harmful genetic activity, or make changes directly to DNA. Unlike conventional medications that must be taken repeatedly, some genetic treatments are designed to work after just one administration.

More than 6,000 rare genetic disorders have been identified, although only a small proportion currently have targets that can be treated. Gene therapies have already achieved important successes against conditions such as spinal muscular atrophy and sickle cell disease.

Now, researchers are exploring whether similar approaches could help prevent or manage far more widespread health problems, including high cholesterol, heart disease, obesity, and diabetes.

That raises a fundamental question: Just because scientists can permanently change a person's genetic activity, does that mean they should?

In a perspective published in JAMA Internal Medicine, University of Michigan Health Frankel Cardiovascular Center cardiologists Eric D. Smith, M.D., and Venkatesh L. Murthy, M.D., Ph.D., outline how doctors and researchers should weigh the potential benefits of genomic therapies against their risks.

The two gene therapy researchers explain why these treatments are so promising, what makes them different from conventional medicines, and what must happen before they can be safely offered to millions of people.

Why One-Time Gene Therapy Is Different From Daily Medication

One of the most appealing features of gene therapy is the possibility of achieving lasting results without repeated treatments.

Traditional medicines generally work only as long as patients continue taking them. Genomic therapies operate differently because they act on genetic material itself. They may provide a healthy version of a gene, suppress a gene responsible for harmful effects, or modify a specific DNA sequence.

This makes it possible to develop treatments intended to work after a single dose. Such therapies are often called "one-and-done" treatments.

However, receiving a treatment only once does not necessarily mean its effects will last a lifetime.

Smith explains that many gene therapies use modified viruses to carry genetic instructions into cells. The immune system can recognize these delivery vehicles and develop a response against them. As a result, administering the same treatment again may be difficult or impossible, even if its benefits begin to fade.

Another important distinction concerns which cells are changed. Current gene therapies generally target somatic cells, which are the body's cells other than those involved in reproduction. Unlike germline editing, these treatments are not intended to create genetic changes that can be inherited by future generations.

Why Gene Editing Common Diseases Raises New Risks

For people living with rare, devastating genetic conditions, the benefits of gene therapy may clearly outweigh the potential dangers. Some patients have few effective treatment options, making even an experimental intervention worth considering.

The situation becomes considerably more complicated when the same technology is used against common diseases.

Conditions such as high cholesterol, heart disease, obesity, and diabetes already have established treatments. Many of these medications can be adjusted as a patient's condition changes or discontinued if troublesome side effects develop.

A permanent genetic intervention may not offer that flexibility.

Murthy also points to a major concern involving the number of people who might eventually receive these treatments. A serious side effect that occurs only rarely could still harm a substantial number of patients if a therapy is administered to millions.

For that reason, treatments intended for widespread use must meet especially demanding safety standards.

Five Questions Scientists Say Must Be Answered

To help determine when genomic therapy is appropriate, Smith and Murthy propose evaluating five essential factors:

The final question may be especially challenging.

Clinical trials typically involve relatively small groups of patients who are monitored for limited periods. Although these studies can identify many important safety concerns, they may miss extremely rare complications or problems that take years to develop.

Some adverse effects might only become apparent after a treatment has reached a much larger population.

The Problem of Tracking Risks That Could Emerge Years Later

Smith argues that long-term monitoring cannot be treated as an afterthought. It needs to be an essential part of how gene therapies are introduced into medical practice.

Patient registries, which collect information about people receiving particular treatments, have already shown how valuable extended follow-up can be.

However, therapies that could eventually reach millions of patients will require monitoring systems capable of operating on a much larger scale.

These systems must be independent and standardized so researchers can consistently evaluate whether treatments remain effective and whether unexpected health problems appear over time.

Without reliable long-term data, doctors may struggle to determine the full consequences of genetic interventions that cannot easily be reversed.

Could Some Genetic Changes Be Too Risky to Make Permanent?

Another concern is whether certain diseases or biological processes are suitable for permanent treatment at all.

Murthy emphasizes that developing the ability to alter a genetic target does not automatically make doing so the best medical decision.

Some conditions require careful adjustments to medication doses over time. In other cases, the difference between an effective treatment and a harmful one can be extremely small. Changing a biological process too much or too little could create serious complications.

Conventional medications offer an important advantage in these situations because doctors can modify or stop treatment as needed.

Permanent gene therapies generally lack that option.

Scientists may eventually overcome this limitation by developing genetic treatments with built-in biological "off-switches" or other methods for reversing their effects.

Until those approaches have been shown to work reliably, the ability to undo or adjust a treatment remains an important safety advantage of traditional medicine.

The Million-Dollar Challenge Facing Gene Therapy

Safety is not the only barrier to bringing gene editing into mainstream healthcare. Cost could also determine whether these treatments become widely available.

Some existing gene therapies have list prices above $1 million for a single patient, and several cost substantially more.

Such prices may be considered justifiable for certain rare, life-threatening conditions, particularly when treatment options are extremely limited.

But applying similar pricing to diseases affecting millions of people would place enormous financial pressure on healthcare systems.

Smith and Murthy argue that affordability and access must therefore be part of the discussion from the beginning.

Even a highly effective gene therapy could create new healthcare inequalities if only a small percentage of patients could obtain it. Researchers and policymakers must consider not just whether these treatments work, but also whether they can be delivered without making existing disparities worse.

Could One Gene-Editing Treatment Prevent Heart Disease for Decades?

Despite these challenges, the possibility of using gene editing to prevent common diseases is becoming increasingly realistic.

Researchers are already conducting early studies to investigate whether a single genetic treatment can produce long-lasting reductions in LDL, commonly known as "bad," cholesterol.

LDL cholesterol contributes to the buildup of fatty deposits inside arteries, which can increase the risk of heart attacks and other cardiovascular problems. Lowering LDL over extended periods is an important strategy for reducing cardiovascular risk.

If gene editing can safely produce sustained reductions, it could eventually offer a new approach to protecting cardiovascular health without requiring patients to take medication indefinitely.

However, promising early results will not be enough to justify widespread use.

Before these therapies become routine options for common conditions, researchers will need convincing evidence that their benefits last, their risks remain acceptably low over many years, and their costs are manageable. Reliable safeguards will also be essential.

For Smith and Murthy, the objective is not to hold back genetic medicine. It is to make sure that a technology with the potential to transform healthcare is introduced carefully and responsibly.

As gene therapy moves beyond rare disorders toward conditions affecting millions of people, the central challenge will be ensuring that the promise of lasting protection does not come at the expense of long-term patient safety.

Materials provided by Michigan Medicine - University of Michigan. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5658. Inside Tommy Lee Jones’ 6,000-Acre Texas Ranch Complete With 2 Polo Fields

Texas native Tommy Lee Jones moved to New York City to pursue an acting career back in 1969, but he knew he had found real success when he realized he could head back to the Lone Star State.

“There was a time when I became aware that I could live anywhere I want to,” “The Fugitive” star told The New York Times in a profile. “So, in my wisdom, I went home.”

These days, “home” for the 80-year-old actor is a sprawling ranch in San Saba, TX. Jones resides on the 6,000-square-foot property with his wife, Dawn Laurel-Jones, 62, who is from San Antonio.

In addition to a two-story limestone residence that was built as a fort in 1856, the massive plot of land is a full-fledged retreat. There is not one, but two polo fields, and an array of animals from horses to dogs to feral pigs.

The property is a fully operable ranch, and in 2006, Jones told Texas Monthly all about what a typical day is like.

"In the summers, we'll work cattle, and then at about 7 o'clock at night, we'll start playing polo," he said. "We'll play until about 9, and then when we're done, we put the meat on the fire and watch the dark come. It's a good life. Everyone is happy."

Although Jones is famously private and has not shared imagery of the home, he did share a quote that piques interest.

“I didn’t want any fences around the house,” he said while telling the Times of the feral hogs that dig up his yard. “As you can see, the house has an architectural statement to make.”

Inside, the abode is just as fascinating. The publication reported that the living room is furnished with two Frank Lloyd Wright slate-top tables and a Gustav Stickley sofa that is more than a century old.

Antiques and collected art pieces can be found throughout the home, as well as other finds from the property itself, such as flint arrowheads, shed antlers, and small animal skulls.

Jones has ridden horses for most of his life and took an interest in polo in the 1970s. He regularly hosts polo matches at his ranch, which is home to 25 horses.

According to Social Life Magazine, Jones has been expanding his cattle ranch for decades after first acquiring it in the 1980s. He has built onto the property with additional parcels of working ranchland over time.

The couple’s passion for polo has made an impression on more than one of their homes. In 2019, Jones offloaded his Florida equestrian estate for $11.5 million. The 55-acre property, known as “San Saba,” the same name as his hometown, is 72 miles north of Miami in a town called Wellington.

While that residence was considerably smaller than the Texas ranch he lives in today, its polo facilities are remarkable.

Bradley A. Scherer, the listing agent who handled the sale, told Mansion Global that the estate was “one of the only, if not the only, property listed during 2019 that was a true, full-service polo facility with existing polo fields.”

Jones had purchased the Florida estate in 2002 for $2.95 million, then acquired a secondary parcel for $550,000 in 2012. With an additional third parcel, the land was all sold in a single transaction, after it lingered on the market for eight years.

The original asking price was $26.75 million.

#5656. The brain’s hidden fear mechanism may explain anxiety and PTSD

The brain has a remarkable ability to recognize danger, but new research suggests that this survival mechanism may also explain why people sometimes feel threatened in situations that are actually safe. The discovery offers a possible explanation for the intense fear responses associated with anxiety and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

For years, scientists believed that fear helps the brain distinguish more clearly between threatening and harmless experiences. However, a study led by researchers at the Douglas Research Centre at McGill University and the University of Toronto-Scarborough challenges that assumption. The findings, published in Nature Neuroscience, suggest that fear may have the opposite effect.

In experiments involving mice, researchers trained the animals to associate one environment with danger and another with safety. Instead of developing increasingly separate neural representations of the two locations, the animals' brain activity began to show overlapping patterns. In other words, the brain's representations of safe and dangerous experiences became less distinct.

"Our findings suggest fear may blur the boundary between danger and safety rather than sharpen it," said senior author Mark Brandon, Associate Professor in McGill's Department of Psychiatry and Researcher at the Douglas. "This could reshape how scientists think about anxiety and PTSD."

How Scientists Watched the Brain Process Fear

To investigate how these changes occur, the research team developed an unusual experimental setup that combined augmented reality with real-time brain imaging.

The researchers created a specialized arena in which mice could be virtually "teleported" between environments associated with danger and safety. By changing the sights and sounds surrounding the animals, scientists could make them experience different settings without physically moving them to another location.

At the same time, miniature microscopes monitored hundreds of neurons in the hippocampus, a brain region essential for learning and memory. This allowed the team to observe how the brain's activity changed as the mice transitioned between experiences associated with safety and threat.

"That gave us something conventional fear conditioning experiments cannot easily provide: a moment-by-moment view of the brain switching between competing maps of dangerous and safe memories," said Robert Rozeske, Assistant Professor in University of Toronto's Department of Psychology and lead author on the publication.

Why the Brain May Confuse Safety With Danger

Although mixing memories of safe and dangerous experiences might seem like a problem, the researchers believe it could serve an important evolutionary purpose.

The experiments suggested that overlapping memory representations allowed the brain to retrieve information about previous threats more rapidly. This could help an animal recognize possible danger and respond before it is too late.

Such a strategy comes with a trade-off. By prioritizing speed over accuracy, the brain may react to a potential threat even when the current situation is harmless. From a survival perspective, responding unnecessarily to a false alarm may sometimes be preferable to overlooking a genuine danger.

"The ventral hippocampus may be part of a system that prioritizes a rapid 'better safe than sorry' response," said Rozeske. "In other words, the brain may sacrifice precision for speed when danger matters."

The ventral hippocampus is a part of the hippocampus involved in processing emotionally significant experiences, including fear and anxiety. The new findings suggest that overlapping memory representations in this region may help the brain switch rapidly into a defensive state.

A Hidden Survival Mechanism May Help Explain PTSD

The discovery could also offer insight into why people with anxiety and trauma-related disorders sometimes experience powerful fear responses in situations that pose no immediate threat.

For someone with PTSD, an otherwise harmless sight, sound, or environment can trigger memories associated with a traumatic experience. The resulting fear can feel immediate and overwhelming, even when the person is objectively safe.

The researchers suggest that such reactions may arise, at least in part, when a normally useful survival mechanism becomes excessively sensitive. Instead of reflecting a system that has simply stopped distinguishing between different memories, these responses might involve a brain mechanism that shifts too quickly from recognizing safety to anticipating danger.

"Our study suggests that's not necessarily a broken pattern-separation system, but possibly an overactive version of a normal survival mechanism gone into overdrive," said Brandon. "That reframing could guide therapeutic approaches to address an overly fast transition to 'danger mode'."

Because the experiments were conducted in mice, additional research is needed to determine whether the same mechanisms contribute to anxiety and PTSD in humans. Nevertheless, the findings provide a new way to understand how fear influences memory and why a brain system designed to protect against danger might sometimes generate fear when no immediate threat exists.

The study, "Overlapping representations in the ventral hippocampus support rapid fear memory retrieval," by Robert Rozeske and Mark Brandon, was published in Nature Neuroscience.

The research received support from the Canadian Institutes of Health Research and the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada.

#5655. Kubernetes had settled into quiet maturity until AI blew the doors back open

Kubernetes has grown from a maturing container orchestrator into the agent substrate that enterprises are counting on to run artificial intelligence. The shift revives old security ideas such as perimeters while raising the stakes for portability across clouds.

Infrastructure providers are racing to make that foundation simpler to deploy and safer to run. Broadcom Inc. used KubeCon to unveil two open-source initiatives, and the show marks a turning point for a project that had seemed settled, according to Dilpreet Bindra (pictured), senior director of engineering in the VCF Division at Broadcom.

“There were a few that were like, Kubernetes is becoming mature, and so things were stabilizing, and they were less energy, I would say. And this KubeCon just blasts those doors wide open because Kubernetes has become the foundation for AI,” Bindra said.

Bindra spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how Kubernetes has become the agent substrate and how Broadcom is adding security in depth and workload conformance to make it portable across clouds. (* Disclosure below.)

Agents are bringing back security concepts the cloud era had declared dead. Broadcom’s approach is security in depth, using its vDefend firewall at the network perimeter and deeper inside to cut off network access when rogue agents appear, Bindra explained.

“How do you then isolate them in a compute boundary in our vSphere Pods, which is a micro VM, so you can have a very secure runtime,” Bindra said. “You can employ things like Agent Substrate to be able to run within them.”

Portability is the other half of Broadcom’s agenda. The company is co-chairing a new working group on Kubernetes workload conformance, aiming to end the separate validations software makers run for each distribution, including VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service, or VKS. It also contributed its VM API project to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation, bringing virtual machines into Kubernetes as first-class citizens.

“We want Kubernetes to be Kubernetes wherever it runs in any environment,” Bindra said. “You don’t have to do individual validations of VKS, and then do individual validations of other Kubernetes distributions. You can do it as one Kubernetes.”

#5652. Goodbye, cavities? Scientists create gel that could regrow tooth enamel

Scientists have developed a new gel that could make it possible to regrow damaged tooth enamel, potentially overcoming one of the biggest limitations in dental care. Unlike bones and many other tissues in the body, tooth enamel cannot naturally regenerate once it has been lost. The new treatment offers a promising way to rebuild this protective layer, strengthen teeth, and help prevent future decay.

The innovation comes from researchers at the University of Nottingham's School of Pharmacy and Department of Chemical and Environmental Engineering. Their new material is inspired by the biological processes that form tooth enamel during early childhood. It is designed to repair enamel that has been weakened by mineral loss or worn away by erosion, while also reinforcing enamel that remains healthy.

The findings, published in Nature Communications, could pave the way for a new generation of dental treatments that go beyond protecting existing enamel and actually help restore its structure.

One of the most promising features of the technology is its simplicity. Dentists could apply the gel directly to teeth using a procedure similar to existing fluoride treatments, making it potentially easy to incorporate into routine dental care.

Unlike conventional fluoride products, however, the new gel contains no fluoride. Instead, it uses a material made from proteins that imitates important characteristics of the natural proteins responsible for guiding enamel formation when teeth first develop.

Once applied, the gel forms a thin but durable coating that penetrates the tooth's surface and fills microscopic cracks and gaps. This coating then provides a framework for rebuilding the mineral structure of enamel.

The process relies on calcium and phosphate ions, two essential mineral components naturally present in saliva. The gel attracts these minerals and helps organize them into new crystals that grow in an orderly pattern.

Scientists call this process epitaxial mineralization. Essentially, it means that new mineral crystals grow in alignment with the existing enamel, allowing the newly formed material to become structurally integrated with the original tooth surface.

This organization is especially important because enamel gets its exceptional hardness and durability from the precise arrangement of its mineral crystals. Simply depositing minerals on a tooth is not enough to recreate the complex structure that makes natural enamel so effective.

By guiding crystal growth, the new gel can restore both the microscopic architecture and the physical properties of healthy enamel.

A Potential Solution for Tooth Sensitivity and Decay

The researchers also discovered that their material can be used on exposed dentine, commonly called dentin in the United States. Dentin is the layer of tooth tissue beneath the enamel. It is softer than enamel and contains tiny channels that can transmit sensations toward the nerves inside the tooth.

When enamel wears away, or gums recede, exposed dentin can make teeth particularly sensitive to hot, cold, sweet, or acidic foods and drinks.

The new gel can encourage the formation of an enamel-like mineral layer over exposed dentin. This could help reduce tooth sensitivity while also improving the attachment of dental restorations, such as fillings and other treatments used to repair damaged teeth.

The potential benefits are significant. Enamel deterioration is a major factor in tooth decay and contributes to dental problems that affect nearly half of the world's population. These conditions can cause pain, infections, and eventually tooth loss. Poor oral health is also associated with broader health problems, including diabetes and cardiovascular disease.

One of the greatest challenges in dentistry is that enamel has no living cells capable of rebuilding it after teeth have fully developed. Although saliva can naturally replace some minerals lost during the earliest stages of enamel damage, the body cannot regenerate substantial amounts of enamel that have been worn away.

Existing treatments, including fluoride varnishes and remineralization products, can help protect teeth and repair early mineral loss. However, they cannot fully reconstruct enamel that has already been lost.

The new technology aims to overcome that limitation by encouraging the formation of new mineral tissue with properties resembling those of the original enamel.

Regenerated Enamel Performs Like Natural Tooth Enamel

The research team tested the mechanical strength and durability of the regenerated material under conditions designed to mimic everyday use.

These experiments examined how the newly formed enamel responded to activities and exposures that teeth routinely experience, including brushing, chewing, and contact with acidic foods.

The results were encouraging. According to the researchers, the regenerated enamel displayed mechanical properties comparable to those of healthy natural enamel, suggesting that the material could provide more than a temporary protective coating.

Dr. Abshar Hasan, a postdoctoral fellow and the study's lead author, explained why recreating enamel's internal structure is so important.

"Dental enamel has a unique structure, which gives enamel its remarkable properties that protect our teeth throughout life against physical, chemical, and thermal insults. When our material is applied to demineralized or eroded enamel, or exposed dentine, the material promotes the growth of crystals in an integrated and organized manner, recovering the architecture of our natural healthy enamel. We have tested the mechanical properties of these regenerated tissues under conditions simulating 'real-life situations' such as tooth brushing, chewing, and exposure to acidic foods, and found that the regenerated enamel behaves just like healthy enamel."

These findings suggest that the gel could eventually offer a way to restore the strength and protective function of damaged enamel rather than simply slowing further deterioration. However, the laboratory results do not yet establish how well the treatment will perform over extended periods in patients.

Beyond its ability to regenerate enamel, the researchers emphasize that the technology was developed with practical dental applications in mind.

The gel is designed to be safe, simple to apply, and suitable for manufacturing on a larger scale. Its versatility could also allow it to be incorporated into several types of dental products, potentially benefiting patients of different ages with enamel erosion, tooth sensitivity, or other problems involving exposed dentin.

Professor Alvaro Mata, Chair in Biomedical Engineering & Biomaterials at the University of Nottingham, led the study and highlighted the potential for translating the discovery into products that dentists can use.

"We are very excited because the technology has been designed with the clinician and patient in mind. It is safe, can be easily and rapidly applied, and it is scalable. Also, the technology is versatile, which opens the opportunity to be translated into multiple types of products to help patients of all ages suffering from a variety of dental problems associated with loss of enamel and exposed dentine. We have started this process with our start-up company Mintech-Bio and hope to have a first product out by next year; this innovation could soon be helping patients worldwide."

The researchers have already begun working toward commercialization through their company, Mintech-Bio, with the goal of introducing an initial product as early as the year following the announcement.

Although further development and clinical validation will be important before the technology becomes an established dental treatment, its ability to recreate the structure and strength of natural enamel represents a promising advance.

If the approach proves successful in patients, it could fundamentally change how dentists address enamel loss, opening the possibility of rebuilding tooth surfaces that previously could only be protected or restored using conventional dental materials.

#5651. A surprising discovery could help aging muscles repair themselves

Muscles can begin losing their strength and ability to recover surprisingly early in the aging process. Over time, muscle tissue may develop scar tissue, accumulate fat, and lose some of the specialized fibers responsible for rapid, powerful movements. These changes can make everyday activities more difficult and gradually reduce mobility and physical independence.

Now, scientists in Japan have identified a promising molecule that could help protect the body's natural muscle repair system and potentially make it more effective. In laboratory experiments, the compound strengthened an important biological signal involved in muscle regeneration, increasing its ability to connect with a key cellular receptor by more than twofold.

The discovery comes from a team led by Professor Ryuichi Tatsumi at Kyushu University's Faculty of Agriculture. Their findings, published in Scientific Reports, suggest a possible new approach to addressing the cellular changes that make aging muscles increasingly difficult to repair.

How Aging Disrupts the Body's Muscle Repair System

Skeletal muscles are the muscles attached to bones that allow us to walk, lift objects, maintain posture, and perform other voluntary movements. Although these muscles experience wear and tear throughout life, they also have a remarkable ability to repair themselves.

Much of that repair depends on specialized stem cells known as satellite cells. These cells normally remain inactive, positioned alongside muscle fibers until they receive a signal that repair or regeneration is needed. Once activated, they can multiply and develop into muscle cells that help restore damaged tissue.

An essential part of this process involves a protein called hepatocyte growth factor, or HGF. Despite its name, HGF plays important roles beyond the liver, including helping activate the stem cells responsible for muscle regeneration.

Under normal conditions, HGF is stored within the supportive material surrounding muscle fibers. When muscles experience an injury or mechanical stimulation, such as physical movement or stretching, the protein can be released.

HGF then attaches to a receptor called c-met on the surface of satellite cells. Receptors are specialized proteins that receive molecular signals and trigger responses inside cells. In this case, the interaction helps awaken dormant satellite cells, allowing them to multiply, mature, and participate in repairing muscle fibers.

But this carefully coordinated system becomes less reliable with age.

A Hidden Chemical Change May Weaken Aging Muscles

The researchers' previous work revealed that HGF can undergo a chemical modification known as nitration. This process attaches a chemical group called a nitro group to particular locations on a protein, potentially changing its structure and interfering with its normal activity.

For HGF, the researchers identified two especially important locations, Y198 and Y250. Both lie within the region involved in attaching to the c-met receptor.

When these sites undergo nitration, HGF becomes less capable of connecting with its receptor. The result is similar to a key that has become damaged and can no longer operate its intended lock.

This disruption could have important consequences for aging muscles. Even if the body continues producing HGF, chemical changes may prevent the protein from properly activating the stem cells needed for tissue repair. The researchers believe this mechanism may contribute to age-related muscle wasting and declining regenerative capacity.

"HGF is not necessarily missing as we age," explains Tatsumi. "Rather, it can be chemically altered after it is made. That led us to wonder whether a compound with strong antioxidant capacity might protect HGF, either by preventing nitration or by compensating for the functional loss it causes."

Scientists Test Two Powerful Sulfur Compounds

To investigate that possibility, the team studied two compounds with strong antioxidant properties: glutathione trisulfide (GSSSG) and lipoic acid trisulfide (LASSS).

Antioxidants can help limit certain types of chemical damage caused by reactive molecules. Such damage can interfere with proteins and other essential components of cells, particularly when the body's normal protective systems become less effective.

The two compounds belong to a chemical family called trisulfides. Their defining feature is a chain of three sulfur atoms connected to one another. This arrangement gives them unusual chemical properties, including an ability to participate in reactions involving the transfer of electrons, known as redox reactions.

Because these reactions play important roles in cellular chemistry, trisulfides have attracted growing interest as potential ingredients in new medicines.

In the first set of experiments, both compounds reduced nitration at the two vulnerable sites on HGF. However, preventing this chemical modification did not completely restore the protein's ability to attach to c-met.

The scientists therefore increased the amount of trisulfide used relative to HGF. They changed the molar ratio, which compares the number of molecules of each substance, from 1:4000 to 1:8000.

That adjustment produced an unexpected result.

An Unexpected Discovery Creates "Super HGF"

At the higher concentration, LASSS did much more than protect HGF from chemical damage. It also dramatically improved the protein's ability to bind to its receptor.

Compared with untreated HGF, the protein exposed to LASSS showed more than twice the binding affinity for c-met. In other words, it could attach to its target receptor much more strongly, potentially enhancing a critical step in the muscle repair process.

The treatment also made HGF more resistant to the loss of function caused by nitration, particularly at the Y198 site.

Notably, the effect was specific to LASSS. Although GSSSG had also reduced nitration in the earlier experiments, it did not produce the same improvement in receptor binding.

"This exceeded our expectations," comments Tatsumi. "We knew trisulfides had diverse biological functions, but we never expected that simply mixing HGF with LASSS would produce such a striking effect.

"What this tells us is that LASSS does more than simply neutralize reactive molecules. It may interact directly with HGF and induce a subtle structural change, creating an enhanced 'Super HGF' form that binds c-met more strongly and resists nitration."

The researchers suspect that LASSS interacts with HGF in a way that slightly alters the protein's three-dimensional shape. Because a protein's shape helps determine how well it interacts with other molecules, even a small structural adjustment could substantially change its activity.

The result is what the team describes as "Super HGF," a potentially enhanced form of the body's existing muscle repair signal.

Importantly, stronger receptor binding does not automatically establish that muscle regeneration itself has improved. Additional experiments will be needed to determine whether this molecular enhancement translates into better muscle healing and strength.

Mouse Experiments Reveal Promising Protection

After observing the effects in laboratory experiments, the researchers wanted to determine whether LASSS could also protect HGF inside living muscle tissue.

They used mice subjected to tail suspension, an established experimental method for studying muscle atrophy. By reducing normal weight bearing and muscle use, this technique produces some of the changes associated with prolonged inactivity, including muscle deterioration.

Mice that received LASSS before the experiment showed significantly less HGF nitration than untreated animals. This suggested that the compound's ability to protect the muscle repair protein was not limited to controlled laboratory conditions.

Once again, GSSSG failed to produce the same protective result.

These findings provide early evidence that LASSS can influence the chemical processes affecting HGF within living animals. However, the mouse experiments demonstrated protection against nitration, not that LASSS restored lost muscle mass or improved physical strength.

The researchers emphasize that studies involving aging animals are still necessary to establish the compound's effectiveness and safety in vivo, meaning within a living organism.

A Potential New Strategy Against Age-Related Muscle Loss

The discovery could eventually contribute to treatments aimed at maintaining muscle function during aging or extended periods of inactivity.

Muscle deterioration is not limited to older adults. It can also occur during prolonged bed rest or other situations in which muscles are used less frequently. When muscle repair mechanisms become impaired, recovering lost strength and function can become especially challenging.

Rather than replacing the body's natural repair machinery, the approach explored in this study seeks to protect and enhance an existing biological signal. If the benefits can be confirmed in future studies, strengthening HGF activity could become one strategy for supporting muscle regeneration.

The scientists also believe that the underlying effects of LASSS on HGF may extend across species. That raises the possibility of applications not only in human medicine but also in veterinary care, particularly for aging companion animals such as dogs and cats.

For now, the findings represent an early step toward understanding how a naturally occurring muscle repair pathway might be strengthened. Whether LASSS can safely and effectively preserve muscle function during aging remains an open question.

Still, the unexpected discovery that a sulfur-based compound can both protect and enhance a critical repair protein offers a promising direction for future research, with the long-term goal of helping people maintain mobility, independence, and a better quality of life as they grow older.

Materials provided by Kyushu University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5650. 5 Packing Tips for a Smooth Move

Moving can be a time-consuming process, but it doesn't need to be stressful. We have some tips to help you enjoy a smooth move from your old home to the new. With the right system in place, there is no need to be overwhelmed by the move.

Before you make the move, check out these 5 packing tips.

A common mistake people make when moving is to pack all of their belongings and move them, only to realize upon unpacking that many of the items should have been donated, sold, or thrown out. Before you pack, ruthlessly declutter your home. Packing things only to get rid of them at the new house is a waste of your time and money.

Some questions to ask yourself as you declutter before packing are:

As you pack and move, things are bound to get misplaced. To avoid the stress of a missing document or essential information, keep a folder (either physical, digital, or both) where you won't misplace it that is filled with essential paperwork. This might include:

Greg Dallaire - Green Bay Real Estate Expert says, "Be sure to set up any utilities in the new place to be turned on and ready when you arrive. Even if it means paying for utilities at two places for a brief overlap, it is often worth the convenience. In addition to basics like water and power, call ahead to make sure you will have internet, TV, and any other services you need."

This is also a great time to move additional services to the new address, like security, pest control, or house cleaning.

Even if you are moving all in one day from one Calgary home to another, don't count on being able to unpack everything you need on night one. Instead, pack a suitcase with a few days' worth of clothes and necessities for everyone in the house. This way, you can settle into your new home without scrambling to find a towel or toothbrush before spending your first night there.

The suitcase should include more than just your change of clothes and toiletries. Anything you might need for 2-3 days should be packed in it, including:

As you pack, or have your movers pack, label each box with not just the contents inside but the room it should be placed in at the new home. This way, whether you have professional movers, a team of friends and family, or just your own household, it will be easy to make sure each box lands in the proper place.

One of the easiest ways to do this is by color coding. Assign a color to each room and label accordingly. For example, let's say the kitchen is blue. All boxes that should be brought to the kitchen will be labeled with blue tape, and on move-in day you can hang a large blue paper in the kitchen. This simple system will make unpacking much smoother.

#5649. Enterprises, not a handful of giants, are becoming the GPU buyers that matter

Enterprises building AI-native applications are discovering that raw GPU capacity is only half the equation. As Kubernetes users move from cloud-native to AI-native stacks, the question is shifting from who has the most accelerators to who can run distributed, secure workloads at global scale.

The first wave of so-called neoclouds stood up massive GPU clusters for a handful of the largest buyers, but enterprise developers need far more than data center capacity. The Constant Company LLC, which does business as Vultr, has bet on AMD silicon and open software stacks to win AI infrastructure deals. It is positioning itself as a full-stack cloud built to close that gap, according to Kevin Cochrane (pictured), chief marketing officer of Vultr.

“In the early market … it was all about just standing up large GPU clusters wherever you could get land, power and shell, and then just selling it on through to a hyperscaler,” Cochrane said. “And somehow in that mix, people forgot that you still need cloud, right? You still gotta run this thing.”

Cochrane spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed why enterprise AI demands distributed cloud infrastructure, how global networking shapes GPU adoption and Vultr’s new programs for open-source builders. (* Disclosure below.)

Every computing supercycle reshapes architecture from the data center up to the application layer, according to Cochrane. In AI, the first iteration was tuned for a narrow group of the biggest GPU buyers, he explained. Enterprises have different requirements, and serving them means returning to computing’s longer trajectory.

“We took a little bit of a step backwards because in that early iteration of the new architecture, when we over-indexed on a limited number of buyers, we went back more to centralized systems,” Cochrane said. “And we have to remember that the long arc of compute is towards decentralized distributed systems driven by open standards and driven by open source.”

Distributed AI also changes how inference gets served. Because many users ask the same question, Vultr aims to maximize token reuse through a global namespace that shares KV cache across nodes, work it is pursuing with partners such as Vast Data Inc., Cochrane noted. Connectivity between data centers matters just as much, since enterprises want private networks isolated from every other tenant on a public cloud.

“In the neocloud moment, I think some of the complexity of what’s required to operate workloads at global scale for enterprises has been forgotten or just assumed it wouldn’t matter,” Cochrane said. “But … it’s the biggest barrier to getting enterprises to actually leverage GPUs from a new cloud because the networking connectivity, it just doesn’t work.”

Vultr is also putting resources behind the open-source community building the AI stack. The company has joined the Cloud Native Computing Foundation as a platinum member, and at KubeCon it highlighted its Open Source Credits Program, which provisions infrastructure for the maintainers behind new CNCF projects.

“All of those projects need compute, right? The maintainers aren’t going to suddenly open up their own personal checkbooks,” Cochrane said. “How can you build the next great CNCF project if you don’t have compute?”

#5648. The 10 Affordable Cities Where Homeowners Are the Least Locked In by Housing Costs

Many homeowners who began the year hoping to move may now be locked in by soaring mortgage rates that threaten to nearly double their monthly payments—but a handful of budget-friendly markets still offer relief.

These rare pockets of affordability are clustered primarily across the Midwest and South, including Pittsburgh; Baltimore; Buffalo, NY; New Orleans; Detroit; Birmingham, AL; San Antonio, TX; Akron, OH; McAllen, TX; and Philadelphia.

Nationally, the typical U.S. mortgage holder pays roughly $1,300 in principal and interest per month. If they were to purchase a home today, that payment would surge by more than 85%, or $1,100, according to a new report on America's "locked-in" homeowners from Realtor.com®.

The market's current predicament can be traced to the COVID-19 pandemic years, when historically low mortgage rates whipped up a buying and refinancing frenzy. As of July 2026, more than a quarter (27%) of all fixed-rate mortgages on record for single-family homes and condominiums were originated in 2020 and 2021 alone.

Once mortgage rates began climbing again in 2022, homebuying and refinancing both hit a wall. Over the subsequent four years, only about 1 in 4 mortgages on record was originated, highlighting the sharp pullback in activity as a result of higher borrowing costs.

"For those who purchased before mortgage rates shot sharply higher, the sentiment of 'I couldn’t afford to buy my home today' continues to ring true in most cases, contributing to historically low mobility and some of the leanest for-sale inventory on record," notes Realtor.com senior economist Hannah Jones.

In other words, homeowners who were fortunate enough to secure a sub-4% mortgage rate at the height of the pandemic are reluctant to list. Trading up or downsizing today means taking out a mortgage with a steeply higher rate, gobbling up a much bigger share of their income.

Just how much bigger? Purchasing a median-priced home at the Oct. 22 rate of 7.32%, assuming a 14.3% down payment, would translate into a monthly principal and interest payment of nearly $2,500, almost double the $1,300 typical owners currently pay.

However, in parts of the U.S. where home prices remain accessible, the "lock-in" effect is felt less acutely, keeping inventory—and people—moving and creating a self-reinforcing cycle.

"The affordability of these markets enables mobility, which means the typical outstanding mortgage rate is higher, which helps reduce the payment jump associated with moving, which reinforces affordability," explains Jones.

In the South and Midwest, approximately three-quarters of mortgages carry a rate below 6%, compared to 78% nationally.

Additionally, nearly a quarter of all outstanding mortgages in these two regions were originated within the past four years at 6% or higher, compared with 21.6% in the Northeast and 17.7% in the West.

"That mix means fewer homeowners in these regions are clinging to 3%–4% rates, which lessens the lock-in effect," says Jones.

Across the 100 largest metros, Pittsburgh stands out as the nation's least "locked in" housing market, where a seller purchasing a new home in town would see a 43% increase in their monthly mortgage payment—a modest penalty compared to the 165% in San Jose, CA.

Baltimore is a close second, with a 45% payment gap, followed by Buffalo, at 46.1%.

"A 3% mortgage is a great reason to stay in a house, but it's not always a great reason to stay in a house that no longer fits your life," Colleen Collier, associate broker at Re/Max Plus in Buffalo, tells Realtor.com.

The latest housing data reflects the market's mobility and affordability. In October, Buffalo posted the largest year-over-year increase in active listings (+34.4%) among the 50 largest metros, paired with the largest growth in new listings (+13.1%).

At the same time, the median listing price in the metro registered at $259,999, down 2.8% from a year ago and sitting more than $155,000 below the national median.

Collier notes that while more local homeowners are willing to make a move, it does not necessarily mean they are comfortable giving up their low rates. They are being compelled by life changes.

"They're retiring, downsizing, or relocating to be closer to family," says the broker. "Many are looking to reduce maintenance and their overall living expenses. Others are relocating to a warmer climate. ... They're taking the equity they've built and putting it toward their next purchase."

Collier recently represented clients who sold their home of 30 years to downsize into an apartment. They were able to get a final sale price well above asking, which was enough to cover at least 10 years of apartment living, and fund future travel plans and a new car.

"What made this experience so rewarding was that the homeowner had more equity than they realized," says Collier. "After more than three decades in their home, selling wasn't simply about moving into a smaller space. It was about creating financial freedom and enjoying the next chapter of life."

In Akron, a typical homeowner currently paying just $868 per month should expect to see that figure rise nearly 62% under present-day market conditions—well above Buffalo’s level but still a far cry from the most locked-in coastal markets.

"The financial difference between staying in a home with a low mortgage rate and purchasing another home may be less dramatic here than in higher-priced markets," Mike Valerino, CEO of Akron Cleveland Association of Realtors, tells Realtor.com. "However, that doesn't mean the mortgage rate lock-in effect has disappeared."

According to Valerino, in Summit County, where Akron is located, new listings and closed sales were down in September while the average sales price increased, suggesting that despite the market's relative affordability, homeowners are still weighing the financial implications of moving.

"Life circumstances remain important drivers of housing decisions," he says, echoing Collier's argument. "Growing families need more space, empty nesters may want to downsize, and job changes, retirement, and family considerations can create reasons to move that outweigh the financial benefits of staying put."

At the same time, Valerino says that Akron's relative affordability does not insulate buyers and sellers from the challenges affecting housing markets nationally.

"The mortgage lock-in effect may be less severe here, but the cost of the next home still plays a major role in whether someone decides to move," he says.

In roughly a third of the 100 largest U.S. metros, a move to a median-priced home would more than double the monthly payment. Ballooning borrowing costs disproportionately penalize expensive coastal and fast-growing markets, leaving local homeowners feeling virtually trapped by their lower mortgages.

According to the latest data, the most "locked-in" markets in the U.S. include Portland, ME, San Jose, and Los Angeles, where anticipated monthly mortgage payments surged by more than 140%, grinding mobility to a halt. That friction has severely squeezed inventory and put upward pressure on home prices, sidelining first-time and budget buyers.

"Because homes in these markets are already expensive, buyers typically rely on larger mortgage balances, which amplifies the impact of rising rates," says Jones.

In Portland, for instance, a current owner holding on to a 4% mortgage rate makes a median payment of $1,270 per month. If they were to purchase a home comparable to theirs with a 26.2% down payment and took out a 7.32% mortgage, their payment would jump a staggering 167% to $3,392.

Mortgage rates would have to drop a long way from their current 7.18% level to close the gap between what current owners pay and what a buyer would pay today.

Rates would need to reach 6% before half of U.S. households could afford the median-priced home, and even then a move would still mean a payment about 62% higher than what the typical mortgage holder spends now.

Crucially, however, Jones stresses that falling mortgage rates alone are not enough. Because home values have appreciated significantly over the past few years, buying a median-priced home with a 4% mortgage would still cost about 29% more per month than what existing homeowners pay on their original COVID-19-era loans.

Valerino agrees, maintaining that there is no one "magic number" that will unlock the market.

"Rates in the 5% range could make moving more attractive to some homeowners, but affordability involves more than the interest rate," he says. "Home prices, property taxes, insurance, and accumulated equity all factor into that decision."

The market is poised to loosen gradually rather than all at once as more households buy in to higher rates, softening price growth narrows the gap, and rising incomes boost buying power.

"The lower-priced Midwest and South markets, where the gap is smallest and more loans carry higher rates, are likely to see the most activity first," predicts Jones. "Large coastal markets will need both lower rates and lower prices or significantly higher incomes before sellers feel free to move."

Snejana Farberov is a reporter at Realtor.com covering the U.S. housing market and the latest domestic real estate trends. She has worked as a general assignment journalist in New York City and Long Island for 16 years, writing for New York Post, Daily Mail, and News 12. Snejana earned bachelor's degrees in journalism and Italian from St. John's University, followed by a master’s degree from Columbia University School of Journalism.

#5647. A compound hidden in broccoli could help fight a devastating genetic disease

A natural substance found in broccoli could offer an unexpected new approach to treating a devastating genetic disease that progressively damages the nervous system. Researchers at Swinburne University have identified promising effects from the compound, raising hopes for a more affordable and accessible treatment for patients with few available options.

The disease, known as Friedreich ataxia, causes nerve cells in the brain and spinal cord to gradually deteriorate. As the damage progresses, patients lose their ability to coordinate movements, walk, and speak. The condition can also shorten life expectancy, and there is currently no cure. Approximately 200 Australians are living with the disease.

In a new study, scientists found that sulforaphane, a naturally occurring compound in broccoli, can increase levels of frataxin, a protein that is present in insufficient amounts in people with Friedreich ataxia. The researchers also found that the compound can help protect vulnerable nerve cells from damage.

How a Broccoli Compound Could Protect Nerve Cells

Frataxin plays an important role in keeping cells functioning properly, particularly those with high energy demands, such as nerve cells. In Friedreich ataxia, a genetic defect leads to reduced production of this essential protein, contributing to the progressive damage that characterizes the disease.

Sulforaphane appears promising because its potential benefits extend beyond increasing frataxin levels. Research indicates that it can also influence several biological processes involved in disease progression, including cellular stress and inflammation. Addressing multiple sources of damage at once could make the compound a valuable candidate for further investigation.

The findings are particularly encouraging for children with Friedreich ataxia. According to lead researcher Associate Professor Faith Kwa of Swinburne University, children account for a large proportion of those affected, yet no treatments specifically approved for pediatric patients are currently available.

"Friedreich ataxia is a devastating rare genetic disease that progressively steals a child's ability to walk, speak, play, and ultimately survive," she says.

"This novel therapeutic agent can target the underlying cause of the disease, while delivering an affordable and accessible therapy worldwide, improving treatment opportunities for families affected by this life-limiting disease.

"This discovery brings us closer to a future where children with Friedreich ataxia experience a better quality of life, greater independence, and an improved chance of long-term survival."

A Potential Treatment That Could Be More Accessible

One of the most encouraging aspects of sulforaphane is that it is not an entirely unfamiliar substance. The compound already has an established safety record in both children and adults, and purified, biologically active forms are commercially available.

These advantages could make it easier to develop a widely accessible treatment if future clinical trials confirm that sulforaphane is effective against Friedreich ataxia. However, further research is essential before scientists can determine whether the promising findings will translate into meaningful benefits for patients.

Kwa explains that the rarity of Friedreich ataxia creates additional challenges for researchers. Because relatively few people have the disease, public awareness is limited, making it more difficult to attract the funding needed to investigate potential treatments.

Researchers Seek Funding for Clinical Trials

The Swinburne team hopes to secure financial support for clinical trials that would examine whether sulforaphane can deliver the same promising effects in people living with the disease.

"We are hoping to gain funding to conduct clinical trials and further prove the positive impact the broccoli compound could have on those suffering from Friedreich ataxia," she says.

"Sulforaphane already has an established safety record in children and adults, and its pure and bioactive form is commercially available. This means if clinical trials prove successful, its rollout could accelerate the path to patient impact."

For patients and families facing a progressive illness with no cure, even improvements in everyday functioning and independence could make a meaningful difference. The researchers hope their work will not only advance treatment possibilities but also bring greater attention to a condition that remains largely unknown to the public.

"Even if we can raise awareness of this debilitating condition or improve one person's quality of life, our efforts will have been worth it."

Materials provided by Swinburne University of Technology. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5646. ‘Wake-Up Call’: Trump’s Former Housing Commissioner Says New Congress Must ‘Get Serious’ About Housing Affordability

Democrats and Republicans both understand Americans are broadly worried about the cost of living, and a former Trump administration official says it's time for both parties to take action.

In a bitterly divided Washington, DC, it remains to be seen whether lawmakers will heed that call when the 120th Congress convenes in January, with Democrats back in control of both the House and Senate.

After campaigning hard on affordability concerns, Democratic leaders say they'll use their new majorities to focus on the cost of living. Republican leaders admit they didn't heed voter concerns about the economy. Meanwhile, President Donald Trump has threatened to use his veto power freely.

The summer's 21st Century Road to Housing Act, with its dozens of provisions aimed at cutting red tape, was a rare example of bipartisan consensus. What follows that landmark legislation remains an open question.

Republicans want more deregulation while Democrats aim for more support for housing. And each side must now contend with an upswell of hard-liners pushing policies that could radically change the market.

Many of the prominent names in both parties who built the housing bill are returning, including Rep. French Hill (R-AR), Rep. Maxine Waters (D-CA), Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-MA), and Sen. Tim Scott (R-SC). They're likely to return to the House and Senate committees on housing and banking.

"Now is a wake-up call," Trump's former Federal Housing Commissioner Frank Cassidy tells Realtor.com®. "Senate, House, White House. Everyone needs to get serious about tackling and addressing housing affordability. It can't be ignored anymore."

Congress had some bipartisan momentum to provide tax incentives that encourage the buying and selling of homes.

Colin Allen, executive director of the American Property Owners Alliance and a former housing issues adviser to Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-SC), said that could mean some ideas pitched in this Congress could come back as part of larger bills.

"They have good working relationships and have already done some bipartisan work," Allen said.

Take, for instance, the Neighborhood Homes Investment Act, which would create a new tax credit to buy and renovate homes in economically distressed areas. The bill drew 70 sponsors from both parties.

Real estate groups put in significant groundwork this year to update the capital gains tax scheme for the first time in more than 30 years. The More Homes on the Market Act came close to 200 sponsors in Congress. It would double the exclusion for many filers. It's been floating around Congress for several years and has been a target of the National Association of Realtors® and other groups.

Trump expressed some support for changing the capital gains tax scheme, though a specific plan hasn't yet materialized from the White House.

"We've done a lot of legwork to get folks behind it," Allen said. "If we're looking at a larger bipartisan bill, you can see a scenario where a few of those ideas get together. The debt limit is coming up, and there are a few other opportunities to package together."

Hill and Republicans have lobbied for more changes to the financing system. They were able to get several banking reform provisions into the Road to Housing bill. They've also floated new financial reforms to change and rescind banking rules codified in the Dodd-Frank Act and the Basel III accords after the subprime mortgage crisis. Republicans say they've chased smaller banks out of the housing market.

This summer, Hill called Dodd-Frank a "massive overreaction."

"For our smaller banks, the new regulations were a poor fit, burying them in compliance work and bureaucratic red tape," Hill said. "Instead of helping customers, their attention was diverted to filling out forms and satisfying examiners."

Mortgage reform is also a lever Congress can pull. A bipartisan group of six members of Congress pitched the First-Time Homebuyer Affordability Act this summer. It would expand access to low-interest mortgages for first-time homebuyers.

"By expanding access to financing, we can help more hardworking families achieve homeownership, strengthen our communities, and build long-term financial security," said Rep. Darin LaHood (R-IL) said.

Then there's the matter of new construction. Democrats and Republicans found some bipartisan ground in cutting some of the federal red tape that blocks construction of new homes.

Republicans also said they favor rolling back Build America Buy America provisions. Builders, they say, have complained that the sourcing requirements are time-consuming and expensive. But they've also targeted some environmental regulations that Democrats passed.

Dennis Shea, chair of the J. Ronald Terwilliger Center for Housing Policy at the Bipartisan Policy Center, tells Realtor.com that some public housing authorities saw costs climb by double digits. The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development's waiver process is every bit as time-consuming for builders.

"A sentiment exists in both parties to change the rules, but ultimately it takes an act of Congress to exempt housing," Shea said.

Hill and other lawmakers such as Rep. Emanuel Cleaver (D-MO) have said that Congress' action should shift some burden onto states to implement reforms at the local and state level. The American Enterprise Institute said this year that state and local policy changes could boost annual homebuilding by six figures. But many of those new homes are accessory dwelling units.

Congress and the White Hose also found common ground on manufactured housing reform. All sides recognize they need to keep eyeing supply-side reforms, says Cassidy.

"Ultimately, the problem in this country is supply," Cassidy adds. "You could lower rates to 2% tomorrow, and all that will do is increase home values. It's not going to solve the underlying issue."

The other big question will be funding of the many provisions created under the Road to Housing Act. While the provisions in the bill were bipartisan, Congress must still approve funding for some of those programs. Some of those discussions are coming in the 2028 fiscal budget and beyond.

Over the months of negotiations on the Road to Housing bill, some Republicans took issue with unfunded mandates in it. Concerns about funding programs, and at what level, could spill over into congressional proceedings in coming years.

Tony Marquez, director of American University's real estate program, who has a long career in real estate and banking, tells Realtor.com that the industry is still amenable to a few different ideas for how to solve housing. It doesn't rely on one side's control of the government.

"My un-professional assessment is we'll have a certain amount of gridlock over a number of years where Democrats may come up with some suggestions," Marquez says. "But the answer to affordable housing is not just one silver bullet. It can have many elements."

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

#5645. Low testosterone linked to 18% higher risk of dying from cancer

Men with very low testosterone levels may face an increased risk of developing cancer and dying from the disease later in life, according to a major international study. The findings suggest that testosterone levels could provide an early clue to future health risks, potentially years or even decades before cancer is diagnosed.

Researchers found that men with low testosterone had an 18 percent higher risk of dying from cancer. However, the relationship was not the same for every type of cancer. Surprisingly, testosterone levels were not associated with prostate cancer risk. Instead, prostate cancer was more closely linked to low levels of two other hormones, sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) and luteinizing hormone.

The research comes from the Androgens In Men Study (AIMS), an international collaboration led by Professor Bu Yeap at The University of Western Australia. The project investigates how different sex hormones relate to cancer risk and other health outcomes in men.

Study Tracks Testosterone and Cancer Risk in 26,000 Men

Published in the journal Lancet Healthy Longevity, the study examined data from more than 26,000 men participating in 11 long-running studies across Australia, the United States, and Europe.

Researchers analyzed hormone concentrations in blood samples collected earlier in the men's lives. They then compared those measurements with cancer diagnoses and deaths recorded over the following decades, allowing them to investigate whether hormone levels were associated with future cancer outcomes.

The analysis included testosterone, dihydrotestosterone (DHT), SHBG, and luteinizing hormone. Luteinizing hormone is produced by the pituitary gland and signals the testes to produce testosterone.

"We wanted to know whether the concentration of these hormones in the blood was related to the risk of men being diagnosed with, or dying from, cancer into the future," Professor Yeap said.

"What we saw was that if a man had low testosterone levels - in the lowest one-fifth compared to the highest one-fifth of the range - their subsequent risk of dying from cancer was higher, even after allowing for age and other health-related factors."

Cancer Risk Increased Below a Key Testosterone Level

The researchers identified a testosterone concentration below which cancer risk began to rise. According to Professor Yeap, testosterone levels in healthy younger men typically range from 10 to 30 nanomoles per liter (nmol/L), although concentrations generally decrease with age.

Testosterone levels can also be influenced by factors that people may be able to change, including body mass index and physical activity. Certain medical conditions, such as diabetes, can affect testosterone concentrations as well.

"We saw that when baseline testosterone was below 8.6 nmol/L, subsequent cancer risk started increasing," Professor Yeap said.

"This suggests low testosterone is an important biomarker, so it's possible that looking at testosterone levels could help us identify men who might do poorly if they get cancer down the track."

These findings raise the possibility that testosterone measurements could help doctors recognize men who may face greater health risks in the future. However, the results show an association and do not establish that low testosterone itself causes cancer.

A Surprising Finding About Prostate Cancer

Because testosterone plays an important role in male reproductive health, researchers also investigated whether naturally occurring testosterone levels influenced the likelihood of developing prostate cancer.

The question has particular medical significance because lowering testosterone is an established treatment for prostate cancer. However, the new analysis found no evidence that a man's natural testosterone concentration was associated with his risk of developing the disease.

"Since reducing testosterone levels is a treatment for prostate cancer there's always been a question of whether the amount of testosterone your own body makes relates to your risk of prostate cancer but based on our findings there's no evidence they are related," Professor Yeap said.

"We did find, however, that men with low levels of SHBG and luteinizing hormone were at higher risk of prostate cancer."

The results highlight an important distinction between testosterone and other hormones involved in male reproductive function. Although low testosterone was associated with higher overall cancer risk and mortality, prostate cancer showed a different pattern of hormonal associations.

Why Low Testosterone Does Not Mean Men Need Supplements

Despite the connection between low testosterone and cancer outcomes, Professor Yeap emphasized that the findings should not be interpreted as a recommendation to take testosterone supplements to prevent cancer.

"While we've shown low levels are associated with increased risk, we haven't got any evidence yet that actually giving men testosterone will reduce that risk," he said.

Instead, unexpectedly low testosterone could be a reason to investigate a person's overall health. A medical evaluation may uncover underlying conditions or risk factors that require attention, even when there is no evidence of a problem affecting the testes.

"What we would say to men is if they are found for whatever reason to be low in testosterone, it's important to go to the doctor for a full checkup. It may not show any sign of testicular disease, but it might show other health issues or risk factors they need to address.

"It could be a wake-up call and encouragement for men to engage in more healthy lifestyle behaviors, and to get regular, holistic checkups to stay on top of their health."

Materials provided by University of Western Australia. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5644. Neoclouds face a shakeout as cloud-native software skills decide who survives

AI infrastructure clouds have multiplied as GPU capital pours into new data centers, but standing up capacity is proving easier than running it at scale. With Kubernetes now hardened into the operating layer for AI factories, the cloud-native community holds expertise that many of these new providers lack.

KubeCon has been shifting toward an AI infrastructure event, with container orchestration for AI and distributed inference now central to the conversation. The newer AI clouds run on the same computing fundamentals as the hyperscalers before them, yet many specialize narrowly and lack a bridge to the enterprise systems that will ultimately consume their capacity, according to Sarbjeet Johal (pictured), chief executive officer of Stackpane.

“I’m afraid that the neoclouds, if they don’t partner with the ones who are appreciating the brownfield, they will suffer,” Johal said. “They can’t survive on their own because, who is going to take that compute from them? It’s the hyperscalers. The neoclouds are the overflow.”

Johal spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed the event’s first-day takeaways, from AI-written code and token economics to the maturing neocloud market and the skills needed to run it. (* Disclosure below.)

Kubernetes spent more than a decade evolving in fits and starts, and the payoff is now showing up in AI. The Cloud Native Computing Foundation added a dedicated AI inference and agentic track to this year’s KubeCon North America schedule, a sign of where practitioner attention has moved. Kubernetes now runs across about two-thirds of the enterprise, sits inside Nvidia Corp.’s reference architectures and underpins the neoclouds, Furrier noted. Skills honed through years of operating Kubernetes are now being applied directly to the commercial buildout of AI factories, where most of the capital is going.

“Now it’s hardened. So when you have hardened Kubernetes, we’re seeing inference being talked about,” Furrier said. “Who would have thought at this show inference would be discussed? Well, guess what? Distributed inference is the hottest area right now.”

That maturity matters because so much AI capital spending is flowing to new providers. SoftBank Group Corp. unveiled plans to enter the U.S. neocloud business this summer, joining a crowded field. Many existing operators started out building data centers for bitcoin mining or arbitraging spot pricing rather than running large-scale software, according to Furrier, who sees a reckoning ahead. The hard part is less about acquiring GPUs than operating them as a true cloud.

“Half the neoclouds will fail,” Furrier said. “To run a big neocloud, you’ve got to look like CoreWeave. Well, guess what CoreWeave is? The founders know data centers. … People who know large-scale software stacks at scale win.”

The rescue, in Furrier’s view, will come from the cloud-native community. He pointed to CoreWeave Inc., whose engineering is run by former Google Cloud LLC executive Chen Goldberg, as the model for pairing data center know-how with large-scale software skills. He also suggested private equity investors could buy smaller Kubernetes companies to fill the gap. Those companies could command billion-dollar valuations as data center owners with land, power and shell seek help with connectivity, multigeneration Nvidia hardware and workloads that span data centers, he explained. Johal, who watched a similar story play out at Rackspace Technology Inc., agreed that software will decide which providers last.

“We have seen this movie earlier. So if you want to be a good hyperscaler, if you don’t have the software chops, you’re dead,” Johal said of the new AI infrastructure clouds. “We knew how to run data centers at Rackspace, but we didn’t have software chops. … Without software chops, you’re dead in the water.”
