#5623. Red Hat and Nvidia’s OpenShell puts AI agents on a deny-by-default leash

Prompt injection attacks and silent data exfiltration have turned AI agent security from a theoretical worry into an urgent enterprise concern.

As agents move from developer laptops into data centers, companies need guardrails that don’t strip away what makes agents useful. Red Hat Inc. and Nvidia Corp. have expanded their partnership to tackle that problem through OpenShell, an open-source project that sets limits on what agents can do. The threat model for agents differs sharply from that of traditional software, so the industry has to build a shared standard to secure them, according to Derek Carr (pictured, left), senior distinguished engineer at Red Hat.

“Agents can’t get access to your secrets. They need deny-by-default networking, and you need a rich policy framework for what happened and when for this class of apps,” Carr said. “Nvidia had reached out to us and noted that they were seeing the same problem domain. No one wants to work on this alone. It’s better to work together.”

Carr and Mrunal Patel (right), distinguished engineer at Red Hat, spoke with theCUBE’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how OpenShell helps enterprises run AI agents in production with safeguards against prompt injection and data leaks. (* Disclosure below.)

Viral projects such as OpenClaw showed the industry that agents could take real actions on their own. Of course, that power also bred anxiety about agents leaking secrets or spending company money, with concrete warning signs appearing early, Patel noted.

“As soon as we started hearing about the prompt injection attacks and how like folks were seeing the data getting exfiltrated outside, that was scary,” Patel said. “We realized we needed a solution.”

To that end, OpenShell lets operators give agents access to specific endpoints while keeping credentials hidden from the agents and scoped to those endpoints, according to Carr. A policy advisor asks agents to justify blocked actions in plain language, while operators can update policies as workloads change. With OpenShell now under open governance at the Cloud Native Computing Foundation following Nvidia’s contribution, Red Hat aims to make deploying agents on OpenShift as routine as running traditional apps, with prompt injection defenses built into the platform.

“Many companies are struggling to get to one agent in production, let alone thousands or millions,” Carr said. “By having a project like OpenShell in the ecosystem, it provides a blueprint for companies to follow — to get from their first idea of ‘I want to do something with agents’ to a point where they’re safely doing one, 10 or 20 in production.”

#5622. Christmas Lights Are Squeezing Homeowner Budgets More Than Ever, but There’s a Way To Pay Less and Still Be Festive

Christmas lights can bring holiday cheer to your home and neighborhood, but they don’t come cheap.

The U.S. Energy Information Administration projects the national average residential electricity price at about 18 cents per kilowatt-hour in 2026—roughly 37% higher than in 2020. This translates to the highest utility bills some homeowners have ever seen, made worse during times of the year when more electricity is needed.

According to a recent study by Payless Power, running a full display throughout December costs $15.36 with LED lights and $92.03 with incandescent lights at the typical electricity rate. That’s a $76.67 difference.

Where you live can affect your electric bill, too.

Hawaii is the most expensive state for holiday lighting, at $42.53 for a full LED display and $254.84 for the incandescent version. Rhode Island ($31.85), Massachusetts ($31.47), Maine ($30.98), and New Hampshire ($26.81) also make the list of the five most expensive states for a full LED display.

Meanwhile, homeowners in North Dakota ($11.25), Nebraska ($11.49), and Missouri ($12.02) pay the least.

The good news is there are ways to lower your electric bill without sacrificing curb appeal or holiday spirit, regardless of where you live. All it takes is a bit of planning and creativity.

A variety of factors are contributing to high electric bills these days.

“The grid is outdated. Infrastructure is old, and utility companies need to replace and upgrade equipment,” says Brandon Young, CEO of Payless Power in Fort Worth, TX.

Extreme weather plays a huge role as well, as the lines and equipment can’t always handle conditions like freezing temperatures and high winds.

Increased electricity demand adds to the problem.

“Demand is growing, and the grid can’t always keep up. Data centers and industrial use are large consumers of energy, and it takes a lot to power those facilities,” Young explains.

Fuel costs also fluctuate and affect how much it costs to generate electricity.

“Prices for residential customers in 2025 went up more than twice the rate of inflation,” says Young.

These high costs are particularly noticeable during the holiday season. Young points out that many homeowners often forget that a higher utility rate doesn’t take December off.

“The higher rate is there all year, and every kilowatt-hour is more costly. The oven and lights for holiday gatherings all cost more to use,” Young adds.

Fortunately, you don’t have to forgo Christmas lights altogether.

These tips can help you enjoy them while keeping your electricity costs in check.

While you don’t get to choose your utility rates, you do get to choose your light bulbs. And LEDs are much cheaper than incandescent bulbs.

“One hundred bulb C9s cost about $19.57 in December to run, and if they're swapped with LEDs, you’ll pay $2.80,” says Young.

LED lights aren’t hard to find either. You'll notice a variety of options at just about any home improvement store.

You don’t have to keep your lights on all day, every day.

Consider displaying them only from 5 to 10 p.m., for example. You could use a timer or smart plug that allows you to turn them on or off manually when you want to.

Also, if you plan to leave town, keep them off until you return.

Lighting every bush in your yard will cost you. Instead, be selective about where you hang lights.

Highlighting your front door, roof line, and a tree in your yard can make just as big of an impact.

If you have inflatables, there’s no reason to keep them on 24/7.

“Unplugging inflatables when you go to bed saves a few dollars. The cost to leave one up for the month is about $1.68, which is a lot to pay [compared with] a 100-bulb LED light strand at 14 cents,” says Young.

In addition, you don’t have to use inflatables for your home to stand out. A light projector can do the trick at a fraction of the cost.

The study says that a projector costs only 17 cents per month to run, compared to $1.68 for an inflatable.

#5620. What Experts Forecast for Mortgage Rates and Home Prices in 2027

When it comes to housing, two of the biggest questions on everyone’s mind right now are:

And if you’re weighing whether to move in the next few months or wait until 2027, here’s what you should know.

When experts look ahead to 2027, they see a steady housing market. No wild swings. No big surprises. Just a calmer, more balanced market.

And steady makes planning a whole lot easier. Let’s break it down.

Lots of people are holding out for lower rates. But the latest forecasts from Fannie Mae, the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA), and Wells Fargo show rates holding fairly flat through 2027 (see graph below):

Lenders see it the same way. In a recent survey from HousingWire, 70% of mortgage executives said they expect rates to be around 7.5% or higher six months from now (see graph below):

And if you’re wondering why, the answer is fairly simple. Chen Zhao, Head of Economics Research at Redfin, says:

“Until the underlying economic fundamentals—everything from oil prices to AI–that are keeping rates high change, mortgage rates are unlikely to fall significantly.”

So what does that mean for you? Instead of trying to guess where rates go next, focus on what you can control. Even if rates don’t budge, there are still ways to get the best rate possible. When you talk with your lender, ask about:

Your credit score. Even a small bump in your score could help lower your rate.

Different loan types. Some programs offer lower rates or smaller down payments than you might expect.

Buying down your rate. Paying a little more upfront (called “points”) can lower your rate and your monthly payment.

That way, you’ll know exactly where you stand and what a comfortable monthly payment looks like for you.

But what about prices? Here’s where steady really works in your favor.

Experts don’t see a home price drop coming. On average, forecasts from Fannie Mae, MBA, and Wells Fargo show prices rising about 1% to 1.5% a year through 2027 (see graph below):

In plain terms, in most places prices are still going up, just not as fast. For sellers, that means your home should hold onto its value. For buyers, slower growth gives you a little more breathing room. Just don’t count on prices getting cheaper while you wait.

But keep in mind, these are national forecasts. Prices can look very different from one area to the next, so what matters most is what’s happening where you live.

When the market is steady, you don’t have to try to time it perfectly. There’s no big swing to wait out.

That puts the focus back on you. Maybe you need more space for a growing family. Maybe you’re ready for less upkeep. A steady market makes it easier to plan for either one.

If you’re asking yourself should you move now or wait? You should know experts see a steady market through 2027, with rates holding near today’s levels and prices rising slowly. So, rather than waiting for a big shift that may not come, connect with a local real estate agent and run the numbers on what a move looks like at today’s rates and prices, so you can decide based on your goals instead of the headlines.

#5619. Inside Billionaire Larry Ellison’s HOA Feud Over His 8-Home Buying Spree

Billionaire Larry Ellison recently spent nearly $10 million on eight homes for his staff in a gated South Florida community—but not everyone was thrilled about his buying spree.

Ellison, 82, co-founder of technology giant Oracle, purchased the properties in spring 2023 in Palm Meadows Estates, an upscale 288-home community in Boynton Beach, FL, known for its sprawling houses, manicured lawns, and lakefront views.

But the plan hit a roadblock when the neighborhood’s homeowners association adopted a new rule limiting owners to just five properties around the same time the deals were closing.

The amendment, obtained by Realtor.com®, was signed on May 30, 2023, and recorded with Palm Beach County on June 2, 2023—during the same period Ellison's eight purchases were finalized. All eight deals were closed between May and June 2023, according to property records.

However, the amendment appears to have come too late to stop the sales from closing, and property records show that a company associated with Ellison now owns the eight homes.

All eight homes were purchased for Ellison’s household staff, which included teachers, therapists, and chefs, according to his real estate agent Kimmie Cruz, who talked to CBS12 about how some of the deals were still in the process of closing when the HOA moved to limit the number of properties a single owner could acquire.

"They tried to stop it," Cruz said. "There were also some neighbors who felt that it was going to change the dynamic of the neighborhood."

The amendment to the HOA rules also requires a year of ownership before a property can be rented out, according to the document obtained by Realtor.com.

Attorneys became involved in the dispute, and all eight purchases ultimately closed.

The HOA did not respond to a request for comment from Realtor.com.

The identity of the buyer initially remained a mystery, with an LLC listed as the buyer on property records.

But Cruz later learned the purchases were being made for Ellison, who has a roughly $200 billion fortune. A year earlier, he had bought a $173 million oceanfront estate in nearby Manalapan.

Cruz, a local real estate agent with LuxeIQ who lives in the community, previously told The Wall Street Journal that she received an urgent call in March 2023 from another real estate agent about a buyer interested in purchasing as many as 10 homes.

The agent told Cruz that it would be “worth it” to arrange the last-minute showings, she recalled. A few days later, Ellison arrived to tour the homes and that night, Cruz received the first of the signed contracts for the houses.

Cruz said the homeowners walked away with sizable profits from the sales.

“Across the homes I sold, I secured sale prices averaging 20% above market value,” she said.

One couple, Paul and Yvonne Carozza, sold their three-bedroom, roughly 2,100-square-foot home to Ellison for $1.2 million, a home they paid $567,000 for in 2019, records show.

Ellison’s purchases highlight an emerging trend among the ultrawealthy who are buying properties to house staff who manage their multimillion-dollar estates on their behalf.

Meta founder Mark Zuckerberg has been buying up a number of homes in Palo Alto, CA, to create a family compound.

Wealthy newcomers to South Florida, including billionaires, tech executives, and hedge fund managers, have poured hundreds of millions of dollars into building out new private and charter schools for their children, according to the Journal.

Some, including Zuckerberg, Elon Musk, WeWork co-founder Adam Neumann, and real estate developer Jeff Greene, have even launched schools of their own.

#5618. What the Silver Tsunami Means if You’re Planning To Sell

If you’re following the housing market, you may have heard the term “silver tsunami” lately. It’s the idea that millions of homes owned by older Americans could come onto the market as more homeowners reach retirement age and make their next move.

And when you hear a phrase like that, it’s easy to picture a flood of houses hitting the market all at once. But that picture doesn’t match the data.

And if you’re planning to sell, it’s not a reason to put your plans on hold. Let’s look at what the research actually says.

According to Realtor.com, about 13.9 million homes owned by older Americans are expected to change hands by 2036. Sure, that’s a big number. But these homes aren’t all expected to come onto the market at once.

The projections show this happening gradually over the next decade, with roughly 1.3 to 1.5 million homes changing hands each year (see graph below):

Rather than a sudden wave of houses flooding the market, this is a gradual shift as longtime homeowners make decisions about where and how they want to live.

The term silver tsunami makes for a dramatic headline, but the actual data tells a much less dramatic story. And there’s another reason these homes won’t overwhelm the market.

After the 2008 housing crash, builders significantly slowed construction. And for years afterward, they didn’t build enough homes to keep up with demand. That led to a housing shortage we’re still dealing with today.

And just how big a gap are we talking about? Estimates vary, but many experts say the U.S. is still millions of homes short. For example, a recent report from the White House Council of Economic Advisers explains:

“If homebuilding and the growth of the single-family housing stock had continued at their historical pace instead of falling dramatically after 2008, there would be 10 million or more additional single-family homes today.”

As more longtime homeowners sell, those homes will help a gap that’s already there. But they won’t push us over the edge. That’s because, at the same time, more households are expected to form in the decade ahead, and they’ll need homes, too.

So, more homes becoming available over time isn’t automatically a bad thing. It can give buyers more options and help create a more balanced housing market moving forward.

Here’s the takeaway if you’re thinking about selling your house. The silver tsunami isn’t something you need to plan your move around. What’s happening in your local market is far more important than a national projection about the next decade.

That’s because real estate is local. Some markets have more homes for sale than others. Some are seeing houses sell relatively quickly, while others are taking longer.

And those are the conditions that matter when you’re deciding how to price, prepare, and market your house.

For example, an agent who knows your area can help you understand:

How many homes are for sale nearby. This tells you how much choice buyers have and how your house will compare.

What similar houses are actually selling for. That’s one of the most important factors in setting a competitive asking price.

What buyers are looking for right now. Knowing which features and improvements matter most can help your house make a strong first impression.

And that’s something you can act on today, regardless of what happens with the silver tsunami over the next decade.

The right strategy starts with understanding your local market and making decisions based on what’s happening there, not what a dramatic national headline suggests might happen years from now.

The silver tsunami may sound like a major wave of homes coming onto the market, but the research points to a gradual shift over the next decade, not a sudden flood of listings.If you're thinking about selling, don't let that headline make you second-guess your plans. Talk to an agent about what's happening in your local market.

#5617. Selling Your Home? What You Should Know About Price Cuts vs. Rate Buydowns.

In today’s market, a growing number of sellers are opting to do something called a price cut – especially when their house has been on the market for a while without any bites.

According to HousingWire Data as many as 4 in 10 (43%) sellers are going this route – that’s the highest it’s been in 4 years. But what if there’s another (potentially better option) for your bottom line? And it’s just as appealing, if not more so, to today’s buyers?

First, let’s set the stage on why some compromise may be necessary in today’s market.

In September, Redfin says there were 63% more sellers than buyers in the market. And with so many sellers active and relatively few buyers by comparison, those purchasers are realizing they have more power. And as mortgage rates continue to put a squeeze on their budgets, they’re leaning in and using it.

One of the most common negotiation points? The price.

That’s because they want to feel like they’re getting a deal and they want to see their monthly payment drop. And since buyers can’t control rates, the price feels like the most obvious lever to pull.

But the savviest sellers realize being flexible doesn’t always mean a lower price, paying for a buyer’s rate buydown might work better.

A buydown is money paid at closing to lower the buyer’s mortgage rate. When you pay it as the seller, you are paying some of the buyer’s interest ahead of time, so the buyer gets a lower rate and monthly payment. And that’s especially appealing to today’s buyers.

Temporary buydowns lower the rate for the first few years, then it goes back to the full rate. The more years a buydown covers, the more it costs. These work well for buyers who expect to refinance within a certain amount of time.

A permanent buydown lowers the rate for the whole loan. These are paid for with “discount points.” One point costs 1% of the loan. According to FICO, each point generally lowers the rate by about a quarter of a percent. This type of buydown works well for buyers who plan to stay in the home for a long time.

And here’s why these can be a win-win for both buyers and sellers. Rate buydowns help sellers stand out in a crowded market and they can have a bigger impact on your buyer than a price cut would.

Here’s an example to show you what that could look like.

Let’s say you’re willing to make a $10,000 concession to help get the deal done. Take a look at these three ways to spend that money and the impact they could have on a buyer’s $420,000, 30-year fixed loan at 7%:

It’s the same $10,000 from the seller. But a 2-1 buydown saves the buyer about eight times more each month in the first year.

And since most buyers shop by monthly payment, that’s what grabs their attention.

That’s what makes a rate buydown worth considering. Instead of reducing your asking price, you may be able to use that same money to have a bigger impact on your buyer’s monthly payments. And depending on what matters most to that buyer, the immediate savings could be more appealing than a price reduction.

The key is working with your agent and the buyer’s lender to compare the options and see which one makes the most sense.

Loan programs cap how much a seller can pay toward a buyer’s costs.

Money toward buydowns doesn’t limit what else a buyer may ask a seller to pay for. Buyers may still ask for repairs or other concessions.

Putting the buydown offer in your listing lets agents and buyers know it’s an option.

Your agent can run scenarios on buydowns and other costs of selling in advance so you’re prepared when an offer comes in.

As Lawrence Yun, Chief Economist at the National Association of Realtors (NAR), says:

“Home sellers need to be realistic about local market conditions, which could require price discounts and other incentives to attract buyers.”

And sellers who offer solutions like buydowns can make meaningful impact where home buyers need it most: in their wallets.

When you're looking for ways to make your house more appealing to buyers, a price reduction isn't your only option. A mortgage rate buydown could help a buyer save more each month, especially in the early years of their loan.Talk to your agent or a trusted lender which incentives could make the biggest difference for buyers in our market, while still protecting your bottom line.

#5616. This New Water Heater Gadget Could Turn Your Hot Showers Into Bitcoin. But Is It Worth It?

Your water heater already uses electricity to keep the showers hot and dishes clean. But what if it could also earn you a little money at the same time?

That's the idea behind Bitwater, an unusual new home appliance from technology company Heatbit that combines an electric water heater's heating element with a bitcoin mining computer.

Rather than purchasing an entirely new water heater, homeowners can install the device inside an existing electric tank, replacing a conventional heating element with one powered by computer chips that generate heat while mining cryptocurrency.

"We were actually looking for areas where electricity is turned into heat, where it's not seasonal," Alex Busarov, Heatbit's founder, told Realtor.com® in a phone interview. The company had already developed bitcoin-mining space heaters, he explained, but household water heating offered an opportunity to put the technology to work year-round.

It's an eye-catching proposition at a time when homeowners are looking for ways to offset utility bills. But can mining bitcoin really make heating water more affordable?

At first glance, Bitwater resembles an oversized heating element, the metal component inside an electric water heater that warms the water.

But instead of a traditional electrical resistance wire, it contains specialized computer chips that perform the calculations involved in bitcoin mining.

But instead of a traditional electrical resistance wire, it contains specialized computer chips that perform the calculations involved in bitcoin mining.

Those chips produce heat as they work. Bitwater transfers that heat into the surrounding water, cooling the computer hardware while heating the tank.

Unlike space heating, which is largely unnecessary during the warmer months, households need hot water throughout the year. That makes a water heater a potentially more practical home for computing equipment that generates heat.

The device replaces only the lower heating element in a conventional electric water heater. The upper element remains in place to provide additional heating when demand increases.

According to Busarov, Bitwater typically operates at approximately 400 to 600 watts, heating water more gradually than a conventional element that might draw several thousand watts for a shorter period.

Busarov said the device automatically stops mining when the water reaches its target temperature. He estimated that the mining hardware operates approximately 80% of the time, although actual utilization would depend on household demand for hot water.

Bitwater can reportedly generate up to 34 terahashes per second, a measure of the computing power used to mine bitcoin, which Busarov estimated could translate to roughly $30 per month in cryptocurrency under current mining conditions.

That would represent approximately $360 annually, although actual earnings depend on bitcoin prices, mining difficulty, operating time, and other factors.

At that rate, a roughly $900 device would require about 2.5 years to recover its purchase price, even before accounting for installation costs, mining fees, maintenance, or changes in cryptocurrency earnings.

There is an important distinction, however, between generating bitcoin revenue and saving energy. Bitwater doesn't eliminate the electricity needed to heat water. Instead, the company argues that the electricity can perform two useful jobs: powering a computer and producing household hot water.

In principle, that gives the homeowner some cryptocurrency in exchange for electricity that would otherwise have gone toward conventional resistance heating.

Busarov says the mining operation shuts down when the tank reaches its desired temperature, so the device isn't intended to consume additional electricity solely to mine bitcoin. It prioritizes heating water, with cryptocurrency mining as a secondary function.

At an illustrative electricity rate of 18 cents per kilowatt-hour, operating a 600-watt device continuously would consume about $78 in electricity each month. Bitwater is not designed to operate continuously, however, and that electricity would not necessarily represent an additional expense if the heat replaces what a conventional electric heating element would otherwise produce.

Heatbit's projected earnings are therefore not the same as guaranteed savings on a utility bill. The calculation depends on how much the device operates and how much cryptocurrency it actually generates.

Heatbit designed Bitwater as a retrofit for conventional electric tank water heaters rather than a complete replacement system.

The device is intended to fit compatible residential tanks equipped with standard screw-in heating elements.

Busarov said installation is designed to be comparable to replacing an ordinary water heater element.

"We really built it for DIY installation," he said.

That doesn't necessarily mean every homeowner should attempt it.

Working on a water heater involves electricity, pressurized water, and potential flooding hazards. Homeowners unfamiliar with those systems should use a qualified professional and check local code requirements.

Heatbit promotes several safety and maintenance features, including leak protection, overheating safeguards, and programmed high-temperature cycles intended to limit the growth of Legionella bacteria.

Busarov said protecting against leaks was a significant part of developing the physical product.

He also described a system that can periodically raise water temperatures to combat bacterial growth without maintaining those higher temperatures continuously.

The company says Bitwater also incorporates a powered anode rod designed to protect the tank against corrosion and anti-limescale technology intended to reduce mineral buildup. Both corrosion and mineral deposits can contribute to water heater maintenance problems, and Busarov saw these features as selling points even for homeowners who aren't interested in cryptocurrency.

However, homeowners should verify that the specific product they receive has the appropriate electrical and plumbing certifications, and that its temperature controls and other protective features operate as advertised.

Independent, long-term reliability data will be especially important as the technology moves beyond its initial testing phase.

For homeowners primarily interested in reducing utility bills, Bitwater faces an established competitor: the heat-pump water heater.

Unlike conventional resistance heaters, heat-pump models use electricity to move heat from the surrounding air into a water tank.

According to Energy Star, an efficient heat-pump water heater can save a four-person household approximately $550 per year compared with a standard electric water heater.

Those savings come from reducing energy consumption rather than producing a separate stream of income.

Bitwater takes a fundamentally different approach. It aims to create financial value from electricity already being used for heating.

That may appeal to homeowners who already have a functional electric water heater and don't want to replace the entire appliance.

But a homeowner considering a major water-heating upgrade should compare installation costs, electricity consumption, maintenance, and expected savings before choosing one technology over another.

For all its ingenuity, Bitwater still faces some crucial, fundamental questions—like does adding cryptocurrency mining to an everyday appliance actually save homeowners enough money to justify the investment?

Regarding the latter, Heatbit claims it tested the system in households in Miami and Rochester, NY, during January, according to Busarov. Both locations maintained adequate hot water despite their dramatically different winter climates, according to the findings.

"People didn't really notice the difference," he said.

Realtor.com asked Heatbit to arrange interviews with the homeowners who tested the devices to independently assess their experiences, but those interviews had not been arranged by publication deadline.

While the concept has generated enthusiasm among cryptocurrency enthusiasts online, others questioned whether the device's mining revenue could justify its upfront cost, particularly if its computing performance declines as the water in the tank heats up.

There is also the question of whether homeowners want to become cryptocurrency miners, even on a small scale.

Bitcoin's value can fluctuate dramatically, and mining profitability depends on competition from other miners around the world. A device generating $30 in one month might earn considerably less in another.

There are also questions about actual mining utilization. Busarov estimated the device can mine approximately 80% of the time, but that figure has not been independently verified. Because the mining operation shuts down when the water reaches its target temperature, households using less hot water may have fewer opportunities to generate cryptocurrency.

Long-term maintenance presents another uncertainty. A conventional heating element is relatively simple and inexpensive to replace, while Bitwater introduces computer chips, electronic controls, and other components into an appliance that homeowners generally expect to operate for years with little attention.

And while the company insists the early household tests suggest the product can provide adequate hot water, the item is still in pre-order phase right now with the first units slotted to ship in the first quarter, so there is no independent evidence of its performance and durability, and real-world earnings remains limited.

Taken together, those uncertainties make Bitwater an intriguing proposition, but not yet a proven way to reduce household expenses.

#5614. British inference chip developer Fractile raises $720M in funding

Fractile Ltd., a British startup that develops artificial intelligence inference chips, has raised $720 million in funding.

Reuters reported today that the Series C round was led by Thrive Capital, Founders Fund, Lightspeed and Redpoint. They were joined by about a dozen others including the U.K. Sovereign AI Fund, the British Business Bank and Alphabet Inc.’s CapitalG investment arm. Fractile is now worth $7 billion.

Fractile was founded in 2022 by AI researcher Walter Goodwin (pictured), who serves as its chief executive. The company reportedly expects its chips to provide up to 100 times better performance than current silicon. Furthermore, Fractile is promising a 90% reduction in energy use. The chips deliver those improvements by removing the need for AI models to move data to off-chip HBM memory.

Large language models generate prompt responses through a workflow that involves numerous steps. When an LLM completes a processing step, it sends the results to an off-chip HBM memory chip. It then retrieves those results to lay the groundwork for the next step. Those repeated data round-trips take a significant amount of time, which slows down inference.

Fractile is not the only AI chip supplier tackling that bottleneck. Cerebras Systems Inc., which went public in May, offers wafer-size accelerators that reduce data movement by keeping information in a large onboard cache. That cache is faster than off-chip HBM modules. The company’s newest processor, the WSE-3T, can hold 44 gigabytes of data.

Cerebras’ on-chip cache is based on SRAM, a type of memory that was historically added to processors in only small quantities. SRAM cells, the technology’s basic building blocks, have six transistors apiece. Those transistors read and write data faster than the single transistor found in HBM cells. At the same time, SRAM’s speed comes with certain trade-offs: it’s expensive and has limited capacity.

Fractile is taking a different approach to reducing data movement. Instead of integrating SRAM into its inference chips, the company is stacking standard DRAM memory on top of them. Placing a memory module immediately above a processor’s logic circuits minimizes the distance that data has to cover. That speeds up traffic while lowering the amount of electricity needed to shuffle it back and forth.

Samsung Electronics Co. is developing a similar technology. In August, the company debuted an HBM variant called zHBM that can be stacked atop AI accelerators. It uses tiny copper wires to move data to and from the host chip. Samsung says the technology will be eight times faster than HBM5, a future iteration of HBM more performant than the versions in use today.

Fractile, for its part, estimates that its chips will enable LLM to process several thousand tokens per second. It plans to ship the processors as part of rack-scale systems that will also include custom software. Many AI chipmakers offer custom compilers, software tools that automatically turn customers’ LLMs into a format compatible with their silicon.

Fractile expects to start shipping its chips next year.

#5613. Hurricane Season Is Over Early, but El Niño Is Not Done With Us Yet

In a typical year, the Atlantic hurricane season runs from June to the end of November. But 2026 has been anything but a typical year.

In fact, the meteorologists at AccuWeather have announced that tropical activity for the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season is over, three weeks before the official end of the season on Nov. 30.

"El Niño has played a significant role in limiting tropical activity across the Atlantic," said AccuWeather lead hurricane expert Alex DaSilva.

"While tropical storms can still develop this late in the season, the weather patterns we're seeing give us confidence that the United States will avoid additional direct tropical impacts this year. It's an unusually quiet conclusion to a season that defied expectations and broke a 121-year-old hurricane record.”

But while the hurricane season might be bowing out early, the country still needs to prepare itself for the coming winter months in a big way.

AccuWeather originally forecasted 11 to 16 named storms for the season last spring, but once El Niño arrived and strengthened much earlier in the year than usual, the forecast dropped to eight to 11 named storms and three to four hurricanes.

To date, only 10 named storms came to fruition, the fewest since 2014, when there were only eight storms. Only one reached hurricane status, with Hurricane Isaias making a destructive Category 2 landfall on the Florida Panhandle in October.

It was the first time since 1925 that there was only one hurricane in the entire season.

That’s not to say that the season wasn’t destructive. The first storm of the season, Tropical Storm Arthur, dumped more than 20 inches of rain in some spots across the Gulf in June and caused an estimated $4 billion to $6 billion in total damage and economic loss, according to a preliminary estimate from experts at AccuWeather.

While the hurricane season is over, homeowners across the country still have to continue with a deluge of wet weather on the way.

Again, all thanks to the Super El Niño still churning away.

Notably, the El Niño could influence winter weather across the United States, bringing warmer-than-average temperatures to Northern states and wetter-than-average conditions to the South and East Coast, according to NOAA’s U.S. Winter Outlook.

Wetter-than-average conditions are most likely across the southern tier, from the Southwest to the Southeast, and along the East Coast. But if the temperatures stay up, the likelihood of snow is slim.

But even without the snow, the storms could be significant for this area this year.

“As we know from decades of observations, a very strong El Nino will likely bring a southward and eastward shift to the jet stream for the contiguous U.S., which tilts the odds toward stormier weather across the South,” said Ken Graham, director of NOAA’s National Weather Service.

“While higher chances of rain and snow may bring relief to drought-afflicted areas, too much precipitation on dry soil can fuel destructive flash floods and mudslides. Now is the time for communities and individuals to plan ahead for the upcoming winter.”

Meanwhile, more snow than average is favored across parts of the Intermountain West, the Plains, and the Appalachians this winter because of El Niño's active storm track, according to The Wall Street Journal.

In fact, most models that were reviewed showed above-average snowfall across the Plains, from South Dakota to northern Texas, and a swath of the central and southern Appalachians.

#5612. Only a Quarter of U.S. Households Have Children at Home

Household composition is a fundamental driver of housing demand, influencing everything from floor plans and bedroom counts to community amenities and long-term land strategies. Understanding how household composition is changing can help inform product planning and identify opportunities to serve different types of buyers.

As of 2024, 25.4% of U.S. households had children under age 18 living at home, according to Zonda’s analysis of U.S. Census data. Put another way, nearly three out of every four households did not have children at home.

The finding is consistent with trends visible among home buyers: the 2025 Home Buyers and Sellers Generational Trends Report from NAR showed that only 24% of buyers had children under 18, a historic low.

Several structural demographic forces help explain this shift, including fertility rates below replacement levels, later family formation, and an aging population that has contributed to more empty nesters, retirees, and older adults living independently. At the same time, households without children, including DINKS (dual income, no kids), represent an important part of housing demand.

These shifts highlight the changing composition of household types shaping housing demand and reinforce the importance of segmentation over assumptions. The traditional family household remains an important customer, but understanding the needs of other household types can help inform product planning and identify opportunities to reach a broader range of buyers.

The insights in this article were taken from more in-depth research reports published in Zonda’s National Outlook subscription.

Zonda’s experts provide objective analysis on housing trends, supply and demand dynamics, and economic drivers. The team of economists, researchers, and analysts blends proprietary data with expert interpretation to help you navigate changing markets and make smarter decisions.

#5609. Sunlight, Weather and Childcare: A Year of New Data on Redfin Home Listings

In 2026, Redfin added information about sunlight, weather, childcare access and more to home listings. Here is everything you need to know about what’s new.

A home listing has always been good at telling you about a house: the square footage, the year it was built, the number of bedrooms. Historically, it has been less good at telling you what living there is actually like. Does the kitchen get morning sunlight? How hot are the summers? Is there a daycare within walking distance?

Those are the questions we set out to answer this year. Multiple new data sets arrived on Redfin in 2026, and they now sit alongside other information that was already there, including scores about a property’s walkability, transit access and climate.

Sunscore shows exactly how much sunlight a home gets

Natural light is one of the hardest things to judge from listing photos or a single showing, and it matters more than you might expect. In a recent Redfin survey, nearly 70% of people said the amount of sunlight in their home affects their satisfaction with where they live, and 11% said it is non-negotiable when searching for a home.

Sunscore is a property-level rating from 0 to 100 that shows how much sunlight a home gets. We co-created it with Shadowmap, a sunlight analysis platform, using 3D modeling that tracks how shadows fall across a home throughout the day and across the seasons. Here are the score breakdowns:

Each score accounts for the home’s 3D shape and structure, surrounding buildings, trees and terrain, the sun’s position throughout the day, and seasonal changes across the year. In other words, it catches the things you would only discover after moving in—like a neighboring building that blocks the afternoon light in winter.

And it is not only about comfort and aesthetics. A home’s sun exposure also says something about its solar potential, which can translate into real savings on energy costs over time.

Weather data helps predict precipitation and heat

Weather turns out to be one of the biggest reasons people move. In a recent Redfin survey conducted by Ipsos, 22% of Americans planning to move to another state said better weather was motivating the move—the most cited reason out of nearly 30 options, ahead of affordability, job opportunities and moving closer to family. Another 21% said concerns about climate change or natural disasters were shaping where they wanted to live.

In July, we partnered with The Weather Company, owner of The Weather Channel app and weather.com, to bring historical weather data to every for-sale listing on Redfin. As our exclusive historical weather provider, it supplies the same data hundreds of millions of people check every month.

Each listing shows ZIP code-level averages for:

Consider this information the difference between the weather on the day you tour a home and the climate you might actually live in.

Childcare data displays daycare and preschool options

For families with young children, childcare access can determine a neighborhood’s fit as much as school boundaries do. However, it’s historically been missing from the home browsing experience. Redfin is the first major real estate portal to partner with Winnie, the largest marketplace for childcare and early education in the U.S., to bring local childcare information to for-sale listings.

Nearby daycare and preschool options now appear on for-sale home listings with details that determine whether a spot is realistic for your family, such as:

Location scores capture everything from wellness access to noise

While Walk Score, Bike Score and Transit Score already existed on home listings, Redfin has expanded these location scores to capture more information about a neighborhood’s vibe using Local Logic data.

#5608. Andersen Partnership Helps Build Accessible Homes for Wounded Veterans

Since 2018, Andersen has worked with Jared Allen's Homes for Wounded Warriors, a nonprofit organization that builds injury-specific, accessible mortgage-free accessible homes for veterans who sustained severe injuries during their military service.

Since 2018, Andersen has partnered with Jared Allen’s Homes for Wounded Warriors to help provide accessible, mortgage-free homes designed around the individual needs of severely injured military veterans.

Through the partnership, Andersen has donated windows and doors to 12 veteran families and home projects across the country. The manufacturer also supports the nonprofit through financial contributions and company matches of employee donations.

Most recently, Andersen contributed to a custom home for Marine Lance Corporal Josh Wege in Fond du Lac County, Wisconsin. Josh Wege, who sustained life-changing injuries while serving in Afghanistan, received the keys to the mortgage-free home alongside his family.

The residence was designed around Wege’s accessibility and mobility requirements, with the broader goal of providing greater independence, comfort, and quality of life.

“Building a home that meets the needs of a critically wounded veteran and their family takes a team of people who believe in our mission,” says Jared Allen, founder of Jared Allen’s Homes for Wounded Warriors since 2009. “Andersen is an important part of that team, and we’re grateful for their support and commitment to the veterans we serve.”

Jared Allen, a Pro Football Hall of Famer and former Minnesota Vikings defensive end, added that the partnership helps create homes “where veterans can live more independently, and families can make memories together for years to come.”

For Andersen, the partnership also provides an opportunity to apply product selection and design considerations to the specific mobility needs of each homeowner. Depending on the project, those considerations can include wider openings, low- or zero-threshold transitions, accessible hardware placement, and patio door configurations intended to make movement easier between indoor and outdoor spaces.

Charlie Jackson, an account sales manager at Andersen, has helped project teams identify window and door solutions based on individual veterans’ accessibility requirements.

“My father was a World War II Marine, so supporting veterans has always been personally meaningful to me,” Jackson shares. “These projects bring Andersen’s work into focus because you can see how thoughtful product choices and accessible design come together to make everyday life easier for a veteran and their family.”

“As a 10-year Andersen employee, I’m proud to contribute my experience to help identify the products and solutions that best support each homeowner’s accessibility, comfort, and long-term needs,” he adds.

The homes are completed through collaboration among Jared Allen’s Homes for Wounded Warriors, manufacturers such as Andersen, local businesses, tradespeople, and other supporters.

#5607. Google tests Tabletop, letting groups build planning tools with an AI agent

Google LLC today began testing Tabletop, a Google Labs experiment in which groups share an online space and ask an artificial intelligence agent to build the planning tools they need.

In a blog post, Roman Nurik, design and engineering lead at Google Labs, wrote that coordinating a family trip or a potluck goes more smoothly when the whole group can pitch in from one place. Whoever sets up a space adds the links, files and ideas the group has collected, and from there a request to @tabletop produces the tool.

Tools Google lists include itineraries, dinner polls, expense splitters and tournament brackets, and there is a set of starter templates that Tabletop users can access as well. Once the space is shared through an invite link posted in the group’s existing chat, everyone can work on those tools at the same time, “like in a Google Doc,” Nurik wrote.

When a guest at an office party in one of Google’s demos ends up seated next to the boss, a request to @tabletop turns the seating chart into one where name badges can be dragged between tables. Any tool can be reworked the same way, according to the Tabletop site.

Google did not say which of its models run Tabletop. When Labs released its Disco browser experiment last December, Gemini 3 was the model it used to turn a person’s open tabs into small web apps.

Tabletop also follows Google’s move in September to let up to six members of a household share the division’s CC agent. Rival OpenAI Group PBC added group chats to ChatGPT a year ago, and up to 20 people can now talk to the chatbot in one thread.

In ChatGPT the chatbot sits inside the conversation as one more member, and OpenAI said at launch that it had taught the model to judge when to join in. Replies in those chats initially came from GPT-5.1 Auto, which chooses a model based on the prompt and on the subscription of whoever ChatGPT is answering. OpenAI also kept personal memory out of group chats entirely.

Tabletop is limited for now to U.S. users 18 and older who sign up through the waitlist at tabletop.google, with Google saying it will let more people in each week. Google’s announcement does not mention pricing or a release outside the U.S.

#5606. Kylie Jenner Faces Fourth Household Staff Lawsuit—Former Housekeeper Alleges Dog Bite, Being Trapped in Closet

Kylie Jenner's former housekeeper is suing the beauty mogul, claiming that she was trapped inside Jenner's closet, bitten by her dog, and pepper-sprayed in the face.

The lawsuit, which is the fourth filed by a member of Jenner's household staff since April, was brought by Dinora Cabria Amaya, who began working for the reality TV star in March 2025.

In the 20-page filing, which was obtained by The Rolling Stone, Amaya claimed that she was denied overtime and experienced a hostile work environment.

She also claimed that she suffered workplace injuries, including being hit with pepper spray, which allegedly caused “severe burning and vision problems.”

According to the lawsuit, she messaged her manager, “Sorry to interrupt you, I had an accident at work, someone left pepper spray and took off safety." The manager then allegedly replied, "Thanks for letting us know."

They then requested that the housekeeper fill out a report and provide it to Jenner's security before seeing a healthcare professional.

She then claimed she experienced “significant eye pain, blurred vision, headaches, burning, irritation, and sensitivity," but received no accommodations due to pain.

“The more plaintiff complained that she was hurt, the harder defendants made her job,” the lawsuit claimed.

Amaya then claimed that she was often "confined in a room because defendant Jenner did not want to see her” and that her “repeated reports of ongoing pain” were not regarded with importance.

In one alleged incident, she described using a passcode to enter the TV personality's closet, only to became locked inside and suffer a panic attack.

“No one is at the house that can let you out, and I cannot give the password to anyone else; you just have to wait,” the housekeeper's manager allegedly replied when Amaya told her she was locked inside.

Amaya claimed that her manager "mocked her" during their call.

The housekeeper then recalled the alleged incident that saw Jenner's dog biting her while she was cleaning the doghouse.

“Again, no meaningful assistance was provided. Plaintiff purchased over-the-counter medication and treated the injury herself. She continued reporting that her eyes hurt, her arm and wrist hurt from the dog bite, and her back hurt from the increasingly physical work," the filing states.

Amaya was fired on Feb. 6, 2026, after requesting mileage reimbursement for her trips to Jenner's homes.

Jenner owns multiple homes in the Los Angeles metropolitan area and a property outside of Palm Springs.

The housekeeper is now claiming that she was fired because she spoke up about her treatment.

The filing names the beauty mogul, her company Kylie Jenner Inc., staff supervisors Laura Dooley and Itzel Sibrian, Tri Star Services, and La Maison Family Services.

The lawsuit claims wrongful termination, false imprisonment, disability discrimination, failure to provide reasonable accommodations, whistleblower retaliation, failure to prevent discrimination and retaliation, and intentional infliction of emotional distress.

Amaya is seeking unpaid wages, past and future monetary earnings, and damages. The housekeeper is being represented by lawyer Della Shaker.

Amaya earned $40 an hour working for Jenner—$23 more than the state's minimum wage. Amaya worked six days a week.

Jenner’s lawyer, Michael Rhodes, noted that Shaker is the same lawyer representing the other members of Jenner's staff who sued earlier this year.

“It’s clear that this lawyer wants to use publicity to try to extract an unwarranted payday. We’re not going to be intimidated into doing that. As such, we’ll defend these meritless cases vigorously and look forward to telling our side of the story," Rhodes told The Rolling Stone.

In response, Shaker told the outlet, “For employees working in high-profile households, the fear of losing future employment opportunities can be overwhelming. When your livelihood depends on discretion, references, and powerful professional relationships, speaking out can feel impossible. But no employer has the right to retaliate against workers for protected complaints. The truth should never be buried behind wealth, fear, or silence.”

Amaya's lawsuit comes after former housekeepers Angelica Hernandez Vasquez and Juana Delgado Soto also filed suits against Jenner, also alleging mistreatment and whistleblower retaliation.

#5605. Invitation Homes Invests in HBI Training for Veterans

The Home Builders Institute (HBI) and Invitation Homes have launched a partnership aimed at helping transitioning military service members, veterans, and their families build careers in construction, property maintenance, and the skilled trades.

The partnership will expand Invitation Homes’ existing Invitation to SkillUp initiative through an investment in HBI’s Military Services program, which provides hands-on, instructor-led skilled trades training, industry-recognized certifications, and job placement assistance.

Through the partnership, HBI and Invitation Homes will connect HBI-trained veterans, military spouses, and family members with career opportunities in the build-to-rent and single-family rental sectors. The organizations also plan to expand recruitment at HBI Military Services locations, including Fort Stewart, Georgia, and Jacksonville, Florida.

Invitation Homes’ Veteran Employee Resource Group will participate in mentorship and career guidance efforts.

“Veterans and their families have dedicated themselves to serving our country, and we are proud to support them as they transition into rewarding civilian careers,” Invitation Homes president and CEO Dallas Tanner says. “Through our Invitation to SkillUp initiative, we are investing in talented individuals whose dedication and service strengthen our communities, while helping create meaningful opportunities in the skilled trades.”

HBI has spent a decade training, certifying, and placing transitioning service members, veterans, and their families in skilled trades careers. According to HBI president and CEO Ed Brady, nearly 90% of graduates from the organization’s military program find jobs, earning an average of more than three times the federal minimum wage.

“We know this model works, and with this important investment from Invitation Homes, we can help more veterans enter the skilled trades every year because the people who served this country deserve a career as strong as their service,” Brady said.

Invitation to SkillUp is Invitation Homes’ national skilled trades development initiative, which works with trade schools and organizations to expand trades education and increase awareness of career opportunities.

Invitation Homes joins other companies supporting HBI’s military programs. The Home Depot Foundation and DEWALT were early supporters, while Google recently provided a $1 million contribution to the effort.

The partnership comes as the housing industry continues to look for ways to strengthen its skilled labor pipeline. For transitioning service members and military families, the effort offers a pathway from military service into construction and housing careers while providing the industry with another source of trained workers.

Leah Draffen is a senior editor at Builder. She earned a B.A. in journalism and minors in business administration and sociology from Louisiana State University.

#5603. Amanda Seyfried Reveals What It Was Like To Be in Elizabeth Holmes’ Texas Home While the Theranos Founder Was in Prison

This article contains spoilers for “You Can See Everything.”

Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s documentary “You Can See Everything” gives viewers an unprecedented look into the home life of Elizabeth Holmes.

The disgraced Theranos founder invited the filmmakers to document the 34 days before she reported to the Federal Prison Camp in Bryan, TX, on May 30, 2023. Two years later, the A24 production team would pick up cameras again, joining Holmes’ partner, Billy Evans, and the couple’s two young children at their home in Austin, TX.

In a surprise twist to viewers, Amanda Seyfried, who portrayed Holmes in the Hulu miniseries “The Dropout,” becomes an important part of the narrative in the second half of the documentary.

The actress opened up about the experience in a Rolling Stone interview with Fielder and Oppenheim, and described what it was really like to enter the family’s Texas home while Holmes was away in prison.

Seyfried—who had been shown footage Fielder and Oppenheim captured in the days leading up to Holmes reporting to prison—explained that she had some preconceived notions about Evans.

She chose to put those feelings aside before visiting the home—a four-bedroom, three-bathroom luxury residence that’s currently on the market for $2.25 million with Amy Deane of Moreland Properties.

“I wanted to turn my disdain off a little bit, because I’m in his house now with his children—with their children,” she emphasized. “I always want to give people the benefit of the doubt, and I felt bad that I had talked a bunch of sh-t about him up until that point.”

The “Mamma Mia!” star noted that although she didn’t particularly “like” Evans, she was careful with her words because she was “coming into this man’s house.”

She explained that “trying to engage with Billy” was “going fine” until he received an unexpected call from Holmes.

“That was just ... what an experience for somebody to have, to say the least,” she reflected, adding that everything she felt was plainly visible on her face in that scene.

“We didn’t know she was gonna call right then. I am sitting there with her children and cuddling with her dog! While she’s in prison!” the star recalled.

Later, the documentary would show Fielder, Seyfried, and Evans having dinner together—a moment that grew tense quickly, due to a stark difference in political opinions between Seyfried and Evans.

“I don’t want to provoke him, but at this point, it’s kind of like, the gloves are off,” she recalled. “I was in the frame of mind where I’m like, ‘OK, this guy is disrespectful, and I’m here in his home, I’m gonna argue this because I actually have a pretty solid stance on things.’”

Seyfried revealed that the dynamic was difficult to balance, as she was torn between being “protective” of herself and “trying to set the record straight,” but she was also hoping to maintain “some kind of rapport” with Evans, so filming could resume in the home without the entire production crew getting kicked out.

The documentary eventually leverages Seyfried’s acting skills—and unique knowledge of the source material—to create a series of reenactments to key the audience into moments that happened before cameras picked up.

These reenactments would take Seyfried and the crew to the ultraprivate Del Mar, CA, beach home Holmes had rented in the weeks leading up to her prison stay.

In the Rolling Stone interview, Fielder remarked that Seyfried had been very “curious” about the objects that were found on the re-creation sets, and wanted to learn which items were placed by the production design team and which had existed in the home when Holmes lived there two years earlier.

“I was just grasping at anything that could ground me back into this world, because it had been so long, and I think I was also experiencing some kind of weird, like, meta-vortex, because I had just seen Elizabeth Holmes in this house, and the house is so specific,” Seyfried explained.

The four-bedroom, four-bathroom home certainly is specific, and became an instantly recognizable location from the moment the “You Can See Everything” trailer dropped. It’s one of just about a dozen residences in the ultraexclusive community called Sandy Lane, about a half-hour from San Diego.

The single-story home was built in 1948 and includes direct access to a private beach. It features tall ceilings, exposed beams, and sizable windows that connect the moody space to its serene surroundings.

The actress said it was “just crazy” to be in the “same place” she had seen Holmes in, through footage Fielder and his team had previously captured.

“Nobody had been in Holmes and Evans’ beach house for two years, or whatever,” she said. “And suddenly, it’s like I’ve time-traveled two years into the past.”

#5602. Lennar, Operation Finally Home Surprise Two Military Families With New Homes

U.S. Army Specialist Jordan Taylor and U.S. Marine Corps Sergeant Kevin Gallmeier with their families.

Two military veterans and their families received life-changing news ahead of Veterans Day when Lennar and Operation Finally Home surprised them with the gift of new homes.

U.S. Army Specialist Jordan Taylor and U.S. Marine Corps Sergeant Kevin Gallmeier were surprised with the announcement during the inaugural Operation Finally Home Golf Classic reception in Austin, Texas, on Nov. 9.

Neither family knew about the plans beforehand and attended the event as guests of Operation Finally Home.

The announcement followed a live performance by country music artist and Army Reserve soldier Craig Morgan. Operation Finally Home founder Dan Wallrath and Lennar San Antonio division president Brian Barron then revealed that each family would receive a new Lennar home.

The partnership builds on Operation Finally Home’s mission of providing mortgage-free homes and home modifications to wounded, ill, and injured veterans, first responders, and their families.

Gallmeier served in the Marine Corps from 2005 to 2015 after being motivated to enlist by the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks. During his service, he deployed twice to Iraq in support of combat operations and later deployed to Okinawa, Japan, as part of the 31st Marine Expeditionary Unit.

Gallmeier sustained a traumatic brain injury following a grenade blast during combat operations in Iraq. He also developed post-traumatic stress disorder and continues to manage PTSD, amongst other conditions, according to Operation Finally Home.

Following his military career, Gallmeier earned bachelor’s and master’s degrees in divinity from Biola University and became a pastor. A formal groundbreaking for the family’s new Lennar home is scheduled for Nov. 10 in the Freedom Crossing community in Killeen, Texas.

Taylor enlisted in the U.S. Army in August 2004 shortly after graduating from high school in Washington state. He served as an infantryman and filled roles including Squad Automatic Weapon gunner, driver, and team leader.

From June 2006 to September 2007, Taylor deployed to Baghdad in support of Operation Iraqi Freedom. His unit lost 21 soldiers during the deployment.

After completing his military service in December 2007, Taylor continued serving his community as a firefighter and emergency medical technician.

A serious back injury in January 2024, combined with the lasting physical and emotional effects of his military service, ultimately forced Taylor to medically retire from firefighting in March 2025.

Following the injury, Taylor and his wife, Aylynn, and their four children faced financial uncertainty and eventually sold their home and moved in with relatives. The family’s new Lennar home will provide a fresh start. A groundbreaking for the Taylor residence is slated in December.

Leah Draffen is a senior editor at Builder. She earned a B.A. in journalism and minors in business administration and sociology from Louisiana State University.

#5601. What’s Next for Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac After the Midterm Elections

President Donald Trump has suggested that Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac's government conservatorship should end. But whether that will happen under his administration remains unclear after the midterms.

Since the federal bailout in 2008, Fannie and Freddie have remained under conservatorship for 18 years, with the terms subjecting them to strict oversight and regulation by the Federal Housing Finance Agency.

For years, the U.S. Treasury has collected nearly all profits from the two entities, an amount surpassing $300 billion and exceeding the government's outlay in the bailout. Trump has floated the idea of ending the conservatorship since his first term in office, an idea that regained attention when he returned to the White House in 2025.

Trump suggested this could mean an initial public offering of the two mortgage giants, with both companies valued at up to $1 trillion combined and selling between 5% and 15% of their stock.

Key Democrats have expressed reservations about privatizing Fannie and Freddie or otherwise ending the conservatorship, raising questions about whether the Trump administration will pursue the matter with Democrats in control of Congress.

Trump has said little about the matter in recent months. Billionaire investor Bill Ackman, who has long pushed for an end to conservatorship, believes that the Trump administration wanted to wait until after the midterms to take action.

“The reason why it’s not being touched right now is, you know, midterms,” he told CNBC on Election Day.

Before the election, a senior Trump administration official said the end of conservatorship for Fannie and Freddie could still be on. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent suggested the government could take up the matter again in 2027 or 2028.

U.S. Federal Housing Finance Agency Director William Pulte supported the idea this spring. He said that changes to their credit scoring requirements introduced this year could increase the chances of success. But only Trump knew the timing, he said.

“We stand ready every day to execute the president’s vision, and if and when he decides he wants to do something, we are locked and loaded and ready to go," Pulte said.

But starting in January, the Trump administration may face stiff opposition in Congress to privatizing Fannie and Freddie, a move that many economists have warned could put upward pressure on mortgage rates.

Rep. Maxine Waters (D-CA), who's running to chair the House Financial Services Committee, has consistently opposed administrative efforts by regulators to rapidly release Fannie and Freddie from conservatorship without comprehensive congressional oversight, public transparency, and safeguards for affordable housing and racial equity.

"To address the affordable housing crisis, Congress must ensure that Fannie and Freddie meet their mission to provide liquidity, sustainability, and affordability to all housing markets in the U.S., and at all times," Waters said at a hearing in April.

Legal and political analysts are divided on whether the executive branch could end the conservatorship by fiat, but such a push would almost certainly face stiff opposition from Democrats in Congress.

The White House didn't respond to a Realtor.com® request for comment about the future of the conservatorship. Waters also didn't respond.

Even as he discussed the end of conservatorship, Trump used Fannie and Freddie as tools to try to help improve affordability in the market. That meant directing them to purchase $200 billion in mortgage-backed securities in an effort to improve the housing market.

Trump's former Federal Housing Commissioner Frank Cassidy told Realtor.com that privatization is a lever Trump could pull without his party controlling Congress. But it needs to be structured in a way that benefits the market. One worry is that the lack of government backing would drive up mortgage rates.

"It hasn't been a priority yet. It would need to be worked on very quickly because it will take some time," Cassidy said. "How do you structure it in a way that makes it more favorable? The idea under conservatorship is implicitly a government guarantee."

In the meantime, the Mortgage Brokers of America reiterated that a positive outcome is still possible.

"MBA continues to believe that GSE release must preserve what works to ensure that it continues to deliver what consumers need and investors expect," it said. "And importantly, any release must include an explicit federal backstop—passed by Congress and paid for by the GSEs—of their mortgage-backed securities to protect consumers, taxpayers, and our best-in-the-world housing finance system."

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

#5600. Attached Housing Stands Out in Baltimore’s Housing Market

Annualized new-home sales declined 5.2% in September to 2,613 units. Attached housing accounted for 1,951 sales versus 662 detached sales during the period. However, the Baltimore market is sending mixed signals as 2026 winds down. By comparison, the market’s average new-home sales rate of 2.4 homes per project matched Maryland and remained above the national rate of 2.0.

That aforementioned product split is one of Baltimore’s defining characteristics. Annualized attached sales fell just 0.9% year over year compared with a 16% decline for detached homes as of September data. The strongest sales activity also sits toward the more attainable end of the new home market, with attached homes priced from $350,000 to $450,000 experiencing the most closing activity over the past year.

Related, affordability remains a constraint. As of July, the median new-home closing price stood at $555,337, down 2.9% year over year, compared with $420,000 for existing homes.

The economic backdrop adds another layer. Total nonfarm employment in the Baltimore metro declined 0.6% year over year in August, while the unemployment rate was 4.1%. Households are estimated to decline 0.1% in 2026 and post flat annual growth through 2028.

One potential longer-term catalyst comes from defense manufacturing. Anduril Industries announced a $3.7 billion investment in a high-tech shipyard at Baltimore County’s Tradepoint Atlantic industrial center. The project is expected to create 3,100 direct jobs and support more than 11,000 indirect jobs, while generating more than $2 billion in annual economic output.

Baltimore’s opportunity is therefore less about broad based growth and more about positioning. Ideal locations, attainable price points, and disciplined starts stand out in a market where buyers are still active but increasingly selective.

#5599. October Marks the First Month in 3 Years With a Decline in U.S. Home-Sale Prices

For three years, U.S. home-sale prices rose from a year earlier every single month, even as mortgage rates climbed and would-be buyers pulled back. That streak has ended.

The median home-sale price declined 0.4% year over year to $388,634 in October. That’s  the first decline since May 2023 and a sharp slowdown from the 2.5% gain just two months earlier. With Americans’ wages growing about 4% year over year, even a slight dip in prices can improve affordability. Sale prices have risen nearly every single month for the last 13 years; the only exception was a handful of months in 2023.

With the total number of homes for sale at its highest level since early 2020 and demand cooling, homebuyers’ negotiating power keeps increasing–and that’s finally showing up in sale prices.

Home-sale prices fell nationwide, but they rose in more than half of the 50 most populous U.S. metro areas. San Francisco led the nation by a wide margin, with the median sale price rising 16.8% year over year. That’s the biggest increase since 2018. Next comes New Brunswick, NJ, with a 7.7% gain. Two other NYC-area metros also had price increases ranking in the top six; the median sale price rose 4.4% in both New York City and Nassau County.

In San Francisco, AI wealth is fueling competition for scarce inventory; active listings were down 7% from a year earlier. In the New York City area, years of limited homebuilding have left buyers competing for relatively few homes in a region with a strong job market.

Home-sale prices fell most in Austin, TX, where they declined 6.5% year over year. It’s followed by Seattle (-5.1%) and Nashville, TN (-4.9%). Austin and Nashville are among the biggest buyer’s markets in the U.S., and Seattle’s shaky tech job market is curbing demand.

National sale prices are losing steam because fewer Americans can afford to buy a home. U.S. pending home sales fell 3.6% from a month earlier in October on a seasonally adjusted basis to their lowest level since 2013, with the exception of April 2020.

This is a real-time indicator of the state of the housing market; fewer homes went under contract in October largely because mortgage rates averaged 7.33%, a three-year high and up from 6.86% the month before.

All figures in this report are seasonally adjusted, with the exception of median sale price data and mortgage rate data. See a more detailed methodology here and view an interactive dashboard here.

“It’s a buyer’s market, but not many people can afford to buy,” said Chen Zhao, Redfin’s head of economics. “That could start to shift a bit, now that sale prices are closer to reflecting the shape of the market. House hunters in most of the country should know that the price they see on a listing may very well be a starting point; they should try offering below the asking price, and negotiating for closing costs, repairs and maybe even mortgage-rate buydowns. If you can’t get the price or monthly payment you want on one house, move on to the next one–with a big pool of inventory sitting on the market, buyers can afford to be picky.”

Pending home sales declined in all of the most populous U.S. metros. That’s the second month in a row that has happened; before September, the last time was three years earlier.

The biggest declines were in Seattle and San Diego, both places where pending sales fell more than 20% year over year. Those West Coast metros are some of the priciest in the U.S., so 7%-plus mortgages hit house hunters’ monthly payments there hard. In Seattle, an uncertain local job market is also curbing demand.

Closed home sales fell to their lowest level in nearly 3 years. They declined 2.1% month over month in October to their lowest level since December 2023; before that, the last time sales dropped that low was 2014. Many of the deals that closed last month went under contract in August and September, when rates were already climbing and economic uncertainty was deterring a lot of house hunters.

With homebuying demand falling, supply is building. The total number of homes for sale rose 0.9% from September to its highest level since early 2020; that’s the biggest monthly gain since May 2025.

More supply gives buyers more homes to choose from and more leverage:

“Buyers are nervous about rates, the economy, and everything they’re seeing in the news– so they need the house and the price to line up perfectly before they’ll make an offer,” said Callie Kimmel, a Redfin Premier agent in Philadelphia. “I’m advising sellers to price just below current market value from day one–and not comps from six months ago, but homes that are listed right now. Otherwise, the home is likely to end up sitting on the market for a bit and selling for less than they hoped. There are a few exceptions: Move-in ready homes in the most desirable neighborhoods are still competitive; in those cases, sellers have the upper hand.”

While total housing supply is growing, fewer sellers are adding new inventory to the pool. New listings of homes for sale fell 1% month over month to the lowest level in more than two years. Would-be sellers are pulling back as homebuying demand slows and sale prices lose steam.

The figures below are based on a list of the 50 most populous U.S. metropolitan areas. Some metros may be removed from time to time to ensure data accuracy. Refer to our metrics definition page for explanations of metrics used in this report. All changes below represent year-over-year changes.
