#5568. ‘It’s Like Facebook Again’: How AI IPOs Could Further Upend the Real Estate Market

A robotic hand presents a house icon with a percentage symbol, symbolizing growth and investment in a modern office space, merging technology with real estate. Synapse

(TNS)– The deluge of wealth the artificial intelligence boom has brought into San Francisco has already pushed luxury home prices to record heights. Now, with Anthropic’s initial public offering poised to bring even more money into the city, could things get even worse?

Real estate professionals say yes—but that a lot of the growth is already baked in.

Let’s take stock of what’s already happened. San Francisco’s home prices have risen most sharply in neighborhoods that were already exclusive, such as Pacific Heights or the Marina. The median home price for luxury homes in the San Francisco metropolitan area—properties sold in San Francisco and San Mateo counties at or above the 95th percentile price—was nearly $7.5 million from July to September 2026, Redfin data shows. That was up a whopping 23% from the same period in 2025, and up more than 60% from 2019.

Now, some experts suggest that AI IPOs could cause demand to spill even further, raising prices for the few home types—or communities—in the Bay Area where middle-income families might still afford a property.

Already, some data indicates that even non-luxury homes in the city have seen strong appreciation over the past year.

“Typical” San Francisco area homes—those in the 35th-to-65th percentile sale price range — saw a record median sale price of $1.6 million in September 2026, an increase of 6.5% from 2025. While that’s a much lower jump compared to the San Francisco area’s luxury market, it still diverges sharply from that of the rest of the United States, where high mortgage rates and economic woes have caused prices to dip.

Redfin economist Daryl Fairweather believes the heat in San Francisco will spread to other parts of the region. In some ways, it already has; the city’s surging rents have caused many tenants to seek refuge in relatively more affordable cities like Oakland, pushing up prices there.

“This has been the story for at least … 15 years: San Francisco prices and rents going up and people being displaced,” Fairweather said.

Demand for fancy homes will likely keep surging

Some real estate agents say that the AI workers and investors fighting bidding wars in San Francisco often don’t want to give up on their dream house, even as prices rise. That’s part of the reason demand has flowed into other expensive cities in Marin County or the Peninsula, where there are more fancy homes for the buying. Phil Chen, a real estate broker at Christie’s International Real Estate Sereno, said that demand for Hillsborough has soared, with buyers citing a desire for strong schools — and security.

“It’s my first time hearing, ‘Is the glass bulletproof and are there panic rooms?’” Chen said.

Zillow data indicates that home values in Hillsborough, Menlo Park and Piedmont have risen faster over the past year than any other Bay Area city with at least 10,000 people except San Francisco, suggesting that some wealthy buyers are expanding their search radius. In some cities, such as in Piedmont, starter home values—those in the 5th to 35th percentile—have actually climbed more than top-tier values. Still, a “starter home” in Piedmont still costs more than a mid-tier property in San Francisco.

It’s unclear how much demand could rise for homes that aren’t luxury properties or in expensive neighborhoods. One 2019 study found that IPOs increase demand for high-priced homes near the company’s headquarters, but not for low-priced properties. The study’s results also indicated IPOs increased the probability low-income residents moved to lower-income neighborhoods.

But Fairweather said that junior tech workers with smaller windfalls than their senior peers could start to make offers in parts of the Bay Area where their money will go further. Vanessa Hatvany Kitchen, a real estate agent with Compass’ Team Hatvany Kitchen, said her team has seen more people buying condos and smaller single-family homes in San Francisco, fearing they won’t be able to get a foothold after companies like Anthropic go public.

But much of the demand increase is baked in

If there’s any silver lining for buyers, though, it’s that a lot of those companies’ impact on the Bay Area real estate market is already here. Arrian Binnings, a San Francisco real estate agent at Christie’s International Real Estate Sereno, said many AI workers have been able to get cash by borrowing against their stocks or selling their shares via company-approved tender offers, while investors have benefitted from the strength of the public equity market. That’s consistent with some research showing that merely filing for IPOs can raise home prices near a company’s headquarters.

“I don’t see the IPO as the starting gun of a new race. I see it as … we’re probably already at the 50-yard line,” Binnings said. “But I do still see plenty of room to run.”

IPOs don’t always result in an explosion of wealth. In the months after Uber went public in 2019, the company’s stock price plummeted, erasing billions of dollars in value. A similar fate for a public Anthropic or OpenAI would send a chill through the real estate market, some real estate agents say.

But many buyers are optimistic. Chen said some of his clients plan to sell their newly purchased homes in five years, expecting to increase their budgets from $10 million to $25 million. after the IPO. Those buyers, he added, are relatively junior-level employees.

“It’s like Facebook again, but 10x,” Chen said.

#5567. Pfizer is tapping Blackstone for up to $1.5 billion to fund its weight-loss drug

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Blackstone would be eligible for milestone payments tied to U.S. approval of monthly berobenatide, while Pfizer keeps full control

Pfizer $PFE and Blackstone Life Sciences announced a co-funding agreement on Wednesday in which Blackstone-managed funds will shoulder as much as $1.5 billion of berobenatide's R&D expenses between now and 2028. The drug is an investigational monthly injection being studied for chronic weight management and obesity-related conditions.

In return, Blackstone could receive payments tied to the achievement of certain milestones, the companies said. The payments depend on U.S. regulatory approval of monthly dosing of injectable berobenatide monotherapy for chronic weight management, and on certain commercial sales milestones. Any payments earned will be made over a multi-year period.

Blackstone does not acquire any rights or ownership in berobenatide, and Pfizer retains full operational control and decision-making over the program, the companies said. Funds managed by Blackstone's perpetual private equity strategy, BXPE, will invest alongside the Blackstone Life Sciences funds.

"Our aim is to bring important new medicines to patients while taking a disciplined approach that pairs internal research investments with targeted investment from capital partners," Pfizer Chief Financial Officer Cecile Guegan said in a statement. "Today's announcement helps us advance our comprehensive obesity program and maintain the financial capacity and flexibility to invest in our broader pipeline across all therapeutic areas."

Nicholas Galakatos, global head of Blackstone Life Sciences, said in a statement: "We are pleased to further expand our relationship with Pfizer and support the broad and rigorous development of berobenatide as the anchor of Pfizer's cardiometabolic pipeline."

Pfizer intends to move forward with over 20 studies covering obesity and related conditions during 2026, the company said. Those include 10 ongoing and planned Phase 3 trials for berobenatide, which is being studied for conditions such as knee osteoarthritis and obstructive sleep apnea. The company is developing the drug as a monotherapy and in combination with other peptides, including amylin analogs.

Pfizer is pushing into a weight-loss field currently dominated by Eli Lilly $LLY and Novo Nordisk, according to Bloomberg. The company acquired Metsera in 2025 in a deal worth up to $10 billion.

#5566. A decade in, KubeVirt pushes virtual machines into the AI agent era

Confidential computing is drawing fresh interest as enterprises weigh where their most sensitive AI workloads can safely run. That shift is giving virtual machines a new role alongside containers on Kubernetes, rather than a slow retirement.

The timing lines up with a milestone for KubeVirt, the open-source project that runs VMs inside Kubernetes clusters, which graduated from the Cloud Native Computing Foundation this week. Its maintainers are now steering the project toward AI isolation, agent sandboxes and confidential computing, a long-standing technology that is regaining momentum, according to Itamar Holder (pictured, left), principal software engineer and KubeVirt maintainer at Red Hat Inc.

“I think it’s one of the blockers for a lot of companies to join public cloud in general, like companies that really care about super sensitive data,” Holder said. “I think it unblocks them to join.”

Holder and Vladik Romanovsky (right), technical lead and KubeVirt maintainer at Red Hat, spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how KubeVirt is evolving from a virtualization tool into an operating layer for AI workloads. (* Disclosure below.)

KubeVirt’s core idea is running VMs and containers on the same Kubernetes cluster without maintaining two separate stacks. That pairing matters more in the AI era, with Nvidia Corp. developers helping the project integrate dynamic resource allocation for GPU hardware, Holder noted. Romanovsky sees the two forms of compute as partners rather than rivals.

“VMs will do kind of the heavy lifting and larger isolation, and the pods that are running around them would provide a better scaling for cache applications,” Romanovsky said. “In general, it belongs together. VMs and containers can run as one application as well.”

The project is also eyeing a role in AI agent sandboxing, an area where Red Hat is building out infrastructure. The maintainers want KubeVirt to become another isolation backend for the Kubernetes agent sandbox repository, Holder explained.

“I think that we can offer a lot of benefits that other isolation backends don’t have,” Holder said. “We can use live migration and complex hardware configurations with DRA and a lot of other sweet stuff.”

#5565. I analyzed 1,133 Instagram posts with Meta’s new AI

Meta Muse for Small Business connects to your Instagram analytics. Here are five prompts to analyze your past posts before asking AI to create more.

Meta quietly released something at the end of September that I think a lot of real estate agents are going to want to play with.

It’s called Meta Muse for Small Business, and while there are plenty of AI tools that can help you brainstorm a Reel or write a caption, what is massive about Muse is that it can connect directly to your Instagram professional account analytics, along with your Facebook Pages, Meta ad accounts and other business tools.

I connected mine and started playing with it, but instead of asking it to make more content, which is how I use AI most of the time, I wanted to see what would happen if I used it to understand all the content I had already made.

Eventually, we analyzed 1,133 of my Instagram posts. It helped me understand why my rolling views had fallen from roughly 4 million to 2.46 million, showed me that at least 27 of my 98 newest followers were real estate professionals, and identified patterns in the topics and formats that have historically performed best for me.

That was when I realized I had probably been using AI backward. If you have been consistently creating content for a few years, you already have your own data set of what works and what doesn’t, so before asking AI for another 10 Reel ideas, there may be more value in asking it to help you understand what your audience has already told you.

Here are five prompts I’m using to do that.

“Analyze my Instagram performance over the past 90 days. Don’t give me content recommendations yet. First tell me where the biggest weakness is between reach, engagement, profile visits, follower growth and conversion, and show me the data that led you to that conclusion.”

A few months ago, my Instagram analytics showed roughly 4 million views in a 30-day window, and more recently that number had fallen to about 2.46 million, so naturally my first reaction was that something wasn’t working.

The story was a little different once I dug into the data. Some of my biggest posts, including videos with more than 1 million views, had simply aged out of the rolling reporting period. I would love to tell you I publish a million-view video every week, and I’m working on it, but I don’t.

My views were down, but roughly 84 percent were still coming from non-followers, and my content had reached more than 1.4 million accounts. The point wasn’t to ignore the decline; it was to understand what was causing it before changing a strategy that might not actually be broken.

“Analyze my most recent followers, and group them into the most common audience types you can identify. Don’t assume who my target audience is. Tell me what the data shows.”

We pulled roughly 100 of my newest followers, and of the 98 we could analyze, at least 27 had Realtor, real estate, broker or realty directly in their name or username.

Initially, I wondered whether that was a problem because I sell houses and still want consumers seeing my content, but last year we closed roughly $12 million in sales volume from referrals, and relationships with other agents have also created speaking opportunities, partnerships and other revenue. Trying to get rid of an audience already producing real business made very little sense.

Instead, I’m leaning into it while becoming more intentional about building consumer-focused lead pillars through my local Dana Point Daddy page and YouTube.

I’m also still making consumer-focused and humorous content on my main account because my past clients, database, sphere, friends and family are seeing and engaging with it. We’re still marketing directly to our database, hosting client events and doing the things that generate real estate business outside social media.

Your unexpected audience might be completely different from mine, but you probably shouldn’t decide whether the audience you’re building is good or bad until you know who is in it and what that audience is worth to your business.

“Analyze my highest-performing posts from the last year and group them by topic, format and hook. Tell me what patterns repeat among my winners and which patterns I seem to be underusing.”

I spend an embarrassing amount of time studying other creators, saving their posts and trying to understand why something went viral, while apparently not spending nearly enough time studying the years of content I already had telling me what my own audience responds to.

We analyzed 447 of my carousel and single graphic posts and isolated 103 that used headline-style hooks. The winners repeatedly included income statistics that create sticker shock, local rankings people want to agree or disagree with, surprising changes in the Southern California housing market and California housing policies translated into something useful for homeowners.

This October, Inman turns its focus to AI and its rapid rise in real estate. During Artificial Intelligence Month, we’re digging into the startups shaking things up and the established players folding AI into their offerings.

I don’t need to make variations of those posts forever, but I can look for new topics that share the DNA of things my own audience has already told me it wants instead of constantly trying to recreate somebody else’s viral post.

“Compare how frequently I publish each content format with how those formats actually perform. Where is my time allocation inconsistent with my results?”

At the time of the analysis, I had published 66 times over 28 days, and Reels were the format I was publishing most frequently even though they weren’t my best-performing format. Carousels were.

I’m not going to stop making Reels because different content has different jobs, but if I’m deciding where to spend another hour this week, I should probably know whether the format consuming most of my time is producing my best results.

“Based only on the patterns you identified in my historically best-performing content, give me 10 new content ideas. For each one, tell me which past pattern it is based on and why you think it fits my audience.”

This is where the first four prompts become useful instead of just interesting because I can ask any AI tool for 10 content ideas and it will happily give them to me, but without context it is essentially making an educated guess.

Once it understands what my audience has historically responded to, I can ask a much better question: What should I make next based on what has already worked for me?

I’m still going to experiment, tell personal stories and make something weird because I think it’s funny, but now my own history gets a vote.

Meta Muse for Small Business has only been out for about a month, so I am sure I’m barely scratching the surface of what I can do with it, but this experiment has already changed the way I’m using AI.

If you’ve been consistently posting for a few years, you may already have hundreds or thousands of experiments sitting inside your Instagram, so before asking AI for another hook, caption or content idea, ask it to help you understand those experiments first.

For me, the most interesting thing AI has done for my content lately isn’t helping me create more of it. It’s helping me make better decisions about what I create next.

Krys Benyamein is a Realtor with Allstars Realty in Southern California. Get connected on Instagram or LinkedIn.

#5564. If you own the asset, you should own the project data

Owners often inherit thousands of closeout files but lose decision context stored in contractor systems. A persistent owner-controlled record improves operations, diligence, portfolio learning and future AI analysis.   AI Summary

Real estate owners spend years making decisions before a shovel hits the ground, then decades living with the consequences of those decisions after construction is complete. Yet during construction, something unusual often happens: The most complete version of the project can end up living inside systems controlled by a project team whose role is temporary.

That is not an argument against general contractors or the technology they use. Contractors need their own systems to execute the work — to manage RFIs, submittals, drawings, schedules, changes, commitments, field activity and the hundreds of other workflows required to deliver a project. The issue is what happens to all of that information when the project ends.

For the owner, construction is only one chapter in a much longer relationship with the asset, and the information created during that chapter should remain just as durable as the building itself.

By the time a general contractor mobilizes, an owner may already have spent months or years developing the project. There has been an investment thesis, underwriting, capital planning, site diligence, entitlements, early budgeting, design development, consultant coordination, procurement decisions, lender requirements and investor approvals.

Each of these steps creates information and, more importantly, context: why one design option was selected over another, why the budget moved, which assumptions drove the underwriting, which risks were identified early and which decisions were deferred into construction.

Then the project moves into delivery, and the volume of information accelerates. Drawings are revised, RFIs are answered, submittals are reviewed, contracts are executed, schedules change, pay applications are processed and change orders are negotiated. Decisions are documented across meetings, email, project-management software and individual files.

When construction ends, the asset’s operating life continues. The asset moves into operations, warranties begin to matter, capital projects follow, systems get replaced, spaces are renovated and new teams inherit the property. The asset may later be refinanced, sold or redeveloped. The asset’s history needs to remain accessible through changes in project teams, operating staff and ownership. The way that history is maintained should reflect that reality.

During construction, it is completely reasonable for the general contractor to operate its own project-management environment; in many cases, that is where the day-to-day execution record is most complete. The problem begins when that environment also becomes the owner’s only durable record of what happened.

At turnover, owners can receive thousands of files — drawings, warranties, manuals, RFIs, submittals, schedules, photos, meeting records and closeout documents. Technically, the information was transferred, but information and usable history are not always the same thing.

A folder can tell you what the final drawing was; it may not tell you why the design changed. A change-order file can tell you what was approved; it may not clearly preserve the sequence of decisions that created the change. A final budget can tell you where the project landed; it may not preserve how the forecast evolved along the way.

The distinction matters because the value of project information is not simply in possessing the files. It is in maintaining enough structure and context to understand what happened and why. When that continuity breaks at turnover, the next team has to reconstruct the story.

The answer is not for owners to dictate every piece of software used by every project participant — that would create a different problem. General contractors, architects, engineers, consultants and trade partners all have tools and workflows that support their roles, and those systems are important to project execution and should continue to be.

What the owner needs instead is a persistent layer of information that remains under its control throughout the asset lifecycle. That record should begin before construction, remain active while the project is being delivered and continue after turnover. During construction, information can move between the owner’s environment and the systems used by the project team through workflows, integrations, APIs, exports or agreed reporting processes.

In practice, that means being able to access, export and reuse the agreed project record without depending on a former project participant’s account. Owners should define the required records, their format and responsibility for maintaining them before delivery begins.

The goal is not to duplicate every click made inside a contractor’s software. It is to make sure the information that matters to the long-term owner does not disappear when the temporary project organization dissolves.

Not everything created during construction has equal long-term value. The enduring record should focus on the information required to understand how the asset became what it is.

That starts with the financial history: approved budgets, commitments, forecast changes, contingency usage, major cost movements and the financial impact of significant project decisions. It also includes the decision history — major approvals, design changes, scope decisions, responsible parties and the supporting information behind those decisions.

Then there is the technical project record: drawings, specifications, RFIs, submittals, schedule information and other documentation that explains what was designed and ultimately built. Finally, there is the turnover record — as-builts, warranties, manuals, punch and closeout documentation and the information future teams will need to operate, maintain or modify the asset.

The important point is not the specific software used to store each item. It is continuity. Five years after completion, someone working on the property should be able to understand the decisions made five years earlier without starting an archaeological dig through old inboxes, shared drives and archived contractor accounts.

Construction information is often treated as though its usefulness peaks at closeout. For owners, the opposite may be true. A complete development and construction history can become increasingly useful as the asset ages: operations teams can use it to understand equipment, warranties and design intent and asset managers can use it when evaluating future capital work.

The same history also supports investment and portfolio decisions. Development teams can compare budgets, scopes and outcomes against previous projects, and executives can benchmark performance across a portfolio. Future project teams can understand why earlier decisions were made instead of repeating the same analysis, and the information can also support underwriting, refinancing and disposition diligence by making the history of the asset easier to understand.

This becomes even more valuable for owners with multiple properties. One project record is useful; a consistent record across 20, 50 or 100 assets begins to create institutional knowledge. Patterns become visible, assumptions can be tested, budget performance can be compared and recurring problems can be identified — lessons learned on one project can actually influence the next one. The organization’s experience stops resetting every time a project team changes.

Artificial intelligence makes this conversation more important, but not because every owner needs an AI strategy for every construction workflow today. The larger issue is much simpler: AI becomes more useful when it has access to complete, structured and trustworthy information.

An owner might want to understand why similar scopes repeatedly generated changes, how contingency usage varied across developments or which underwriting assumptions proved wrong. Answering those questions requires more than a collection of final documents; it requires a traceable history of decisions and outcomes.

If each project’s information is fragmented across contractor platforms, consultant systems, shared drives, inboxes and archived files, an AI model faces the same problem a human does: the information may technically exist, but reconstructing the story becomes difficult. The owners that preserve a consistent project history today are not simply improving document retention — they are building the information base from which future analysis becomes possible.

There is an important distinction between controlling a project and controlling the enduring record of a project. Owners do not need every contractor to abandon the systems that help them build effectively, and they do not need to centralize every workflow or capture every administrative action performed during construction. What they do need is continuity over the information that explains the asset they ultimately own.

The owner owns the building. It carries the financial consequences of the decisions made during development, operates the asset after the project team leaves, funds the next capital program, and answers the questions of the next lender, investor, buyer or development team. The information describing how that asset was conceived, financed, designed, built and changed should be treated accordingly.

Construction teams move on, and ownership can change. The project record should remain with the asset, available to the people responsible for its future.

Adam Stark is a Special Forces veteran and construction technology executive with experience spanning development, project delivery, construction management and operational systems in the built world.  This column does not necessarily reflect the opinion of HousingWire’s editorial department and its owners. #5563. Op-Ed: Open Real Estate Shouldn’t Need an Announcement

The announcement of Open Real Estate was welcome news. It also raised an uncomfortable question: How did we reach the point where keeping the housing market open required an announcement?

Buyers should be able to find available homes. Sellers should understand who can see their property and what they may sacrifice by limiting its exposure. Brokerages should compete on the quality of their advice, service and results.

These principles should be ordinary expectations of our profession. The fact that they now need a name, a coalition and a public defense is a troubling sign of how far the conversation has veered off course.

Brown Harris Stevens, where I serve as executive director, is an initial participating member of Open Real Estate. I support the initiative’s stated commitment to broader access, informed seller decisions and fair competition. But the larger issue extends beyond any platform or participating company. Openness should be how we conduct business every day.

The appeal of exclusive inventory to a brokerage is easy to understand. If buyers believe they need a relationship with a particular company to see certain homes, that company gains an advantage. Exclusive inventory can help attract buyers, recruit and retain agents and strengthen the firm’s position.

The benefit to the seller is less easy to understand and requires a separate explanation. A brokerage’s ability to use a listing to grow its business does not establish that limiting the property’s exposure is the best strategy for the homeowner. Those interests may align in a particular transaction, but that does not make them interchangeable.

Compass has made private exclusives and phased marketing central to its offering, promoting the opportunity to test pricing and generate interest before a broader public launch. Those claims deserve scrutiny because they concern decisions sellers are trusting their advisors to help them make.

What does the seller gain during that period? Which potential buyers cannot see the property? How representative is pricing feedback from a limited audience? What opportunities might the seller lose while broader exposure is delayed?

The recruiting appeal of the strategy is clear: Access to inventory agents and their buyers might otherwise miss. But sellers deserve to hear the other side of that pitch. The inventory attracting people into the network is their home, and restricting access may exclude buyers who could compete for it.

A large brokerage network can provide meaningful exposure, but it still represents only part of the market. The strength of that network does not, by itself, establish that a seller benefits from postponing access to everyone else.

For sellers seeking the strongest price within a practical time frame, I believe broad exposure should be the starting point. Making a home available to more potential buyers creates more opportunity for competing offers and gives the seller a fuller picture of demand. A recommendation to delay that exposure should explain what the seller stands to gain and what they may give up.

The pricing argument also deserves scrutiny. Sellers hire brokers in part for their ability to analyze comparable sales, assess competing inventory and recommend a pricing strategy. If an agent recommends testing a price privately, the seller should ask: Why is feedback from a limited audience more useful than feedback from the broader market? What uncertainty does this approach resolve, and why does resolving it require restricted exposure?

A broker should be prepared to answer those questions with evidence specific to the property and the seller’s circumstances. And the answer shouldn’t be just about obfuscating days on market. When we evaluate how quickly the strategy produces a sale, we should count any private marketing period. The absence of public days on the market does not mean the seller’s clock has stopped.

Some sellers have legitimate reasons to limit exposure. Security, personal circumstances, timing and discretion can all matter. A thoughtful advisor should understand those priorities and recommend a strategy that reflects them.

Those needs existed long before private exclusives became the manufactured proposition they are today. They deserve individual solutions. Their existence does not justify making restricted access the default starting point for sellers.

Seller choice matters. So does how an advisor presents that choice. Which option is introduced first? Which benefits are emphasized? Are the limitations explained with the same conviction? Did the conversation start by asking what the seller’s goals are in the selling process, or did the broker prescribe a strategy without first understanding the specific circumstances and goals?

A signed disclosure is needed, sure, but the quality of the conversation that leads to that signature matters even more.

An individual brokerage may argue that its private network is large enough to serve its sellers well. But imagine that argument becoming the operating model across the industry. Buyers would need to navigate multiple networks to understand what is available.

Their selection could depend on which brokerage they contacted. Sellers could reach substantial audiences while still missing qualified buyers connected to other firms. Each company might describe its own network as an advantage. Together, those networks could create a more fragmented and less useful marketplace.

Consider Southwest Airlines. For years, travelers searching online travel agencies would not see its fares. They had to search Southwest separately. In 2025, Southwest expanded distribution to Expedia, Priceline and the other aggregators, making its flights available where more travelers were already shopping.

The parallel has limits, but the visibility question matters: How many potential customers never consider an offering because it doesn’t appear where they are looking?

In real estate, that question carries an additional responsibility. An airline decides how to distribute its own inventory. A brokerage advises a homeowner on how to market theirs. If a brokerage recommends limiting exposure, it should explain why that serves the seller better than reaching the broader market.

Brokerage leaders have a responsibility to consider the marketplace our decisions create. Our clients, buyers and sellers alike, depend on it, and the practices we normalize shape its usefulness.

Open Real Estate’s promise deserves support. Its implementation will deserve scrutiny. Its governance, participation rules and distribution practices must deliver the openness it advocates. Every participating company, including my own, should be held to that standard. The initiative must demonstrate that it expands access in practice.

The underlying principle should already guide our decisions: a homeowner’s marketing strategy should serve the homeowner’s goals. Any benefit to the brokerage must be evaluated alongside that responsibility, and any conflict should be explained candidly.

Our advantage should come from understanding a property, interpreting the evidence, negotiating effectively and helping a client make a sound decision. Those are the capabilities clients hire us for. They should also be the basis on which we compete.

I welcome an initiative that helps protect those conditions. But its announcement should prompt industry-wide reflection. When keeping the housing market open becomes a position companies must organize to defend, we’ve let the conversation drift too far from the people we serve.

Open Real Estate should not be a novel idea. It should describe how we do business.

Jared Antin is the executive director of Brown Harris Stevens.

#5562. Michael Burry warned Jensen Huang affair could invite antitrust crackdown on Nvidia

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The investor said the affair could revive U.S. scrutiny of Nvidia's China chip trade and the Justice Department's antitrust probe

Michael Burry attends the "The Big Short" New York premiere at Ziegfeld Theater on November 23, 2015 in New York City. (Jim Spellman/WireImage)

Michael Burry warned that the scandal involving Nvidia $NVDA CEO Jensen Huang could reopen examination of how Nvidia sells its top-end chips into China, as well as the Justice Department's antitrust probe, according to Benzinga. The investor made the argument in a Substack post.

Nvidia’s board has ordered an independent review of Jensen Huang’s ties to a businesswoman suspected by intelligence agencies of spying for China, according to Benzinga. Huang is said to have had an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Nvidia customer Megaspeed. Investors sent Nvidia stock lower after the news.

Burry thinks the affair is unlikely to hurt the underlying profitability of Nvidia's operations, according to Benzinga. He wrote that he had not seen the news coming and described himself as "a bit shocked" by the rush of shareholders to exit the shares.

Burry said Nvidia's dealmaking is the real exposure. Nvidia's "mafia-like behavior investing in and making requirements of many players in the AI space has, to me, long seemed ripe for anti-trust prosecution," he wrote, according to Benzinga.

"There is a lot there if Justice and Commerce and various enforcement agencies stop ignoring and start investigating," Burry said, according to Benzinga. Until recently, he had no idea what would trigger that change, and the Huang news altered his view. "The mighty are only mighty until they have fallen. The fallen attract all manner of opportunists, both righteous and repugnant," he wrote.

The Justice Department has been examining whether Nvidia attempted to sidestep antitrust review of its licensing agreement with the AI chip startup Groq, The New York Times reported in September.

Burry said he has no interest in holding the stock over the long haul. "I believe Nvidia's competitive advantage will shrink over the next five years," he wrote, adding that the scandal makes it more likely the decline will arrive sooner. He holds puts on the VanEck Semiconductor ETF, the Nasdaq $NDAQ-100 index, Oracle $ORCL and Palantir $PLTR Technologies, among other names, according to Benzinga.

Burry has maintained a short position in Nvidia this year. In August, he said all of his short positions were profitable except his bet against Nvidia. Earlier this year, he added to that bet by buying January 2027 puts on Nvidia with a $115 strike price at $3.30 per contract.

#5561. A Halloween tale: Spooky events and a haunted house sale

Author and trainer Bernice Ross shares a spooky tale of unusual home happenings and a sale process plagued by tragedy.

When you’re in the real estate business, sooner or later there will be a house that someone says is haunted. The story below is true. Were these events just coincidence, or were they something else?

When I was working on my doctorate, my closest friend and study partner was living in a new house in Orange County. She was in the antique business. Her home was like a showcase, every last inch of it beautifully decorated. When I met her, she was in the process of getting a divorce.

Although her house was a little over a year old, it already had the makings of a strange history. While the house was being built, a little girl was sexually assaulted in it. A few months after she and her husband moved in, he became manic-depressive.

Over the next few months, he had numerous confrontations with the police. He refused to take his meds. Unbeknownst to his wife, he placed a warranty deed on the property to access part of the equity. He then took off to Hawaii, where he was reportedly living in the bush outside the Honolulu airport.

We would normally study together at her house about twice per month. The lights would flicker periodically. If we went out for dinner, it was common for pieces of the furniture to be moved away from the wall.

Since my friend had changed the locks and placed a security system on the house, there was no one who had access to move the furniture. There was also a window in the family room overlooking the canyon that would vibrate for no apparent reason. You could put your hand on the window and tell it to stop vibrating, and it did.

After spending the afternoon preparing for our upcoming qualifying exams, we decided to go out to dinner to take a break. When we returned, the lights were flickering, and a number of pieces of furniture were moved again.

As we sat back down to hit the books again, there was a loud rustling in the garage where she refinished her antiques. Her German shepherd, a very mellow dog who never barked, started barking and scratching crazily at the door to the garage.

Although this didn’t disturb my friend, I made sure the dog was between me and whatever was in the garage. As soon as she opened the door, the dog broke away from me and raced into the garage. The dog raced to the other side of the garage, sat down and acted as if nothing had happened.

After consuming a carton of chocolate ice cream to soothe our jangled nerves, we decided to watch a movie — The Ghost of Flight 401. This probably wasn’t the smartest movie choice, but that was the best of the evening’s shows back in the days of seven TV channels and no cable.

As I was getting ready to leave, we were standing by the front door adjacent to the stairway. Her stairs had beautiful wrought iron work topped with a heavy oak banister.

As we were standing there talking, the banister and the wrought iron started to vibrate. Everything else in the house was still. I turned and asked her, “Do you see what I see?” She did.

We were both mesmerized because nothing else was moving. This went on for about five minutes, and then it stopped. At that point, I was out of there, and there was no way I was going back.

My friend wanted out of the house. Needless to say, there were numerous challenges that had to be addressed before she could legally sell the property. California law allowed her to list the property, but both she and her husband had to sign the grant deed to close the transaction.

The lender who held the warranty deed was demanding payment as per the terms of the note. Normally, their option would have been to foreclose. The challenge was that the police reports documented the fact that the husband was probably not legally competent at the time he signed the deed.

Since he was nowhere to be found, my friend and the lender petitioned the court to order the sale as part of the divorce proceedings. The court granted her request.

The house was listed and finally went under contract. The buyer was a deputy sheriff. Two days after opening escrow on the property, the escrow officer had a heart attack and died. The title officer handling the file also had a heart attack but recovered.

About four weeks into the transaction, the deputy sheriff’s right arm became mysteriously paralyzed. He saw several specialists, but no one could find a cause for the problem. He was forced to take disability leave from his job. This meant he didn’t have sufficient income to qualify for the loan. The transaction was canceled. Within a few days after he canceled, the paralysis disappeared.

After almost a year, the house finally sold. The buyer was a psychiatrist.

Fortunately, this transaction took place prior to California passing its disclosure laws. I have to wonder how you would make those disclosures today. Much of what happened could be coincidence. I still don’t have an explanation for the moved furniture, the strange window and, most of all, the vibrating staircase. Perhaps it’s just as well that I don’t.

Bernice Ross is president and CEO of BrokerageUP and RealEstateCoach.com, the founder of Profit.RealEstate and a national speaker, author and trainer with over 1,500 published articles.

#5560. Winning in a buyer’s market

With inventory rising and pending sales hitting historic lows, today's buyers have leverage they haven't seen in years. Jennifer Beeston breaks down three common client hesitations—high rates, high prices and closing costs—and outlines how agents and lenders can use seller concessions and buydowns to get deals across the finish line.   AI Summary

As we head into the end of the year, we are at a truly magical moment for buyers across much of America.

Buyers have more houses to choose from, along with the ability to inspect the property, negotiate repairs and make homeownership more affordable. It is something buyers have been wanting for years, but where are all the buyers? Pending sales were recently recorded as the lowest since they started tracking pending sales!

Currently, many buyers are holding back for three main reasons. As a mortgage lender or real estate agent, knowing these reasons and how to solve them is the key to helping your buyers win right now. Would I recommend waiting for lower rates?  Absolutely not; the lower the rates, the more competition, and it is the lack of competition where true opportunity lies.

Ask the seller to pay to buy down the mortgage rate.  I like a permanent buydown as it gives certainty for the long run. Many buyers can afford the house when the rate starts at 6%, so use a seller buydown to get there.

Offer less. Many buyers do not know that you can offer less. They are waiting for the seller to drop the price when, in reality, they should just write an offer now with what they want to pay.  It is up to the seller to say yes or no.

Whether the seller agrees depends on their financial situation and their motivation to sell. I have chatted with clients who want the house, but not at the current price and are afraid to offer $10,000 less. To me, that’s a missed opportunity.  The seller could be sitting on the other side praying they get an offer.  Write the offer.

Did you know many buyers don’t realize they can ask the seller to pay for closing costs? Over 42% of recent sales have seller concessions, but many buyers still do not know you can ask for this. You could have a buyer you talked to last year who was in a seller’s market, who is saving away, who does not even know that their market is now a buyer’s market. This is your opportunity as a real estate professional to help them get home. Ask the seller to pay their closing costs and help them get home for the Holidays.

As I type this, we have buyers across the country negotiating for lower sales prices, closing costs and rate buydown covered by the seller. Does every seller say yes?  No, but that is the beauty of the buyer’s market; there are so many sellers to choose from. There is tremendous opportunity in the market right now for buyers to win. Help them seize it.

Jennifer Beeston is the EVP of National Sales at Chairman’s Circle (NMLS ID: 247743). This column does not necessarily reflect the opinion of HousingWire’s editorial department and its owners. To contact the editor responsible for this piece: [email protected].

#5558. Bitcoin slips to about $73,000 as Nvidia CEO turmoil rattles risk appetite

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Nvidia stock fell as much as 10% in late trading Wednesday, and U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs have seen roughly $2.5 billion in net outflows since Oct. 30

Bitcoin fell as much as 2.2% on Thursday as reports of a possible leadership change at Nvidia $NVDA weighed on technology stocks and risk appetite. The cryptocurrency traded between about $72,900 and $73,400 in the early morning, and Nasdaq $NDAQ-100 futures were down 0.6%.

Nvidia stock fell as much as 10% in late trading Wednesday and was down about 7% in premarket trading Thursday. Nvidia is working with an outside firm to find possible successors to CEO Jensen Huang after reports that he had two extramarital affairs, one of them with a woman believed to have been spying on behalf of China, according to Bloomberg. Nvidia has yet to make any decision public, according to CoinDesk.

Withdrawals from U.S. spot bitcoin exchange-traded funds added to the pressure. Flows into the funds turned negative on Oct. 30, and net outflows since then total roughly $2.5 billion, according to Bloomberg. The funds shed $299.9 million Wednesday, extending their run of withdrawals to a fifth consecutive day, according to CoinDesk.

Bitcoin dropped to its weakest level in three months on Tuesday, when a stronger-than-forecast U.S. inflation reading strengthened bets on additional rate increases, according to Bloomberg. The Federal Reserve holds its next meeting Dec. 8-9, and CME $CME FedWatch pricing puts the odds of a rate increase near 90%, according to CoinDesk.

"Bitcoin is showing signs of a changing market structure, with selling pressure concentrated in derivatives while spot market activity remains comparatively resilient," wrote Dean Chen, who works as an analyst for the crypto exchange Bitunix, in a Thursday note, according to Bloomberg. Chen said traders are pulling back on leverage, though investors' positioning does not point clearly in one direction.

Open interest in bitcoin futures fell 2.9% over 24 hours, and bitcoin led all coins in liquidations with $62.9 million, according to CoinDesk. Render, a token tied to a decentralized network of graphics processors, fell 3.1% as Nvidia stock slid.

Nvidia's board was set to meet Wednesday evening to weigh removing Huang over two extramarital affairs, and no clear successor exists. Huang apologized to employees Sunday for being unfaithful to his wife. The board announced an independent investigation that day and said it had confidence in him.

Nvidia is scheduled to report fiscal third-quarter earnings on Nov. 17. Three House Republican committee chairs have asked Huang to appear for a private session with lawmakers on Nov. 18.

#5557. ‘Haunted as a matter of law’: How real estate agents handle stigmatized listings in 2026

Stigmatized homes have long sold at a steep discount. Agents and attorneys say an unaffordable, low-inventory 2026 market may be shrinking it.

Many may assume that the rule of thumb on stigmatized homes is simple: A murder, suicide or infamous ghost story knocks a big chunk off the price. Real estate agents who’ve sold these homes say it’s more complicated, and today’s unaffordable, short-on-inventory market may be shrinking the discount.

A “stigmatized” property can mean many things. It can be a home tied to a violent crime, a suicide, a notorious former owner or an alleged haunting.

Would you live in the Amityville Horror house, where Ronald DeFeo Jr. killed six members of his family in 1974?

Or what about the Menendez mansion in Beverly Hills, where Lyle and Erik Menendez killed their parents, José and Kitty, in 1989, a case that has stayed in the headlines for more than three decades?

These gruesome crimes may not always change the bedroom count or the square footage. But they can change who’s willing to buy, and for how much.

Ahead of Halloween, Inman asked real estate agents and attorneys how they handle stigmatized listings in 2026.

Their answers suggest the discount is real but uneven. It often depends less on the stigma itself than on how many buyers it drives away. And in a market with increasingly few affordable options, fewer buyers may be walking away.

The best-known estimate for stigmatized listings comes from real estate economist Randall Bell, who has put the typical “murder-house” discount at 10 to 25 percent. Bell has also said he’s seen some stigmatized homes sell at full value — usually smaller, more affordable homes — while others sit unsold for a long time.

Bell is an expert on real estate damage, earning the nickname “Master of Disaster,” and he runs the advisory firm Landmark Research. He has consulted on some of the most notorious crime-linked properties in history, from the Rancho Santa Fe mansions where the bodies of 39 Heaven’s Gate cult members were found to the home of Sandy Hook shooter Adam Lanza.

While Bell’s estimates are frequently cited, academic research suggests the price discount effect on stigmatized properties may fade over time.

A 2020 study of Tokyo apartment buildings by economist Taisuke Sadayuki found that a homicide in one unit initially cut rents on other units in the same building by about 10 percent, with the effect disappearing after roughly seven to eight years.

Survey data suggests buyers may also be less squeamish than agents assume. In a 2023 Zillow survey, 67 percent of prospective buyers said they could be persuaded to buy a “haunted” house with the right features, location or price.

When Inman covered stigmatized homes more than a decade ago, we framed them as bargains. The market has changed a lot since then.

Rebecca Chambliss, an agent with Carmody Real Estate in the Santa Monica, California, area, recently sold a home in a gated community where the previous owner had died by suicide only a few months before it was listed. All of the neighbors knew.

Chambliss disclosed the death to serious buyers who were discussing an offer. In her experience, buyers don’t spread out along a spectrum of tolerance. They split into two groups.

“Some people will never buy a home where a suicide or other non-natural death occurred no matter what, and then there are people who it doesn’t bother,” Chambliss told Inman. “There aren’t people in between.”

One interested buyer made an unexpected offer. When Chambliss disclosed the death, he demanded to know exactly where in the house it happened and how. Chambliss had chosen not to learn those details herself and told him as much. He wouldn’t move forward without them and withdrew the offer.

The home did eventually sell at a discount because of the suicide, Chambliss said. The buyer understood that he’d have to disclose the death if he ever sold. He relisted it about a year later, asking $1 million more than he paid, and the home still hasn’t sold.

Chambliss also brought in an energy clearer before marketing the home. It’s a reminder that for some agents, handling a stigmatized listing takes more than paperwork.

The discount doesn’t always stay with the property. Sometimes a savvy investor who knows about it collects it.

Jonathan Carcone, principal of 4 Brothers Buy Houses and a licensed agent in Washington state, bought a home in Poulsbo, Washington, with local ghost stories attached.

He said the home was listed at $640,000, while comparable homes were selling for about $650,000. Carcone said the listing didn’t mention ghost stories, but neighbors told him about them.

Carcone used the ghost stories in negotiations and bought the house for $585,000, about 9 percent below list and roughly 10 percent below comps.

Carcone’s company buys, renovates and sells dozens of houses every year, including “challenging properties.” After renovating the house in Poulsbo, he sold it for $660,000 about two months later.

“The ghost stories had no influence on the sale, and we made a good profit,” Carcone told Inman.

He said Washington law doesn’t require agents to disclose a home’s reputation, including ghost stories, so he didn’t. No buyer asked about it during showings, either. So, in this case, Carcone used the stigma to his advantage.

Because the resale price reflects a renovation, it isn’t a clean before-and-after comparison. Still, the pattern is worth noting. The seller absorbed a 10 percent discount for the stigma, and the next buyer paid none.

What agents must disclose for stigmatized properties varies widely by state.

California sets a three-year line. Under California Civil Code Section 1710.2, sellers and agents aren’t required to disclose a death that occurred on the property more than three years before a buyer’s offer. They also can’t be sued for staying silent. Whether it must be disclosed depends on whether it’s material, and the common practice is to disclose to be safe.

Answering a direct question is a separate matter. The law doesn’t protect anyone who lies when asked.

“The main point of contention between sellers and buyers is whether answering questions truthfully violates the seller’s wishes,” Nick Heimlich, founder and attorney of San Jose, California-based Nick Heimlich Law, told Inman. “Under California Civil Code, a seller’s agent cannot refuse to answer questions about the property’s history.”

Texas Property Code Section 5.008(c) says a seller or seller’s agent has no duty to disclose a death on the property from natural causes, suicide or an accident unrelated to the property’s condition. But not homicide, which may still be a material fact that must be disclosed.

Tennessee goes further. Tenn. Code Ann. § 66-5-207 lists a homicide, felony or suicide on the property among the things sellers don’t have to disclose. It also covers any act or occurrence that didn’t affect the property’s physical structure.

Ghost stories bring their own risk. In the famous case of Stambovsky v. Ackley (1991), a New York appellate court let a buyer back out of buying an allegedly haunted home in Nyack, New York.

The seller had publicized the ghost stories herself in Reader’s Digest and the local press, then didn’t tell the out-of-town buyer. In effect, the court held that because she’d told everyone else the house was haunted, it was haunted as a matter of law.

Donald Leeth, managing partner at Leeth & Gaglione, has spent 27 years as a criminal defense attorney and former prosecutor in Monroe County, Pennsylvania, and the Poconos. During that time, he’s encountered many homes where crimes took place. He advises disclosing rather than gambling on the legal minimum.

“It’s always best to be honest up front so you’re not dealing with misrepresentation claims once your transaction has closed,” Leeth said.

The more interesting question for 2026 is whether affordability is eroding the discount stigmatized listings usually have.

Median prices for new and existing homes now both top $400,000, according to Harvard University’s Joint Center for Housing Studies. Existing-home prices have climbed 54 percent nationwide since 2020 and sit at nearly five times median income, well above the 3-to-1 ratio that held in the 1990s.

Leeth thinks the affordability crisis is negating the discount effect on stigmatized listings.

“Many buyers won’t care if there’s an infamous story behind a house because they simply don’t have other options,” he said. “Stigma isn’t as much of a factor as it once was because the price will determine what someone buys.”

That fits with Chambliss’s two-camp theory. If the buyers who’ll never consider a stigmatized home stay out no matter what, the discount depends on how many buyers are left in the other camp. In a tight, low-inventory market, more buyers are in that camp, and they may have fewer alternatives.

Heimlich said the type of event still matters. Buyers might shrug at a home that sat empty for a long time, he said, but something like a murder “can severely influence the property value.”

Still, he added, it likely depends on the market. And if stigma leads to a bargain, that helps, too.

“Some buyers may be willing to invest in stigmatized real estate if it falls within an affordable price range,” Heimlich said.

For agents, the practical takeaway is that a stigmatized listing’s real challenge is finding the buyers who don’t care, not pricing in a fixed discount, and disclosing in a way that doesn’t create legal exposure after closing.

Sometimes the stigma bothers the buyer’s friends and family more than the buyer themselves.

Years ago, Chambliss, the California-based agent, sold a home where a murder had taken place in the front yard. The buyer was a young single father whose Italian immigrant parents were involved in the buying process and may have been helping with the purchase. Chambliss took him outside and told him what had happened there.

He became very concerned, then immediately asked, “Do you have to tell my parents?”

His whole body relaxed, and he laughed. Then he said, “OK, I have no issue with it. But my parents would never let me buy this house if they knew.”

He bought the house, and Chambliss assumed he never told them.

#5556. Homebuilders and their partners team up to salute our veterans

Builders recognized Veterans Day through nonprofit partnerships, including mortgage-free home giveaways and support for transitioning service members. Regional builders also promoted limited-time military savings, typically $1,000 to $3,000, and some offered up to $2,500 toward closing costs in select communities.  AI Summary

Each Veterans Day, millions of Americans take a moment to honor the sacrifices that our military veterans have made for generations.

On a personal note, today I’m remembering both of my late grandfathers. One served in the Navy, while the other received a Purple Heart and numerous other medals for his bravery and service during the Vietnam War.

Across the country, homebuilders are marking Veterans Day with a range of initiatives, including special promotions and discounts for military families, mortgage-free home donations and workforce development programs designed to support veterans transitioning into civilian careers.

The following are some of the ways homebuilders are recognizing and supporting veterans this year.

PulteGroup, in partnership with Operation Homefront, announced that it gifted multiple newly constructed homes to military service members in cities like Anna, Texas, Wixom, Michigan and Richmond Hills, Georgia.

Meritage Homes, also in partnership with national military nonprofit Operation Homefront, will donate a brand-new, mortgage-free home to a military family in Gulfport, Mississippi.

The lucky recipient of Meritage Homes’ giveaway was Navy Personnel Specialist 2nd Class Maggie Coleman, who served 13 years in the Navy. Coleman will receive a 2,000-square-foot home with four bedrooms and three bathrooms.

“I want to give my children everything I didn’t have. I want this home to be a place where my kids and I can share stories and make memories,” Coleman said in a press release.

Lennar partnered with national nonprofit Operation Finally Home and country music artist and U.S. Army Reserve soldier Craig Morgan to surprise two military families with brand-new, mortgage-free homes in celebration of Veterans Day. The surprises unfolded Monday evening in Austin, Texas, during a reception in which the veterans believed they were simply attending as honored guests of the foundation.

And earlier this week, Invitation Homes announced that it has teamed up with Home Builders Institute to fund hands-on training, industry credentials and job placement for transitioning service members and veterans.

Many smaller, regional homebuilders, which don’t have the resources to give away homes for free, are honoring Veterans Day by offering temporary promotions for Veterans and military service members.

Taylor Homes, which builds in Kentucky, Indiana and Ohio, announced that it doubled its “We Salute You” bonus to $2,000 throughout November, giving military members a price reduction on a new home.

Tennessee-based Pratt Home Builders, meanwhile, is offering veterans, active-duty military and reservists $3,000 in savings toward a new home during November and December. Buyers can apply the savings toward the purchase price, design upgrades or appliances.

Other builders are offering similar incentives in select markets, either temporarily or on an ongoing basis. D.R. Horton, for example, is offering up to $2,500 toward closing costs through its Home of the Brave program in select San Antonio-area communities.

Landmark Homes offers active-duty military members and veterans a $1,000 incentive that can be combined with other promotions in Northern Colorado.

In Idaho, Hubble Homes offers a $2,500 Homes for Heroes discount, as does Drees Homes in markets like Jacksonville and San Antonio.

David Weekley Homes, meanwhile, provides military personnel with $1,000 in Flex Dollars in the Charleston, South Carolina market.

Many of these programs extend beyond veterans and military personnel to include teachers, police officers, firefighters and other first responders, grouping them under broader Hometown Heroes or similar initiatives.

The National Association of Home Builders (NAHB) reported that remodeling activity was flat in the second quarter amid a broader nationwide housing slowdown, in its latest State Projections of Remodeling (SPR).

The SPR showed a near-even split in the second quarter: Remodeling spending declined in 26 states and increased in 24 states, according to a release. The average growth rate across all states broke even at 0.0%.

“These flat results are consistent with NAHB’s forecast for remodeling spending in 2026,” NAHB Chief Economist Robert Dietz said. “Second-quarter spending growth was concentrated in smaller states. Among the 10 states with the largest market shares, only North Carolina and Illinois recorded growth.”

“Rising construction costs and weak consumer sentiment are weighing on projects and keeping spending flat, but the remodeling sector has solid long-term growth potential,” Elliott Pike—NAHB Remodelers chairman—stated. “An aging housing stock, the mortgage rate lock-in effect, home equity gains and more home owners choosing to age in place will support future growth.”

Remodeler confidence has also held steady. The release noted that NAHB’s Remodeling Market Index (RMI)—which measures confidence in the sector—has remained above 60 for the past year.

#5554. Nebuly wants to help enterprises understand exactly what their AI investments are worth after raising $21M

An Italian startup called Nebuly S.r.l. says it’s going to help organizations better understand the impact their investments in artificial intelligence have on their bottom lines after raising $21 million in funding today.

The round was led by Planven and saw participation from backers including Exor Ventures, Tenacity Capital, TGVG Capital, Fastweb, Vodafone and CDP Venture Capital’s Digital Transition Fund.

The world’s biggest companies have been spending millions of dollars on artificial intelligence, but very few can actually say how much value those investments have returned. Though some leaders might be able to point to a few vanity metrics, they’ll likely stumble if pressed to come up with concrete numbers.

This is a problem because enterprise leaders are increasingly feeling the pressure to justify their investments in AI. A recent Gartner Inc. survey of business leaders found that 85% of respondents plan to step up their AI spending in the next year, but at the same time, only 22% say they have managed to scale the technology across multiple business units.

Meanwhile, spending is spiraling out of control at many companies. Famously, Uber Technologies Inc. revealed earlier this year that it had eaten up the entire budget it set aside for AI in 2026 in just four months.

Nebuly co-founder and Chief Executive Franceso Signorato told SiliconANGLE that one of the main challenges when it comes to understanding AI’s return on investment is that many companies have deployed a jumbled patchwork of AI models and applications. They’re using tools from OpenAI Group PBC, Anthropic PBC, Microsoft Corp., Google LLC and others, as well as developing in-house tools under their own steam.

That makes it harder to see which projects are actually paying off and generating real business revenue. Although companies can track superficial metrics like token consumption and prompt tallies, genuine productivity gains remain obscured.

“Every enterprise is about to face the same question from its board, if it hasn’t already: What is AI actually worth to us? Nebuly exists to answer that question,” Signorato said. “Until now companies have measured AI by counting users, prompts and responses, which has fueled the rise of tokenmaxxing, where usage itself becomes the goal.”

Though it can be useful to keep track of who is using AI the most, Signarato said it doesn’t reveal if the technology is actually providing a net benefit to the company. “It doesn’t tell you whether an employee got back an hour of work or if a customer got the answer they needed,” he explained.

The lack of real insights can be risky, because AI is already starting to influence how business strategies and how companies spend money in other areas. “Companies are making decisions about hiring and head counts based on assumptions about AI productivity, not evidence,” Signorato said. “Decisions of that weight need real data.”

So it’s just as well that Nebuly claims to have the solution for these organizations. It has created an AI measurement platform that connects directly to the AI agents operating within its customer’s information technology environments, so it can study their behavior through a unified control plane.

Nebuly seeks to evaluate agentic productivity across two dimensions. In the case of internal, employee-facing agents, it tracks operational efficiency metrics, such as the number of hours of work they save human employees and the amount of capacity they free up.

It also takes into account net-new work that human teams couldn’t previously do. In addition, it identifies the kinds of work staff are applying AI to – such as routine, mundane tasks or higher-level strategic work, in order to help companies understand where their agents are most useful.

The platform also tracks external, customer-facing agents. With them, it monitors how they influence revenue, their impact on customer churn and their ability to generate upsell opportunities.

Auditability is a key concern, and so Nebuly ensures flexibility in terms of the financial assumptions it makes. This means financial teams can dig in and inspect the math it has come up with, to verify the performance insights it generates. The platform can be deployed on-premises or in private cloud environments in order to keep sensitive business data secure.

Nebuly’s insights are especially appealing to larger organizations. Almost all of its customers pull in annual revenue of more than $100 million, with about half exceeding $1 billion per year. They include Carl Zeiss AG, Iveco Group N.V. and Oura Health Oy. Most of those customers are based in Europe, but the funds from today’s round should help to change that, with Signorato planning to increase go-to-market hiring in the U.S.

Planven’s Giovanni Canetta Roeder said he’s backing Nebuly because he’s convinced that every large organization is going to need a way to measure AI’s return on investment. “Nebuly is building the way to do it,” he said. “The team turns what AI agents actually do into evidence of business value. That capability and the traction Nebuly has built among major enterprises made this a compelling investment for us.”

#5553. Commission settlement accounts hold $711M as claim payouts await (EXCLUSIVE)

New disclosures show that the settlement fund accounts received about $17.7 million in interest during the first nine months of 2026.

That’s how much money was held in accounts associated with the sweeping real estate commission antitrust settlements as of Sept. 30, according to newly filed federal court documents offering a fresh look at the money from the nationwide agreements.

The disclosures, filed Thursday in federal court in Missouri, show that the accounts received about $17.7 million in interest during the first nine months of 2026, while roughly $5.8 million was transferred out during the same period.

The filings also come amid an ongoing court-ordered audit of settlement administrator JND Legal Administration, which reported earlier this year that it had received and processed more than 2.7 million claim submissions.

The financial accounting follows a series of appellate rulings upholding the commission settlements, although questions remain about when eligible homesellers will receive payments.

According to a declaration signed Oct. 13 by Isaac Lim, a senior vice president and senior risk officer at Morgan Stanley Smith Barney, and filed by plaintiffs Oct. 29, the settlement accounts had a combined balance of $711,251,720.86 as of Sept. 30.

The funds were transferred from Huntington Bank to Morgan Stanley on Oct. 23, 2025, at class counsel’s direction.

Lim reported that $17,705,101.82 in interest was paid into the accounts between January and September 2026, while $5,780,467.43 was transferred out during the same period. The declaration does not identify the purpose of those transfers or establish whether any money has been distributed directly to eligible homesellers.

According to the filing, the money is invested in a BlackRock institutional money market fund yielding about 3.63 percent annually, Morgan Stanley’s preferred savings program paying 4 percent or a combination of both. The yields are estimates and subject to change.

The reported balance represents funds held in the identified Morgan Stanley accounts, rather than necessarily the full amount collected through the broader commission settlements. The declaration does not provide a complete accounting of earlier distributions, expenses or outstanding settlement contributions.

In a June declaration, Jennifer Keough, CEO of JND Legal Administration, said the company had received and processed more than 2.7 million claim submissions. In June 2025, more than 2.5 million claims had already been submitted, while JND had invoiced approximately $32.8 million for its administrative work.

Keough said JND’s original assignment expanded into six separate notification campaigns involving more than 138 million emails and 44 million postcards. Four of those direct-mail campaigns cost about $18.7 million in postage alone, which JND characterized as a pass-through expense.

In May, Missouri-based U.S. District Judge Stephen Bough ordered JND to stop receiving payments while the court considered appointing a special master to audit the company’s past and future bills.

On July 27, the judge appointed Chris Hellums and Randall Sansom as special masters.

Hellums was tasked with overseeing the audit and helping establish future administration arrangements, while Sansom, a certified public accountant, was directed to audit JND’s billing and expenses dating back to the beginning of its work.

The order requires JND to provide detailed financial records, including employee timesheets, vendor invoices, billing records and information about rebates, credits or other financial incentives.

JND opposed the need for an independent audit, arguing in a June filing that the process would be expensive and burdensome and that its work had been performed appropriately. The company said it would cooperate if the audit proceeded, but requested confidentiality protections for commercially sensitive pricing information.

JND also said its responsibilities had expanded substantially at class counsel’s direction and that it had advanced nearly $3 million in out-of-pocket costs on behalf of the class.

The dispute escalated in August when JND sought to disqualify Hellums, alleging he had demonstrated bias against the company through his involvement in a separate antitrust settlement proceeding.

Bough denied the motion Aug. 26, finding that JND, as a nonparty, could not seek disqualification under the applicable rules. He added that even if JND could bring the challenge, it had failed to establish sufficient grounds to question Hellums’ impartiality.

The ruling also examined a question Hellums had raised in the Blue Cross Blue Shield case about potential vendor rebates and credits, which Bough said JND never answered in its email exchange with him and only partly addressed at the Aug. 20 hearing. Keough acknowledged at the hearing that separate vendor agreements govern how rebates and credits are calculated.

JND has maintained in sworn declarations that it has received no rebates, credits or other financial benefits from banks or vendors in connection with the commission settlements.

In its latest accounting, JND reported $155,932 in additional administrative invoices covering July through September, bringing the outstanding balance shown on its October invoice to $494,249.

Keough said JND continues submitting invoices and performing administrative work despite not currently receiving payments.

JND did not respond to Inman’s request for comment by the time of publication.

Despite a series of appellate rulings upholding the real estate commission settlements, it remains unclear when eligible homesellers can expect to receive payments.

On Aug. 19, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit unanimously upheld the landmark Sitzer | Burnett settlement, rejecting seven appeals challenging its scope, fairness and accompanying industry practice changes.

The court subsequently affirmed another $110.6 million in brokerage settlements in the related Gibson litigation on Sept. 1, bringing the total collected for the class to about $1.02 billion, according to the appellate opinion.

After rejecting three additional objector appeals on Sept. 15 and denying rehearing petitions from objectors Robert Friedman and Monty March on Sept. 24, the 8th Circuit issued its mandate in the main Sitzer | Burnett appeals Oct. 2, concluding those proceedings before the appeals court. Objectors may still seek review from the U.S. Supreme Court.

The 8th Circuit issued its mandate in the Gibson appeals Oct. 14.

Despite those developments, the latest financial disclosures do not establish when eligible homesellers will receive distributions or precisely how much of the $711 million held in Morgan Stanley accounts is available for payment.

Eric Dirks, an attorney with the Kansas City-based Williams Dirks Dameron, one of the plaintiffs’ co-lead counsel firms, did not respond to Inman’s request for comment regarding the account balance, interest earnings and anticipated distribution timeline.
